entries.name: Mohenjo-daro
entries.desc: Mohenjo-daro is an archaeological site beside the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan, the remains of one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, built about 2500 BCE and abandoned by about 1700 BCE. Its buildings, mostly of fired brick, stood on a grid plan, with covered drains along the streets and more than 700 wells, for a population tentatively estimated at about 40,000. Public buildings include the Great Bath, a pool 12 metres long waterproofed with bitumen. First excavated in the 1920s, it became South Asia's first World Heritage Site in 1980.

entries.name: Harappa
entries.desc: Harappa is an archaeological site in Punjab, Pakistan, near a former course of the Ravi River, the remains of a major city of the Indus Valley Civilisation. Settled from about 3300 BCE, it was at its largest in the Mature Harappan phase, about 2600–1900 BCE, covering some 150 hectares. The first site of the civilisation excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India, it gave the civilisation its other name, Harappan. In 1857 railway builders took bricks from its ruins as ballast for the Lahore–Multan line.

entries.name: Dholavira
entries.desc: Dholavira is an archaeological site on Khadir Bet, an island in the Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, India, the remains of a city of the Indus Valley Civilisation. It was probably occupied from about 2650 to 1450 BCE, though recent research puts its start near 3500 BCE. Its buildings were largely of stone rather than brick, and it had sixteen or more reservoirs, some cut into the living rock. Ten large Indus signs of gypsum, once set in a wooden board about 3 metres long, lay in a side room of its northern gateway.

entries.name: Lothal
entries.desc: Lothal is an archaeological site in Gujarat, India, one of the southernmost towns of the Indus Valley Civilisation, believed to have been built from about 2300 BCE and ruined by a great flood about 1900 BCE. Excavated from 1955 to 1960, it has a basin of baked brick about 215 metres long that the Archaeological Survey of India and S. R. Rao identified as a dock, while others have argued that it was chiefly an irrigation tank. Its bead-makers supplied a wide trade, and a round seal from Bahrain was found there.

entries.name: Rakhigarhi
entries.desc: Rakhigarhi is a village and archaeological site in the Ghaggar plain of Haryana, India, the remains of one of the five largest settlements of the Indus Valley Civilisation. Its remains span the pre-Harappan, Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases, the last about 2600–1900 BCE. Most scholars put its main mounds at 80 to over 100 hectares; the Archaeological Survey of India's figure of 300–350 hectares includes outlying mounds. Excavations since the 1960s have found paved streets, drains and a cemetery, and DNA from one skeleton, published in 2019, showed no trace of steppe ancestry.

entries.name: Priest-King
entries.desc: The Priest-King is a small steatite sculpture of a bearded man, found at Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, Pakistan, in the 1920s and dated to about 2000–1900 BCE, in the city's Late Period. Broken off at the bottom and perhaps unfinished, it is 17.5 centimetres high, with a fillet round the head, an armband and a one-shouldered cloak patterned with trefoils that once held a red filling. Its name is a modern guess at the man's role. It is kept in the National Museum of Pakistan in Karachi.

entries.name: Indus script
entries.desc: The Indus script, also called the Harappan script, is the set of signs used by the Indus Valley Civilisation, found chiefly on stamp seals, seal impressions and pottery. Early examples date from about 2800–2600 BCE, and by 1992 some 4,000 inscribed objects bearing over 400 distinct signs were known, generally read from right to left. Because the inscriptions are very short, averaging about five signs, and no bilingual text has been found, it remains undeciphered, and scholars disagree whether it records a language at all.

entries.name: Knossos
entries.desc: Knossos is an archaeological site on Kephala hill near Heraklion in Crete, Greece, occupied from about 7000 BCE into the early Byzantine period and the largest centre of the Minoan civilisation. Its first palace, built about 1900 BCE, was rebuilt after a destruction about 1700 BCE, and after about 1450 BCE Knossos became a Mycenaean administrative centre that kept records in Linear B. The palace's complex plan probably contributed to the later Greek tradition of the Labyrinth. Arthur Evans excavated most of it from 1900 and partly reconstructed it in reinforced concrete.

entries.name: Phaistos
entries.desc: Phaistos is a Bronze Age archaeological site in south-central Crete, Greece, with the remains of a Minoan palace and the town around it, one of the largest cities of Minoan Crete. First settled about 3600 BCE, it had a palace from about 2000 BCE, which was destroyed and rebuilt three times before its final destruction in the 15th century BCE. Federico Halbherr and Luigi Pernier excavated it from 1900, and in 1908 the Phaistos Disc was found in a basement room of the palace.

entries.name: Palace of Malia
entries.desc: The Palace of Malia is a Minoan palace and settlement site 3 kilometres east of the town of Malia in Crete, Greece. Dating from the Middle Bronze Age, the palace was destroyed by an earthquake and rebuilt, and most of the visible ruins belong to the rebuilding. With about 7,500 square metres of floor around a central court of 48 by 23 metres, it is smaller and less elaborate than the palaces of Knossos and Phaistos. Joseph Hadzidakis uncovered it in 1915, and the French School at Athens excavated it from 1922.

entries.name: Minoan eruption
entries.desc: The Minoan eruption was a catastrophic eruption of the Thera volcano on the Aegean island of Santorini about 1600 BCE, one of the largest volcanic events in human history, which buried the settlement of Akrotiri in pumice and ash. It occurred late in the Late Minoan IA phase, but its date is debated: radiocarbon dating has favoured the late 17th century BCE and archaeological links with Egypt about 1550–1480 BCE. Earthquakes and tsunamis struck Crete, where Minoan society recovered quickly, though the eruption's longer-term effects are disputed.

entries.name: Bull-leaping
entries.desc: Bull-leaping is an acrobatic feat in which a performer vaults over a charging bull, shown above all in the art of Minoan Crete, where it is thought to have been a key ritual of the elite and perhaps of religion. Leapers, possibly both men and women, are shown grasping the horns or somersaulting over the bull's back, though whether the images record a real performance is debated. Similar scenes occur in Hittite Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt, and the feat survives as a sport in France and Spain.

entries.name: Mycenae
entries.desc: Mycenae is an archaeological site near Mykines in the Argolis, north-eastern Peloponnese, Greece, the seat of the legendary King Agamemnon, which gave its name to the Mycenaean period of Greek history, about 1600–1100 BCE. Its shaft graves of the 17th and 16th centuries BCE held rich grave goods, and about 1350 BCE its walls were rebuilt in Cyclopean masonry, with the Lion Gate added about 1250 BCE. Destroyed around 1200 BCE and only partly rebuilt, it was captured by Argos in 468 BCE. Heinrich Schliemann began excavating there in 1876.

entries.name: Tiryns
entries.desc: Tiryns is a Mycenaean archaeological site in the Argolis, in the Peloponnese of Greece, a hill fort that was at its most important between about 1400 and 1200 BCE. Its walls, usually 6 metres thick and once 9–10 metres high, with tunnels running through them, gave it the Homeric epithet "mighty walled" and enclose a palace with a megaron. Greek myth made it the home of Heracles during his labours. The palace was destroyed about 1200 BCE, and Argos destroyed Tiryns in 468 BCE.

entries.name: Grave Circle A
entries.desc: Grave Circle A is a royal cemetery just south of the Lion Gate of Mycenae in southern Greece, a circle 27.5 metres across with six shaft graves used from about 1600 to 1500 BCE. Its nineteen burials of men, women and children held weapons, jewellery, gold and silver cups and gold death masks, among them the Mask of Agamemnon, with an estimated 15 kilograms of gold in all. First outside the walls, it was enclosed in the citadel when the fortifications were extended about 1250 BCE. Heinrich Schliemann and Panagiotis Stamatakis excavated it in 1876–1877.

entries.name: Mask of Agamemnon
entries.desc: The Mask of Agamemnon is a gold funerary mask found by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 in Grave V of Grave Circle A at Mycenae, now in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Hammered from a single thick sheet of gold, it shows a face with a pointed beard and moustache. Schliemann named it after the king of Homer's Iliad, but it dates to around the 16th century BCE, centuries before the mythical Trojan War. Its authenticity has been questioned by William Calder III and David Traill, but modern research suggests it is genuine.

entries.name: Palace of Nestor
entries.desc: The Palace of Nestor is a Mycenaean palace site on the hill of Epano Englianos in Messenia, Greece, about 17 kilometres north of Pylos, traditionally identified with the palace of Homer's King Nestor at "sandy Pylos". A two-storey building with storerooms, workshops, baths and drains, destroyed by fire, it is the best-preserved Mycenaean palace yet discovered. Excavations by the University of Cincinnati and the Greek Archaeological Service, begun in 1939, found more than a thousand Linear B tablets, part of a royal archive showing that it was the administrative centre of Mycenaean Messenia.

entries.name: La Venta
entries.desc: La Venta is an archaeological site of the Olmec civilisation in Tabasco, Mexico, on an island in a coastal swamp, which was the pre-eminent Olmec centre from after 900 BCE until it was all but abandoned around 400 BCE. Built largely of earth and clay, it has a Great Pyramid 34 metres high, one of the earliest in Mesoamerica, four colossal heads and buried offerings of serpentine blocks. Described by Frans Blom and Oliver La Farge in 1925, it was excavated from 1940 by Matthew Stirling and Philip Drucker.

entries.name: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán
entries.desc: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán is the collective name for three related Olmec archaeological sites in south-eastern Veracruz, Mexico: San Lorenzo, Tenochtitlán and Potrero Nuevo. San Lorenzo, on a plateau 50 metres above the Coatzacoalcos floodplain, was the major Olmec centre from about 1400 to 900 BCE and, from about 1200 BCE, the largest city in Mesoamerica. Its people reshaped the plateau with vast earth fills and stone drains, and ten colossal heads have been found there. Matthew Stirling, the first to excavate there, found colossal heads in 1945 and 1946.

entries.name: Tres Zapotes
entries.desc: Tres Zapotes is an archaeological site at the western edge of the Los Tuxtlas mountains in Veracruz, Mexico, sometimes called the third Olmec capital, though it remained a regional centre for some 2,000 years, from perhaps 900 BCE until about 900 CE. The first colossal head to be discovered was found nearby in 1862. In the Epi-Olmec period the Isthmian script appeared there, and its Stela C, whose lower half Matthew Stirling found in 1939, bears a Long Count date corresponding to 32 BCE, among the earliest known.

entries.name: Olmec colossal heads
entries.desc: The Olmec colossal heads are seventeen heads carved from basalt boulders by the Olmec civilisation of Mexico's Gulf Coast: ten from San Lorenzo, four from La Venta, two from Tres Zapotes and one from La Cobata. Up to 3.4 metres high, each wears a distinctive headdress, and they are thought to be portraits of individual rulers; they cannot be dated precisely, but the San Lorenzo heads were buried by about 900 BCE. The stone was brought from the Sierra de los Tuxtlas by means still unknown. The first head was found at Tres Zapotes in 1862, and all remain in Mexico.

entries.name: Nok terracottas
entries.desc: The Nok terracottas are fired-clay sculptures of the Nok culture of central Nigeria, named after the village of Nok in southern Kaduna State, where the first was found in tin workings in 1928. Hollow and nearly life-size, they show human heads and figures with stylised features, detailed hairstyles and abundant jewellery; the earliest may date from about 900 BCE. Excluding ancient Egyptian art, they are regarded as the earliest large figurative sculpture in Africa. Their function is unknown, and over 1,000 have been illegally dug up and smuggled abroad.

entries.name: Taruga
entries.desc: Taruga is an archaeological site of the Nok culture in central Nigeria, about 60 kilometres south-east of Abuja, known for terracotta figurines and early iron working. A trial excavation of eight days in January 1961 found the bases and walls of smelting furnaces still in place, with iron slag, fragments of tuyères, pottery and figurine fragments. Bernard Fagg's excavations there in the 1960s gave radiocarbon dates of about the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, among the earliest for iron working in West Africa.

entries.name: Lapita pottery
entries.desc: Lapita pottery is the dentate-stamped earthenware that defines the Lapita culture of the western Pacific, which appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago about 1500 BCE. Low-fired and tempered with shell or sand, it bears fine geometric patterns pressed into the clay with toothed stamps and closely resembles pottery from Nagsabaran in northern Luzon. First found on Watom Island in 1909 and named after a site in New Caledonia excavated in 1952, it is known from more than 200 sites between the Bismarck Archipelago and Samoa.

entries.name: Teouma
entries.desc: Teouma is an archaeological site on the island of Efate in Vanuatu with the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands, a Lapita burial ground thought to be about 3,200 to 3,000 years old. Found in late 2003, its 26 burials held 36 individuals, with decorated red pottery; their skulls had been removed once the bodies decomposed and replaced with rings of cone shell. Isotopes mark four of the seventeen people tested as probable immigrants, and DNA extracted in 2016 from three women is closest to that of peoples of Taiwan and the northern Philippines.

entries.name: Mesa Verde
entries.desc: Mesa Verde is a plateau cut by canyons in south-western Colorado, where Ancestral Puebloans farmed until about 1285 and a national park now protects more than 4,000 archaeological sites, some 600 of them cliff dwellings. The first pueblos there were built after 650, and from the end of the 12th century villages of stone were raised in alcoves of the canyon walls, the largest being Cliff Palace. After prolonged droughts the last inhabitants moved south into Arizona and New Mexico. The park was created in 1906 and became a World Heritage Site in 1978.

entries.name: Cliff Palace
entries.desc: Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling in North America, an Ancestral Puebloan village in an alcove of Mesa Verde, Colorado, built and lived in from about 1200 to 1300. Made of sandstone, mortar and wooden beams, it has some 150 rooms and 23 kivas and is thought to have housed 100 to 120 people. Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason came upon it in December 1888 while looking for stray cattle. Damage and looting by visitors over the next decade spurred the campaign for the national park, created in 1906.

entries.name: Chaco Canyon
entries.desc: Chaco Canyon is a canyon cut by the Chaco Wash in north-western New Mexico, which between 900 and 1150 was a major centre of the Ancestral Puebloans. Its builders raised 15 major complexes of quarried sandstone and hauled timber, which remained the largest buildings in North America until the 19th century, and largely straight roads linked it with outlying communities. The Chacoan system began to unravel around 1140, perhaps triggered by a 50-year drought that began in 1130. A national monument from 1907, it has been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

entries.name: Pueblo Bonito
entries.desc: Pueblo Bonito is the largest great house of Chaco Canyon in northern New Mexico, built in stages by the Ancestral Puebloans and occupied between 828 and 1126. It had some 800 rooms, rising four and five storeys in places, two great kivas and more than thirty other kivas. Room 33 held the richest burial excavated in the South-West, and most of those laid there over some 330 years were related through the female line. In 2009 traces of cacao from Mexico were found in its pottery.

entries.name: Kiva
entries.desc: A kiva is a room used by the Pueblo peoples of the American South-West for rites and political meetings; among the Hopi and most other Pueblos it is a round, underground chamber. Kivas evolved from pit-houses: at Mesa Verde, square protokivas of the late 8th century had become smaller round kivas by the early 11th century. These included a sipapu, a hole thought to represent the Ancestral Puebloans' place of emergence from the underworld. Great kivas, larger and set apart from the room blocks, are believed to be the region's first public buildings.

entries.name: Moundville Archaeological Site
entries.desc: Moundville is an archaeological site on the Black Warrior River in Alabama, the remains of a Mississippian town occupied from about 1000 to 1450. From around 1150 it grew into the centre of a regional chiefdom; its rectangular plaza, ringed by 29 surviving platform mounds, and a bastioned palisade date from the early 13th century. Perhaps 1,000 to 3,000 people lived within the walls and 10,000 in the valley. From about 1300 it served more as a religious and political centre than a town, and by the mid-16th century it was abandoned.

entries.name: Etowah Indian Mounds
entries.desc: The Etowah Indian Mounds, south of Cartersville, Georgia, are the remains of a Mississippian town on the Etowah River, occupied in three phases between about 1000 and 1550. Three main platform mounds, the largest 19 metres high, stand beside a plaza, and the town was at its peak about 1325–1375. Elite burials held copper tools, weapons and ornamental plates, and finds from Mound C helped define the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex. Paired stone statues of a seated man and a kneeling woman, found in the area, are thought to represent lineage ancestors.

entries.name: Spiro Mounds
entries.desc: Spiro Mounds is an archaeological site on the Arkansas River in eastern Oklahoma, a centre of the Caddoan Mississippian culture from about 800 to 1450. Craig Mound, one of its twelve earthen mounds, held a hollow burial chamber, the Great Mortuary, that preserved textiles, feathers, copper and engraved conch shell cups and gorgets. Most people moved to nearby villages around 1250, but Spiro remained a ceremonial centre and burial ground. Treasure hunters who tunnelled into Craig Mound in the 1930s sold its contents to collectors, prompting a state law protecting the site.

entries.name: Hallstatt culture
entries.desc: The Hallstatt culture was the main archaeological culture of western and central Europe in the early Iron Age, from about 800 to 450 BCE, and is commonly associated with speakers of Proto-Celtic. It grew out of the Urnfield culture and is named after Hallstatt in Austria, where Johann Georg Ramsauer found a cemetery in 1846 and the salt mines preserved textiles, wood and leather. Towards its end people of high rank were buried under mounds with Greek imports, as at Vix and Hochdorf; the La Tène culture followed in much of its area.

entries.name: Gundestrup cauldron
entries.desc: The Gundestrup cauldron is a richly decorated silver vessel thought to date from between 200 BCE and 300 CE, or more narrowly 150–1 BCE, found dismantled in a peat bog near Gundestrup in Himmerland, Denmark, in 1891. The largest known piece of European Iron Age silver work, 69 cm across, it is kept in the National Museum of Denmark in Copenhagen. Its gilded repoussé plates combine Thracian silverworking with Celtic figures, such as carnyx players and an antlered figure commonly identified as Cernunnos, and motifs from the Near East.

entries.name: Battersea Shield
entries.desc: The Battersea Shield is the bronze facing of a vanished wooden shield, decorated in the Celtic La Tène style and now in the British Museum, which dates it to about 350–50 BCE. It was dredged from the River Thames at Battersea in London in 1857, during the building of the first Chelsea Bridge. It is made of several riveted pieces, with repoussé circles and spirals and 27 small compartments of red enamel. Too thin to protect in battle, it is thought to have been cast into the river as a votive offering.

entries.name: Waterloo Helmet
entries.desc: The Waterloo Helmet is a Celtic bronze horned helmet of about 150–50 BCE, dredged from the River Thames near Waterloo Bridge in London in 1868 and now in the British Museum. Made of riveted bronze sheets with two conical horns, it bears repoussé decoration in the La Tène style. Too fragile for battle, it was probably made for ceremony and is thought to have been thrown into the river as a votive offering. It is the only actual horned helmet of the Iron Age known from Europe.

entries.name: Vix Grave
entries.desc: The Vix Grave is a burial mound at the foot of Mont Lassois, near Vix in northern Burgundy, where a person of high rank, usually identified as a woman, was buried about 470 BCE. Excavated undisturbed in 1953, it held a gold torc and imported vessels for wine from Italy and the Greek world. Chief among them is the Vix krater, a bronze vessel 1.64 metres high, the largest known metal vessel from western classical antiquity. The krater and a reconstruction of the grave are in the museum at Châtillon-sur-Seine.

entries.name: Hochdorf Chieftain's Grave
entries.desc: The Hochdorf Chieftain's Grave is a Celtic burial chamber of the Hallstatt period near Hochdorf an der Enz in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, dating from about 530 BCE. Excavated in 1978–1979, it held a man laid on a bronze couch 2.75 metres long with eight wheels, wearing a gold-plated torc and gold plaques on his shoes. In the chamber were also a four-wheeled wagon, drinking horns and dishes enough for nine people, and a cauldron imported from Magna Graecia that had held about 400 litres of mead.

entries.name: Liver of Piacenza
entries.desc: The Liver of Piacenza is a life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver inscribed in Etruscan, dated to the late 2nd century BCE and found in 1877 near Gossolengo in the province of Piacenza, Italy. Divided into sections for haruspicy, divination from animal livers, it bears the abbreviated names of Etruscan gods. The 16 sections of its rim have been compared with the 16 regions into which, according to Pliny and Cicero, the Etruscans divided the heavens. It is kept in the Municipal Museum of Piacenza in the Palazzo Farnese.

entries.name: Pyrgi Tablets
entries.desc: The Pyrgi Tablets are three gold plates of about 500 BCE, two inscribed in Etruscan and one in Phoenician, found in 1964 at ancient Pyrgi, on the Tyrrhenian coast of Lazio. They record the dedication of a temple by Thefarie Velianas, ruler of nearby Caere, to the goddess called Astarte in the Phoenician text and Uni in the Etruscan. Though not a word-for-word translation, the bilingual text helps scholars interpret Etruscan and shows Phoenician or Punic influence in the western Mediterranean. They are in the National Etruscan Museum, Villa Giulia, Rome.

entries.name: Banditaccia necropolis
entries.desc: The Banditaccia necropolis is an Etruscan cemetery at Cerveteri, ancient Caere, in Lazio, Italy, with about 1,000 tombs over some 400 hectares dating from the 9th to the 3rd century BCE. The earliest are pits for the ashes of the dead. Later tombs are round tumuli of tuff over rock-cut chambers laid out like houses, with a corridor, hall and rooms, or square tombs in rows along streets. With the Monterozzi necropolis at Tarquinia it became a World Heritage Site in 2004.

entries.name: Monterozzi necropolis
entries.desc: The Monterozzi necropolis is an Etruscan cemetery on a hill east of Tarquinia in Lazio, Italy, used from the Villanovan period of the 9th century BCE into Roman times. About 200 of its some 6,000 graves are rock-cut chambers painted with scenes of daily life, rituals, dance and music, and in later tombs with underworld demons escorting the dead. The best known include the Tombs of the Leopards, of Hunting and Fishing, and of the Augurs. With the Banditaccia necropolis at Cerveteri it became a World Heritage Site in 2004.

entries.name: Liber Linteus
entries.desc: The Liber Linteus, or Linen Book of Zagreb, is the longest surviving Etruscan text and the only surviving linen book, written about 250 BCE, probably in south-eastern Tuscany near Lake Trasimeno. It survived as the wrappings of a mummy from Ptolemaic Egypt, bought in Alexandria in 1848 and kept in Zagreb since 1867, now at the Archaeological Museum. In 1892 Jakob Krall identified its language as Etruscan. Only partly understood, its 230 lines name gods and dates and appear to form a calendar of rituals.

entries.name: Phoenician alphabet
entries.desc: The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 consonant letters, written from right to left, used in Phoenicia and across the Mediterranean for most of the 1st millennium BCE. Conventionally dated from about 1050 BCE, it developed from the Proto-Sinaitic script, itself derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs, and appears essentially fully formed on the sarcophagus of Ahiram at Byblos. Spread by Phoenician merchants, it was adopted in the 9th or 8th century BCE by the Greeks, who added vowels, and is the ancestor of the Aramaic, Hebrew, Arabic, Greek and Latin scripts.

entries.name: Sidon
entries.desc: Sidon, or Saida, is a city on the Mediterranean coast of southern Lebanon, about 40 km south of Beirut, inhabited since prehistoric times. One of the most important Phoenician cities, it was known for its glass and purple dye, and under Persian rule it eclipsed Tyre as the leading city of Phoenicia. Crusaders took it in 1110 and made it the seat of the Lordship of Sidon, and under the Ottomans it was the capital of a province. It is now the third-largest city in Lebanon.

entries.name: Ahiram sarcophagus
entries.desc: The Ahiram sarcophagus is a carved limestone coffin from Byblos, Lebanon, generally dated about 1000 BCE, though the date is disputed, and found in 1923 by the French archaeologist Pierre Montet in a shaft tomb of the city's royal necropolis. Its 38-word inscription, in which Ahiram's son records making it for his father and curses anyone who disturbs it, is the oldest known text of any length in the fully developed Phoenician alphabet. Its reliefs show a king on a throne of winged sphinxes; it is kept in the National Museum of Beirut.

entries.name: Sogdian Ancient Letters
entries.desc: The Sogdian Ancient Letters are private and business letters written in the early 4th century by Sogdians living in China, found by Aurel Stein in 1907 in an abandoned watchtower near Dunhuang. In two, Miwnay, left destitute in Dunhuang with her daughter by her husband, asks her mother for help and tells him she would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than his. Another, from Nanai-vandak to Sogdians in Samarkand, reports the sack of the Jin capital, Luoyang, and the death of the Sogdians and Indians living there.

entries.name: Dresden Codex
entries.desc: The Dresden Codex is a Maya book of the 11th or 12th century, probably from the region of Chichén Itzá in Mexico, and one of four Maya hieroglyphic books to survive. Painted by eight scribes on folded bark paper, it contains Venus tables, lunar tables linked to eclipses and ritual calendars. It was long thought the oldest surviving book from the Americas, until the Maya Codex of Mexico proved older in 2018. Bought in Vienna in 1739, it is held by the Saxon State Library in Dresden and was badly damaged by water in 1945.

entries.name: Temple of the Inscriptions
entries.desc: The Temple of the Inscriptions is a stepped pyramid at Palenque in Chiapas, Mexico, built as the funerary monument of the 7th-century Maya ruler K'inich Janaab Pakal. Begun in the last decade of his life, it was completed by his son K'inich Kan Bahlam II shortly after 683. Its name comes from three tablets in the temple whose 617 glyphs form one of the longest known Maya inscriptions. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier reached Pakal's tomb by a stairway beneath the temple floor, finding his carved sarcophagus and jade death mask.

entries.name: Karl Marx
entries.desc: Karl Marx was a German philosopher, political theorist and revolutionary socialist whose theory of historical materialism analysed social change through class struggle and predicted that communism would replace capitalism. Born in Trier, he co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels; it was first published in February 1848. Expelled from Germany after the revolutions of that year, he settled in London, where he wrote Das Kapital, whose first volume was published in 1867. Elected to the General Council of the First International at its founding in 1864, he opposed the anarchists led by Mikhail Bakunin.

entries.name: Robert Owen
entries.desc: Robert Owen was a Welsh textile manufacturer and social reformer, and a founder of utopian socialism and the co-operative movement. From 1800 he managed the New Lanark cotton mills in Scotland, where in 1816 he opened an Institution for the Formation of Character offering free education. By 1817 he had formulated the goal of an eight-hour working day, with the slogan "eight hours' labour, eight hours' recreation, eight hours' rest". His community at New Harmony, Indiana, lasted about two years, and the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union, which he briefly led, collapsed in 1834.

entries.name: Flora Tristan
entries.desc: Flora Tristan was a French-Peruvian writer and socialist activist who argued that the progress of women's rights was bound up with the progress of the working class. Her account of a journey to Peru in 1833–1834, Peregrinations of a Pariah, appeared in 1838. In 1843 she published The Workers' Union and toured France to win workers to her plan for a universal union of working men and women, across the barriers of trade and region; she died suddenly in 1844. In 1848 French workers placed a monument on her tomb.

entries.name: Keir Hardie
entries.desc: Keir Hardie was a Scottish trade unionist and politician, a founder of the Labour Party and its first parliamentary leader, from 1906 to 1908. A miner in Lanarkshire from the age of ten, he became a union organiser in 1879 and in 1886 secretary of the Ayrshire Miners' Union. Elected for West Ham South as an independent in 1892, he helped to form the Independent Labour Party in 1893 and in 1900 the Labour Representation Committee, which became the Labour Party. He later campaigned for women's suffrage and against the First World War.

entries.name: Samuel Gompers
entries.desc: Samuel Gompers was a British-born American cigar maker and trade union leader who founded the American Federation of Labor and was its president, but for one year, from 1886 until his death. Born in London's East End, he emigrated with his family to New York in 1863 and joined the cigar makers' union the next year. He favoured organisation and collective bargaining to win shorter hours and higher wages. In 1919 he chaired the Commission on International Labour Legislation, whose recommendations for a workers' rights charter entered the Treaty of Versailles.

entries.name: Lech Wałęsa
entries.desc: Lech Wałęsa is a Polish trade unionist and statesman who led the Solidarity movement and was president of Poland from 1990 to 1995. An electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, he was dismissed in 1976 for his union activity. In August 1980 he led the strike committee that negotiated the Gdańsk Agreement, which permitted an independent trade union, and he became chairman of Solidarity. Imprisoned under martial law in 1981–1982, he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 and in 1989 informally led the opposition side in the Round Table talks.

entries.name: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
entries.desc: Elizabeth Cady Stanton was an American writer and activist, a leader of the women's rights movement in the United States. In 1848 she was the main force behind the Seneca Falls Convention and the primary author of its Declaration of Sentiments, whose grievances included the denial of women's right to vote. After opposing the Fifteenth Amendment, which gave the vote to Black men but not to women, she founded the National Woman Suffrage Association with Susan B. Anthony in 1869 and became its first president. She wrote most of the first three volumes of the History of Woman Suffrage and of The Woman's Bible (1895–1898).

entries.name: Kate Sheppard
entries.desc: Kate Sheppard was a New Zealand suffragist who led the campaign for women's right to vote. Born in Liverpool, she emigrated to Christchurch and in 1887 became national superintendent for franchise and legislation of New Zealand's Women's Christian Temperance Union. She wrote pamphlets and organised three petitions to Parliament between 1891 and 1893, the last signed by 31,872 women, before the Electoral Act of September 1893 made New Zealand the first self-governing country in which women could vote in parliamentary elections. She was the first president of the National Council of Women of New Zealand, founded in 1896.

entries.name: Millicent Garrett Fawcett
entries.desc: Millicent Garrett Fawcett was an English political activist and writer who led the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, Britain's largest women's rights association, from 1897 to 1919. She campaigned for the vote through changes in the law and distanced herself from the militancy of the Women's Social and Political Union. She co-founded what became Newnham College, Cambridge, in 1871, and in 1901 led a commission of women sent to investigate the concentration camps of the South African War. In 2018 she became the first woman honoured with a statue in Parliament Square, London.

entries.name: Carrie Chapman Catt
entries.desc: Carrie Chapman Catt was an American women's suffrage leader who campaigned for the Nineteenth Amendment, which gave American women the vote in 1920. Chosen by Susan B. Anthony as her successor, she was president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association from 1900 to 1904 and from 1915 to 1920. Her "Winning Plan" of 1916 made a federal amendment the goal, and she led the battle for its ratification. She helped found the International Woman Suffrage Alliance, which she led from 1904 to 1923, and in 1920 founded the League of Women Voters.

entries.name: Olaudah Equiano
entries.desc: Olaudah Equiano, known for most of his life as Gustavus Vassa, was a writer and abolitionist in Britain. By his own account he was kidnapped as a child from an Igbo village in what is now Nigeria, though the historian Vincent Carretta, citing a baptism record that places his birth in Carolina, has questioned this. Enslaved in the Americas, he bought his freedom in 1766, and in 1783 he told Granville Sharp of the Zong massacre. His Interesting Narrative (1789) is credited with helping win support for the Slave Trade Act of 1807.

entries.name: Joaquim Nabuco
entries.desc: Joaquim Nabuco was a Brazilian statesman, diplomat and writer, a leading voice of his country's abolitionist movement. Raised in a family of slaveholders, he campaigned against slavery in the Chamber of Deputies from 1878, founded the Brazilian Anti-Slavery Society and in 1883 wrote O Abolicionismo; slavery was abolished in 1888. A founder of the Brazilian Academy of Letters, he portrayed Brazil's slave-holding society in his memoir Minha formação (1900). From 1905 until his death he was Brazil's first ambassador to the United States, where he promoted Pan-Americanism.

entries.name: Harriet Tubman
entries.desc: Harriet Tubman was an American abolitionist and social activist who was born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland. After escaping to Philadelphia in 1849, she made some thirteen missions back to rescue about seventy enslaved people, among them members of her family, through the network known as the Underground Railroad. During the Civil War she served the Union Army as an armed scout and spy, and guided the raid at Combahee Ferry in 1863, which freed more than 700 people. In her later years she worked for women's suffrage.

entries.name: William Lloyd Garrison
entries.desc: William Lloyd Garrison was an American abolitionist, journalist and social reformer who founded the anti-slavery newspaper The Liberator in Boston in 1831 and published it until slavery was abolished in 1865. Born in Newburyport, Massachusetts, he rejected the American Colonization Society and gradual abolition, demanding the immediate and uncompensated emancipation of the enslaved. He organised the New-England Anti-Slavery Society in 1832 and helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833. He also supported women's rights and in the 1870s became a prominent voice for women's suffrage.

credit.artist: Liljenquist Family Collection of Civil War Photographs

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.desc: Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer and philosopher, regarded as one of the founding feminist philosophers. Born in London, she won fame with A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790), a reply to Edmund Burke's critique of the French Revolution. In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) she argued that women only appeared inferior to men because they lacked education, and that both should be treated as rational beings. Her widower, the philosopher William Godwin, published a memoir of her life in 1798 that damaged her reputation for almost a century.

entries.name: Émilie du Châtelet
entries.desc: Émilie du Châtelet was a French mathematician and physicist. At Cirey, the du Châtelet château where Voltaire settled in 1734, the two worked closely together and shared an interest in Isaac Newton. Her Institutions de Physique (1740) discussed the ideas of both Newton and Leibniz, and in the vis viva debate she repeated and publicised an experiment showing that kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity. Her French translation of Newton's Principia, with her commentary, completed in 1749 and published after her death, remains the standard French version.

entries.name: Philip Melanchthon
entries.desc: Philip Melanchthon was a German Lutheran reformer, Martin Luther's collaborator and the first systematic theologian of the Protestant Reformation. A scholar of Greek and a Christian humanist, he became professor of Greek at Wittenberg in 1518, and his Loci communes of 1521 was the first systematic account of its teaching. He was the main author of the Augsburg Confession, presented at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, and through his grammars, textbooks and work in education he became the founder of the learned schools of Protestant Germany.

credit.artist: Lucas Cranach the Elder and workshop

entries.name: Robert Boyle
entries.desc: Robert Boyle was an Anglo-Irish chemist, physicist and theologian, regarded as one of the founders of modern chemistry. He studied the properties of air with a pump built by Robert Hooke and in 1662 published Boyle's law: at a constant temperature, the volume of a gas varies inversely with its pressure. For him chemistry, the subject of his Sceptical Chymist (1661), was the science of the composition of substances. Named to the council of the Royal Society in its charter of 1663, he left money in his will for lectures defending Christianity.

entries.name: Andreas Vesalius
entries.desc: Andreas Vesalius was an anatomist and physician from Brussels, often referred to as the founder of modern human anatomy. Professor at Padua from 1537, he dissected human bodies himself and found that Galen's anatomy rested on the dissection of animals; he showed, for instance, that the lower jaw is a single bone, not two. His De humani corporis fabrica, published in Basel in 1543 with 273 illustrations, was a major advance on the long-dominant work of Galen. He later served as physician to the emperor Charles V and to Philip II of Spain.

entries.name: William Harvey
entries.desc: William Harvey was an English physician, the first known to describe completely and in detail the circulation of the blood, pumped by the heart through the lungs and around the body. Taught at Padua by Fabricius, he served St Bartholomew's Hospital in London from 1609 and was physician to James I and Charles I. His De Motu Cordis, published at Frankfurt in 1628, combined experiments with a calculation: if Galen were right, the liver would have to make 498 pounds of blood a day. The theory took twenty years to win general acceptance.

entries.name: Friedrich Schlegel
entries.desc: Friedrich Schlegel was a German literary critic, philosopher and Indologist who was, with his brother August Wilhelm, one of the main figures of Jena Romanticism. The brothers founded the journal Athenaeum, whose fragments and essays stated the principles of the Romantic school, and his novel Lucinde of 1799 caused a scandal. On the Language and Wisdom of India, published in 1808, compared Sanskrit with Latin, Greek, Persian and German, noting many similarities of vocabulary and grammar. Received into the Catholic Church that year, he later served Metternich in Vienna as a diplomat and journalist.

entries.name: William Wordsworth
entries.desc: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet who, with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, helped to launch the Romantic Age in English literature with their joint collection Lyrical Ballads in 1798. In the preface to its second edition, in 1800, he sought verse in the language "really used by men" and defined poetry as "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings". He settled at Grasmere in the Lake District, the region of his birth, and was Poet Laureate from 1843. The Prelude, the autobiographical poem generally considered his masterpiece, was published by his widow after his death.

entries.name: Caspar David Friedrich
entries.desc: Caspar David Friedrich was a German Romantic landscape painter, generally considered the most important German artist of his generation. Born in Greifswald in Swedish Pomerania, he studied in Copenhagen and settled in Dresden in 1798. In many of his paintings contemplative figures, often seen from behind, stand against night skies, morning mists, barren trees or Gothic ruins, and he helped make landscape a self-contained emotive subject rather than a backdrop to human drama. He died in obscurity, but a Berlin exhibition of 1906 revived interest in his work, which influenced Expressionists and Surrealists.

entries.name: Frédéric Chopin
entries.desc: Frédéric Chopin was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the early Romantic period who wrote primarily for solo piano. Raised in Warsaw, he left Poland less than a month before the November Uprising of 1830 broke out and settled in Paris in 1831, never to return. There he gave only some thirty public performances, preferring the salon, and lived by selling his compositions and teaching the piano. His mazurkas and polonaises have been credited with bringing a new sense of nationalism to music, and he created the ballade as an instrumental genre.

entries.name: Mary Shelley
entries.desc: Mary Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, considered an early example of science fiction. The daughter of William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft, she eloped with Percy Bysshe Shelley in 1814 and married him in 1816. The novel grew from Lord Byron's proposal, during a wet summer beside Lake Geneva in 1816, that they each write a ghost story, and was published anonymously in 1818. Widowed in 1822, she became a professional author, writing novels such as The Last Man and editing her husband's poems.

entries.name: W. E. B. Du Bois
entries.desc: W. E. B. Du Bois was an American sociologist, historian, writer and Pan-Africanist civil rights activist, the first African American to earn a doctorate at Harvard. In The Souls of Black Folk of 1903 he wrote that "the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color line". A founder of the NAACP, he edited its journal The Crisis from 1910 and, after the First World War, helped to organise several Pan-African Congresses. He settled in Ghana in 1961 and died in Accra.

entries.name: Henry Sylvester Williams
entries.desc: Henry Sylvester Williams was a Trinidadian lawyer, activist, councillor and writer, among the founders of the Pan-African movement. As a law student in London he founded the African Association in 1897 with Alice Kinloch and Thomas Josiah Thompson, and in July 1900 organised the first Pan-African Conference at Westminster Town Hall. He became the first black man called to the bar in the Cape Colony in 1903 and in 1906 won a seat on Marylebone Borough Council, among the first people of African descent elected to public office in Britain.

entries.name: George Padmore
entries.desc: George Padmore was a Trinidadian Pan-Africanist, journalist and author. A Communist Party member from 1927, he headed the Negro Bureau of the Red International of Labour Unions in Moscow and edited The Negro Worker, but broke with the Comintern in 1933 over what he saw as its flagging support for colonial independence. Settled in London from 1934, he chaired the International African Service Bureau and organised the Fifth Pan-African Congress at Manchester in 1945. He advised Kwame Nkrumah and moved to Ghana, where his ashes were buried after his death in London.

entries.name: Rosa Parks
entries.desc: Rosa Parks was an American civil rights activist, best known for refusing on 1 December 1955 to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama, to a white passenger, in defiance of Jim Crow segregation laws. A seamstress and, from 1943, secretary of the city's NAACP chapter, she was arrested and fined, and the bus boycott that followed lasted 381 days, until bus segregation was ruled unconstitutional in Browder v. Gayle. She moved to Detroit in 1957 and is sometimes called the "mother of the civil rights movement".

entries.name: Thurgood Marshall
entries.desc: Thurgood Marshall was an American lawyer and the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, serving from 1967 to 1991. A student of Charles Hamilton Houston at Howard University, he led the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund and won 29 of the 32 civil rights cases he argued before the Supreme Court, among them Brown v. Board of Education, in which the court held segregated public education unconstitutional in 1954. On the court he frequently dissented as it grew more conservative, and fervently opposed the death penalty.

entries.name: Ella Baker
entries.desc: Ella Baker was an American civil rights and human rights activist, a largely behind-the-scenes organiser whose career spanned more than five decades. The NAACP's director of branches from 1943, she was later the first staff member of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. In 1960 she had the SCLC invite student sit-in leaders to Shaw University, where they founded the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and she urged them to stay independent of the older leaders. She held that "strong people don't need strong leaders" and promoted grassroots organising.

entries.name: John Lewis
entries.desc: John Lewis was an American civil rights activist and a member of the United States House of Representatives for an Atlanta district from 1987 until his death. He joined the Nashville sit-ins in 1960 and was beaten as one of the original Freedom Riders. He chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee from 1963 to 1966 and was one of the "Big Six" leaders of the March on Washington. On "Bloody Sunday" in 1965 he led marchers across Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge, where state troopers and police attacked them and fractured his skull.

entries.name: Fannie Lou Hamer
entries.desc: Fannie Lou Hamer was an American voting and women's rights activist, community organiser and leader of the civil rights movement. A plantation timekeeper in Mississippi, she was fired after trying to register to vote in 1962 and became a field secretary of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Beaten almost to death in jail after an arrest at Winona in June 1963, she went on to help organise the Freedom Summer. As vice-chair of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party she gave televised testimony to the credentials committee of the 1964 Democratic National Convention.

entries.name: Malcolm X
entries.desc: Malcolm X was an African American Muslim minister and civil rights leader. Born Malcolm Little, he joined the Nation of Islam in prison and from 1952 was its public face, urging Black empowerment and separation from white Americans and criticising the mainstream civil rights movement's emphasis on non-violence and integration. He left the Nation in 1964, made the pilgrimage to Mecca, embraced Sunni Islam and founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity. He was assassinated in New York in February 1965; his ideas were an important influence on the Black power movement.

entries.name: Albert Luthuli
entries.desc: Albert Luthuli was a South African anti-apartheid activist and traditional leader who led the African National Congress from 1952. Elected a Zulu chief at Groutville in 1935, he was deposed by the government in 1952 for refusing to choose between the chieftaincy and the ANC. Repeatedly banned, he led non-violent resistance inspired by his Christian faith and by Gandhi, and received the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize in 1961. The official account was that a train struck him in 1967, but in October 2025 a reopened inquest ruled that apartheid police had beaten him to death.

entries.name: Oliver Tambo
entries.desc: Oliver Tambo was a South African anti-apartheid politician and activist who led the African National Congress from 1967 to 1991. With Nelson Mandela and Walter Sisulu he helped found the ANC Youth League in 1944, and became the ANC's secretary-general in 1955. After the Sharpeville massacre of 1960 the ANC sent him abroad to rally international opposition to apartheid; based in London, he became acting president on Albert Luthuli's death and was directly responsible for organising guerrilla units. He returned in December 1990 after more than thirty years in exile.

entries.name: Robert Sobukwe
entries.desc: Robert Sobukwe was a South African anti-apartheid leader, a founder of the Pan Africanist Congress and, from 1959, its first president. A lecturer at the University of the Witwatersrand, he held that black South Africans must "liberate themselves" without the help of non-Africans. He launched the PAC's non-violent campaign against the pass laws in March 1960 and was jailed for three years for incitement. Under the "Sobukwe Clause" of 1963 he was held six more years in solitary confinement on Robben Island, and from 1969 lived under house arrest in Kimberley.

entries.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
entries.desc: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, called Lokmanya, was an Indian nationalist and an early, forceful advocate of swaraj, self-rule, known for the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it". He founded the weeklies Kesari and Mahratta and, with Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal, led the radical wing of the Indian National Congress, urging swadeshi and the boycott of foreign goods after the partition of Bengal. Imprisoned for sedition at Mandalay from 1908 to 1914, where he wrote the Gita Rahasya, he later helped found the All India Home Rule League.

entries.name: Seneca Falls Convention
entries.desc: The Seneca Falls Convention was the first women's rights convention, held in the Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls, New York, on 19–20 July 1848. Organised by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and local Quaker women during a visit by Lucretia Mott, it adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modelled on the Declaration of Independence, signed by 100 of some 300 people present. Its resolution on women's suffrage passed after Frederick Douglass spoke for it. Stanton and Susan B. Anthony later presented it as the beginning of the women's rights movement, a view historians have since questioned.

entries.name: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
aka: Vindication of the Rights of Woman
entries.desc: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman is a 1792 essay by the British philosopher Mary Wollstonecraft, considered a pioneering work of feminist philosophy. Prompted by Talleyrand's 1791 report to the French National Assembly, which proposed only a domestic education for women, it argues that women deserve the same fundamental rights as men and a rational education. Well received at first, it acquired an aura of ill repute after William Godwin's memoir of 1798 revealed its author's private life. It influenced 19th-century campaigners for women's rights, notably at the Seneca Falls Convention.
links: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
Vindication of the Rights of Woman

entries.name: Olympe de Gouges
entries.desc: Olympe de Gouges was a French playwright and political activist, best known for her Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen. Writing plays in Paris from the 1780s, she was also one of France's earliest public opponents of slavery. Her declaration of 1791, an answer to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, advocated equal rights for women. Associated with the Girondins, she opposed the execution of Louis XVI; her writings against the Montagnards led to her arrest, and she was guillotined in November 1793.

entries.name: Tolpuddle Martyrs
entries.desc: The Tolpuddle Martyrs were six agricultural labourers from Tolpuddle in Dorset, England, convicted in 1834 of swearing a secret oath as members of a friendly society. Led by the Methodist local preacher George Loveless, they had formed the Friendly Society of Agricultural Labourers in 1833 to protest against wage cuts. Charged under the Unlawful Oaths Act of 1797, they were sentenced to seven years' transportation to Australia. After mass protests and the collection of 800,000 signatures for their release, they were pardoned in March 1836 and returned to England between 1837 and 1839.

entries.name: Chartism
entries.desc: Chartism was a working-class movement for political reform in the United Kingdom, named after the People's Charter of 1838 and active until 1857. The Charter demanded a vote for every man aged 21 or over, the secret ballot, payment of members of parliament and no property qualification for them, equal constituencies and annual parliaments. Parliament rejected its mass petitions of 1839 and 1842, the second signed by over three million people, and the Newport Rising of 1839 was put down. After the movement died out, Britain adopted all its demands except annual parliaments.

credit.artist: William Edward Kilburn (1818 - 1891) Details on Google Art Project

entries.name: Peterloo Massacre
entries.desc: The Peterloo Massacre took place at St Peter's Field in Manchester, England, on 16 August 1819, when cavalry charged into a crowd of tens of thousands gathered to demand parliamentary reform. An estimated eighteen people were killed and 400–700 injured. Magistrates sent the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry to arrest the radical orator Henry Hunt, then ordered the 15th Hussars to disperse the crowd. The radical Manchester Observer coined the name in ironic reference to the Battle of Waterloo, and the government answered with the Six Acts, aimed at suppressing radical meetings and publications.

entries.name: Luddites
entries.desc: The Luddites were English textile workers who, between 1811 and 1816, wrecked certain kinds of machinery in organised raids, out of concern for their pay, working conditions and the quality of goods. Named after the legendary Ned Ludd, whose name appeared in threatening letters to mill owners and officials, the movement began in Nottinghamshire and spread to Yorkshire and the North West. Parliament made machine-breaking a capital crime in 1812, and some 12,000 troops were deployed against the Luddites; a mass trial at York in 1813 led to executions and transportation.

credit.artist: Unknown. 195 years since publication, copyright extinguished

entries.name: The Communist Manifesto
entries.desc: The Communist Manifesto, originally the Manifesto of the Communist Party, is a political pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, commissioned by the Communist League and published anonymously in German in London in February 1848. It argues that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles" and predicts that the proletariat will overthrow the bourgeoisie and bring about a classless society. It fell into obscurity after the defeat of the revolutions of 1848, revived in the 1870s and has become one of the world's most influential political documents.

entries.name: International Workingmen's Association
entries.desc: The International Workingmen's Association, commonly known as the First International, was a political international that aimed to unite left-wing groups and trade unions of the working class. It was founded at a meeting of some 2,000 workers in St Martin's Hall, London, on 28 September 1864, and Karl Marx drafted its Inaugural Address and Provisional Rules. Conflict between Marx's supporters and the anarchists around Mikhail Bakunin led to a split at the Hague Congress of 1872, which expelled Bakunin and moved the General Council to New York. The International was formally disbanded in 1876.

entries.name: Solidarity (Polish trade union)
entries.desc: Solidarity is a Polish trade union that emerged at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in August 1980, the first independent union in a Warsaw Pact country to be recognised by the state. Led by Lech Wałęsa, it had 10 million members at its peak in September 1981, a third of the working-age population. The government tried to destroy it with martial law from December 1981, but it survived underground. In the elections agreed at the Round Table talks of 1989 it won 99 of the 100 Senate seats, and a Solidarity-led government followed.

entries.name: Zong massacre
entries.desc: The Zong massacre was the killing of more than 130 enslaved Africans by the crew of the British slave ship Zong, who threw them overboard over several days from 29 November 1781. The crew said water had run short after navigational errors, and the Liverpool owners claimed insurance for the dead as lost cargo. A jury found for the owners in 1783, but on appeal Lord Mansfield ordered a retrial on learning that rain had fallen during the killings. Brought to Granville Sharp's attention by Olaudah Equiano, the massacre stimulated the abolitionist movement.

entries.name: Underground Railroad
entries.desc: The Underground Railroad was an organised network of secret routes and safe houses by which enslaved people in the United States escaped, chiefly to the free Northern states and Canada. It took shape in the 1780s among abolitionist societies in the North and grew steadily until the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863. Primarily the work of free and enslaved African Americans, aided by abolitionists, it used railway terms: escapees were "passengers" and those who aided them "conductors". One estimate holds that about 100,000 people had escaped through it by 1850.

entries.name: Uncle Tom's Cabin
entries.desc: Uncle Tom's Cabin is an American anti-slavery novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe, serialised in The National Era from 1851 and published in two volumes in 1852. Stowe wrote it in response to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, and it sold 300,000 copies in the United States in its first year. The best-selling novel of the 19th century in the United States, it is credited with helping fuel the abolitionist cause in the 1850s. The book and the plays it inspired also helped popularise negative stereotypes of black people, including the "Uncle Tom".

entries.name: Royal Society
aka: Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge
entries.desc: The Royal Society is a learned society and the United Kingdom's national academy of sciences, founded at Gresham College in London on 28 November 1660 and granted a royal charter by King Charles II. Its founders, among them Christopher Wren, Robert Boyle and John Wilkins, set out to promote experimental learning, and its early meetings included experiments performed by Robert Hooke. In 1665 it began the Philosophical Transactions, edited by its secretary Henry Oldenburg, the world's first journal devoted exclusively to science. Its motto, Nullius in verba, means "Take nobody's word for it".
links: Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge

entries.name: Sidereus Nuncius
entries.desc: Sidereus Nuncius, known in English as the Sidereal Messenger or Starry Messenger, is a short astronomical treatise in Latin by Galileo Galilei, published on 13 March 1610. It was the first published scientific work based on observations made through a telescope, reporting a mountainous Moon, hundreds of stars invisible to the naked eye and four bodies that appeared to circle Jupiter. Galileo, then a mathematician at the University of Padua, named them the Medicean Stars and dedicated the book to Cosimo II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, in hope of patronage.

entries.name: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
aka: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres
entries.desc: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, is Nicolaus Copernicus's account of his heliocentric theory, printed in Nuremberg in 1543, shortly before his death. Following the layout of Ptolemy's Almagest, its six books describe an Earth that turns daily on its axis and circles the Sun with the other planets, though Copernicus kept uniform circular motions and epicycles. An unsigned preface by the Lutheran preacher Andreas Osiander presented the system as an aid to computation, not literal truth. In 1616 the Congregation of the Index suspended the book until corrected.
links: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres

entries.name: Lyrical Ballads
aka: Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems
entries.desc: Lyrical Ballads is a collection of poems by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, first published in 1798 and generally considered to have marked the beginning of the English Romantic movement. Coleridge's four poems in the first edition, about a third of its length, included The Rime of the Ancient Mariner; the other nineteen were Wordsworth's. The poets set out to overturn what they considered the learned, highly sculpted forms of 18th-century English poetry and to write in common, everyday language. Wordsworth's preface to the 1800 edition became known as the manifesto of Romanticism.

credit.artist: William Wordsworth (1770-1850) and Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772-1834).

links: Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems

entries.name: Frankenstein
entries.desc: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus is a Gothic novel by the English author Mary Shelley, published anonymously in London on 1 January 1818. Its protagonist, the young scientist Victor Frankenstein, creates a living creature from body parts and is horrified by what he has made. Shelley, aged 18, conceived it by Lake Geneva in the cold summer of 1816, when Lord Byron proposed that he and his companions each write a ghost story. It spawned a genre of horror stories, films and plays and is generally considered one of the first science fiction novels.

entries.name: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
entries.desc: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog is a painting of about 1818 by the German Romantic artist Caspar David Friedrich. A man seen from behind stands on a rocky precipice above a sea of fog pierced by ridges, trees and mountains, a landscape Friedrich composed in the studio from sketches of the Elbe Sandstone Mountains. It has been interpreted as an emblem of self-reflection, as an evocation of the sublime and as an expression of his German liberal and nationalist feeling. It has been displayed at the Hamburger Kunsthalle in Hamburg since 1970.
links: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

entries.name: Montgomery bus boycott
entries.desc: The Montgomery bus boycott was a protest campaign against racial segregation on the buses of Montgomery, Alabama, and a foundational event of the civil rights movement. It began on 5 December 1955, the Monday after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white person, and was led by Martin Luther King Jr. and the Montgomery Improvement Association. Black residents, three-quarters of the riders, organised carpools or walked despite bombings and arrests. It ended on 20 December 1956, after the Supreme Court upheld a ruling in Browder v. Gayle that bus segregation was unconstitutional.

entries.name: Brown v. Board of Education
aka: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
entries.desc: Brown v. Board of Education was a unanimous ruling of the United States Supreme Court on 17 May 1954 that state laws establishing racial segregation in public schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause. The case began in Topeka, Kansas, was heard with four similar cases and was argued by the NAACP's chief counsel Thurgood Marshall. In Chief Justice Earl Warren's words, "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal"; the decision partially overruled Plessy v. Ferguson of 1896. A second decision in 1955 only ordered states to desegregate "with all deliberate speed".
links: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka

entries.name: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People
entries.desc: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People is an American civil rights organisation founded in 1909 by an interracial group including W. E. B. Du Bois, Mary White Ovington and Ida B. Wells to advance justice for African Americans. The NAACP campaigned against lynching and disenfranchisement through publicity, lobbying and lawsuits, and Du Bois edited its magazine, The Crisis, from 1910. Its legal department, headed by Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall, waged a decades-long campaign against the "separate but equal" doctrine that culminated in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954.

credit.artist: New York World-Telegram and the Sun staff photographer: Al Ravenna

links: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People

entries.name: Selma to Montgomery marches
entries.desc: The Selma to Montgomery marches were three protest marches for African American voting rights, held in 1965 along the 54-mile (87 km) highway from Selma, Alabama, to Montgomery, the state capital. On 7 March, "Bloody Sunday", state troopers and a county posse attacked an estimated 525 to 600 marchers with batons and tear gas at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. The third march, under federal protection, reached Montgomery on 24 March; the next day 25,000 people demonstrated at the Alabama State Capitol. The marches contributed to the passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

entries.name: Fifth Pan-African Congress
entries.desc: The Fifth Pan-African Congress was a meeting of the Pan-African movement held at Chorlton-on-Medlock Town Hall in Manchester, England, from 15 to 21 October 1945. An estimated 87 to 90 delegates from some 50 organisations attended, with more representatives from the African continent than at the four earlier congresses. Among them were Kwame Nkrumah, Jomo Kenyatta and Hastings Banda, who later became the first presidents of their independent countries. Amy Ashwood Garvey chaired the opening session and W. E. B. Du Bois the rest, and the congress demanded independence for Africa's colonies.

entries.name: Universal Negro Improvement Association
aka: Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League
entries.desc: The Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League is a Black nationalist fraternal organisation founded by Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood Garvey in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1914. Based in the United States, it had by 1920 over 1,900 divisions in more than 40 countries, published the weekly Negro World and founded the Black Star Line shipping company. Its first convention, in August 1920, adopted the Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World and the red, black and green flag. Its influence declined after Garvey's deportation to Jamaica in 1927.
links: Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League

entries.name: Négritude
entries.desc: Négritude is a framework of critique and literary theory developed in the 1930s, mainly by French-speaking Black intellectuals and writers, to raise Black consciousness across Africa and its diaspora. Its founders included the Martinican poet Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor, later the first president of Senegal, and Léon Damas of French Guiana. Césaire first used the word in its present sense in 1935 in L'Étudiant noir, a magazine he had started in Paris with fellow students. Rejecting colonialism, racism and Eurocentrism, its writers drew on Marxism and Surrealism and celebrated African history and culture.

entries.name: Khilafat movement
entries.desc: The Khilafat movement was a political campaign of Muslims in British India against British policy towards Turkey and the planned dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire after the First World War. Its leaders, among them Abul Kalam Azad and the brothers Mohammad Ali Jauhar and Shaukat Ali, formed the All India Khilafat Committee to protect the caliphate. In 1920 they allied with Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Congress, and the Khilafatists became a major part of the Non-cooperation movement. Noted for promoting Hindu–Muslim unity, it faded after that campaign was called off in 1922, and Turkey's abolition of the caliphate in 1924 ended its cause.

entries.name: Kabir
entries.desc: Kabir was an Indian mystic poet and saint of Varanasi whose verses influenced the Bhakti movement; some historians place his life in 1398–1448, others in 1440–1518. A few accounts say he was raised by a Muslim weaver and his wife, and he is believed to have been a disciple of Ramananda. His songs and couplets, composed orally and gathered in collections such as the Bijak, attacked the hypocrisy and misguided rituals he saw in Hinduism and Islam alike. Verses attributed to him form the largest non-Sikh contribution to the Adi Granth.

entries.name: Andal
entries.desc: Andal was a Tamil poet-saint, probably of the 8th century, and the only woman among the twelve Alvars, the saints devoted to Vishnu in the Bhakti movement. Tradition holds that Periyalvar found her as a child under a tulasi plant at Srivilliputhur and that she would marry no one but Vishnu. She is credited with the Tiruppavai, 30 verses in which she imagines herself one of Krishna's cowherd girls, and the Nachiyar Tirumoli, about 140 verses of longing for Vishnu. Both are recited during the Tamil month of Margazhi, in December and January.

entries.name: Tulsidas
entries.desc: Tulsidas was a Hindu poet-saint of 16th-century northern India, devoted to the god Rama, who spent most of his life in Varanasi and Ayodhya. A Brahmin schooled in Sanskrit and the Vedas, he is best known for the Ramcharitmanas, a retelling of the Sanskrit Ramayana in the vernacular Awadhi, which he began at Ayodhya in 1574. Popular belief also makes him the author of the Hanuman Chalisa, and he is credited with founding the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple in Varanasi and with starting the Ramlila plays, a folk-theatre version of the Ramayana.

entries.name: Tukaram
entries.desc: Tukaram was a 17th-century Marathi poet-saint of the Varkari tradition, born at Dehu in Maharashtra and devoted to the god Vithoba, a form of Vishnu. In his abhangas, devotional poems in a simple folk style, he attacked caste hierarchy, mechanical ritual and the misconduct of certain religious leaders, which brought him opponents such as a local monastery head, Mambaji Gosavi. Tradition credits him with some 4,500 abhangas, collected in the Tukaram Gatha, whose manuscripts were reworked for about two centuries after his death. Among his disciples was a Brahmin woman, Bahinabai.

credit.artist: Anant Shivaji Desai, Ravi Varma Press

entries.name: Namdev
entries.desc: Namdev was a Marathi poet-saint of the Varkari tradition and a devotee of the god Vithoba of Pandharpur; tradition dates his life to 1270–1350, but scholars have proposed dates from the 13th to the 15th century. Born into a caste of tailors, he composed simply worded songs of praise and taught that all could be saved by devotion, without regard to caste. His companions in worship included Gora, a potter, Janabai, a maid, and Chokhamela, of a caste treated as untouchable. Sixty-one songs under his name are in the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture.

entries.name: Ravidas
entries.desc: Ravidas was an Indian mystic poet-saint of the Bhakti movement who lived in the 15th and 16th centuries, though the details of his life are uncertain. Born near Varanasi to parents of the leather-working Chamar caste, treated as untouchable, he taught the removal of divisions of caste and gender and worshipped God as nirguna, without attributes. Forty-one of his poems are in the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture, and tradition names the Rajput princess Mirabai as his disciple. He is the central figure of the Ravidassia religious movement.

entries.name: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi
entries.desc: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi was a 19th-century Egyptian writer, teacher and translator, an early figure of the Nahda, the Arab renaissance. A scholar of al-Azhar, he went to Paris in 1826 as imam to a student mission sent by Muhammad Ali and read Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu there; his account of France, Takhlis al-ibriz fi talkhis Bariz, appeared in 1834. In 1835 he founded the School of Languages in Cairo, and he supervised the translation of more than 2,000 foreign works into Arabic. His guide to educating girls and boys alike was published in 1873.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Zerida at English Wikipedia.

entries.name: Butrus al-Bustani
entries.desc: Butrus al-Bustani was a writer and scholar from Mount Lebanon, a major figure of the Nahda, the Arab renaissance. Born a Maronite, he became a Protestant while working for American missionaries in Beirut and helped translate the Bible into Arabic. After the 1860 civil war his Nafir Suriyya, the Clarion of Syria, appealed for unity in a Syrian homeland, and in 1863 he founded the secular National School in Beirut, open to all religions. He compiled the dictionary Muhit al-Muhit, founded the journal al-Jinan in 1870 and in 1876 began the encyclopedia Da'irat al-Ma'arif.

entries.name: Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq
entries.desc: Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq was an Ottoman scholar, writer and journalist from Mount Lebanon, considered one of the founding fathers of modern Arabic literature. Born a Maronite, he became a Protestant in Egypt, where he lived from 1825, and from 1848 worked in England on an Arabic translation of the Bible, published in 1857. In Paris in 1855 he published al-Saq 'ala al-saq, a long, digressive novel drawing on his own life. In 1860 he converted to Islam, taking the name Ahmad, and in 1861 he founded the Arabic newspaper al-Jawa'ib in Istanbul.

entries.name: Muhammad Abduh
entries.desc: Muhammad Abduh was an Egyptian Islamic scholar, judge and reformer, a central figure of the Nahda and of Islamic modernism. A disciple of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani from his student years at al-Azhar, he argued that Muslims must use reason rather than simply rely on medieval interpretations of the texts. Exiled in 1882 for supporting the Urabi revolt, he published the journal al-'Urwa al-wuthqa with al-Afghani in Paris in 1884. After his return in 1888 he became a judge, and from 1899 until his death he was Grand Mufti of Egypt.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Zerida at English Wikipedia.

entries.name: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani
entries.desc: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani was a political activist and Islamic thinker who travelled across the Muslim world in the late 19th century, one of the founders of Islamic modernism. He claimed Afghan origin, but several scholars hold that he was born into a Shia family in Asadabad, Iran. In Cairo he gained a disciple, Muhammad Abduh, with whom he published the journal al-'Urwa al-wuthqa in Paris in 1884, calling for unity among Muslims. He was implicated in the plot of his follower Mirza Reza Kermani, who shot Naser al-Din Shah of Iran in 1896.

credit.artist: Yacquub cAbd al-cAziiz Abul Ala Maududi

entries.name: Qasim Amin
entries.desc: Qasim Amin was an Egyptian jurist and Islamic modernist, a co-founder of Cairo University and often counted among the Arab world's first feminists. Born in Alexandria, he took a law degree in Egypt and studied at Montpellier in France, and from 1885 served in Egypt's courts. He criticised veiling, seclusion, early marriage and the lack of education for women, and his book The Liberation of Women, published in 1899, called for an end to the veil. His advocacy stirred debate across the Arab world, though scholars such as Leila Ahmed have questioned his feminism.

entries.name: Jurji Zaydan
entries.desc: Jurji Zaydan was a Lebanese novelist, journalist and teacher of the Nahda who settled in Cairo and founded the magazine al-Hilal there in 1892. Born in Beirut to an Orthodox Christian family, he studied medicine at the Syrian Protestant College before moving to Egypt. His historical novels, about one a year from 1891 and serialised in al-Hilal, aimed to teach ordinary Arabs their own history. His secular History of Islamic Civilisation, published from 1901 to 1906, was controversial, and in 1910 public objections cost him a chair at the new Egyptian University.

entries.name: Prince Gong
entries.desc: Yixin, Prince Gong, was a Qing imperial prince and statesman, the sixth son of the Daoguang Emperor and a leader of China's Self-Strengthening Movement. Left behind with full powers when the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing in 1860, he signed the Convention of Peking with the British, French and Russians. In 1861 he set up the Zongli Yamen, in effect a foreign ministry, and joined the Empresses Dowager Ci'an and Cixi in a coup against the late emperor's regents, serving as prince-regent until 1865. Cixi dismissed him in 1884 and recalled him in 1894.

entries.name: Wenxiang
entries.desc: Wenxiang was a Manchu statesman of China's Qing dynasty, a bannerman of the Plain Red Banner, and one of the architects of the Self-Strengthening Movement. After gaining the jinshi, the highest degree of the imperial examination, in 1845, he joined the Grand Council in 1858. When the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing during the Second Opium War, he stayed and took part in the negotiations with the British and French. A founder of the Zongli Yamen, he was instrumental in devising the government's policy of cooperation with the Western powers between 1861 and 1876.

entries.name: Zhang Zhidong
entries.desc: Zhang Zhidong was a Chinese official of the late Qing dynasty who advocated controlled reform and the modernisation of the army, serving as viceroy of Huguang from 1889. He ordered an iron and steel plant from England, which began production in 1894 but made substantial losses, and founded a mint, mills and factories.
