entries.name: Biblical Hebrew
entries.desc: Biblical Hebrew, also called Classical Hebrew, is an archaic form of the Hebrew language, of the Canaanitic branch of the Semitic languages, spoken by the Israelites in the Land of Israel. It is attested in inscriptions from about the 10th century BCE, when it was almost identical to Phoenician, and persisted as a spoken first language through the Second Temple period, which ended in 70 CE, before developing into Mishnaic Hebrew. It was first written in the Paleo-Hebrew alphabet, displaced after the Babylonian captivity by the Imperial Aramaic alphabet, and its vowel marks, the Tiberian vocalization, were added by the Masoretes in the Middle Ages.

entries.name: Vedic Sanskrit
entries.desc: Vedic Sanskrit, also called the Vedic language, is the earliest attested form of the Sanskrit and Prakrit languages, of the Indo-Aryan subgroup of the Indo-European family. It is attested in the Vedas and related literature compiled from the mid-2nd to the mid-1st millennium BCE, and was preserved orally, predating the local advent of writing by several centuries. The oldest hymns of the Rigveda are generally estimated to roughly 1500 BCE. The late form of the language was formalized as Classical Sanskrit in Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, and its literature has been a major source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Indo-Iranian history.

entries.name: Walter Rodney
entries.desc: Walter Rodney was a Guyanese historian, political activist and academic, born into a working-class family in Georgetown. After a PhD in African History in London in 1966, he taught at the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania; his ban from Jamaica in 1968 set off protests known as the Rodney riots. His How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) argued that exploitation by European imperialists led directly to the modern underdevelopment of most of the continent. A Pan-Africanist and Marxist, he joined the Working People's Alliance in Guyana and was killed by an explosive device in his car in 1980; a Commission of Inquiry concluded it had been a state-ordered killing.

entries.name: William Morris
entries.desc: William Morris was an English textile designer, poet, artist, writer and socialist activist associated with the British Arts and Crafts movement and the revival of traditional British textile arts. In 1861 he founded the decorative arts firm Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. with Edward Burne-Jones, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Philip Webb and others, designing tapestries, wallpaper, fabrics, furniture and stained glass; from 1875 it was Morris & Co. His poems and novels, among them the utopian News from Nowhere (1890), helped to establish the modern fantasy genre. He founded the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings in 1877, the Socialist League in 1884 and the Kelmscott Press in 1891.

entries.name: Corded Ware culture
entries.desc: The Corded Ware culture was a broad archaeological horizon of Europe between c. 2900 and 2300 BCE, from the Late Neolithic to the early Bronze Age, reaching from the Rhine in the west to the Volga in the east. Friedrich Klopfleisch named it in 1883 after the cord-like impressions on its pottery; it is also called the Single Grave culture, after its burials under tumuli in a crouched position, and the Battle Axe culture, after the stone axe placed in men's graves. Genetic studies suggest that it arose from the westward migration of Yamnaya-related people from the steppe, and it is considered a likely vector for the spread of many Indo-European languages.

entries.name: Guru Granth Sahib
entries.desc: The Guru Granth Sahib is the central holy scripture of Sikhism, regarded by Sikhs as the final, sovereign and eternal Guru after the ten human gurus. Its first rendition, the Adi Granth, was compiled by the fifth guru, Guru Arjan, completed in 1604 and installed in the Golden Temple in Amritsar; Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth guru, added the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur and affirmed the text as his successor in 1708. It has 1,430 angs (pages), arranged by 31 main rāgas, and is written in the Gurmukhi script. Composed mainly by six Sikh gurus, it also holds the teachings of Hindu Bhakti sants such as Kabir and Namdev and of the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid.

entries.name: Black power movement
entries.desc: The Black power movement emerged in the 1960s from the civil rights movement in the United States, reacting against its moderate and incremental tendencies and demanding more immediate action to counter white supremacy. Influenced by Malcolm X, whose assassination in 1965 helped ignite it, and by pan-Africanism, Black nationalism and socialism, it saw the Black Panther Party, founded in 1966, as its cornerstone. Its followers founded Black-owned stores, clinics and schools; some groups ran social programs while the Black Liberation Army carried out bombings and murdered police officers. It declined by the mid-1970s and 1980s, but influenced later movements such as Black Lives Matter.

entries.name: Chichen Itza
entries.desc: Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people, whose ruins lie in Yucatán, Mexico, between Valladolid and Mérida. It was a major focal point of the Northern Maya Lowlands from the Late Classic into the early Postclassic, and in the 10th century rose to be a regional capital controlling the area from central Yucatán to the north coast. Its buildings mix central Mexican styles with the Puuc and Chenes styles of the region, among them the Temple of Kukulcán (El Castillo), the Great Ball Court and the Sacred Cenote. It declined as a regional center by 1100, and Francisco de Montejo the Younger, who tried to make it a Spanish capital, abandoned it in 1534.

entries.name: Eric Hobsbawm
entries.desc: Eric Hobsbawm was a British historian of the rise of industrial capitalism, socialism and nationalism and a life-long Marxist. Born in Alexandria, Egypt, he grew up in Vienna and Berlin and moved to London in 1933; at King's College, Cambridge, he joined the Communist Party of Great Britain. He taught at Birkbeck College, University of London, from 1947 and was its president from 2002 until his death. His best-known works are his books on the long 19th century, among them The Age of Revolution: Europe 1789–1848, The Age of Capital and The Age of Empire, The Age of Extremes on the short 20th century, and an edited volume that introduced the idea of invented traditions.

entries.name: Guru Arjan
entries.desc: Guru Arjan was the fifth of the ten Sikh Gurus, born in Goindval in the Punjab, the youngest son of Guru Ram Das, whom he succeeded in 1581. He compiled the hymns of the earlier Gurus and other saints into the Adi Granth, the first edition of the Sikh scripture, completed the Darbar Sahib at Amritsar, and is credited with founding Kartarpur, Hargobindpur and Tarn Taran. He asked Sikhs to give a tenth of their income, the dasvandh, which financed gurdwaras and langars. Arrested on the orders of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, who accused him of supporting a rebellion under Khusrau Mirza, he was tortured and executed in 1606 after refusing to convert to Islam.

credit.artist: Family workshop of Purkhu of Kangra

entries.name: Marija Gimbutas
entries.desc: Marija Gimbutas was a Lithuanian archaeologist and anthropologist known for her research into the Neolithic and Bronze Age cultures of Old Europe and for her Kurgan hypothesis, which located the Proto-Indo-European homeland in the Pontic Steppe. Born in Vilnius, she fled Lithuania before the advancing Soviet army and moved to the United States, where she was professor at UCLA from 1963 to 1989 and directed excavations of Neolithic sites in southeastern Europe. Her Goddess books described a goddess-centred Old Europe supplanted by patriarchal Kurgan invaders; mainstream archaeology dismissed these later works, while three genetic studies in 2015 gave support to her Kurgan theory.

entries.name: Rashid Rida
entries.desc: Muhammad Rashid Rida was an Islamic scholar, reformer, theologian and revivalist, born in al-Qalamoun, in present-day Lebanon, in 1865. He joined his mentor Muhammad Abduh in Cairo and in 1898 began publishing al-Manar, through which he became one of the most influential Sunni jurists of his generation and a leader of the Arab Salafi movement. An early Salafist, he later turned from rationalist leanings to a stricter scripturalist approach, supported the Wahhabi movement and revived the works of Ibn Taymiyyah. He opposed secularism, nationalism and European imperialism and championed a pan-Islamist program to re-establish a Caliphate.

entries.name: Feargus O'Connor
entries.desc: Feargus O'Connor was an Irish Chartist leader, Member of Parliament and advocate of the Land Plan, which sought to provide smallholdings for the labouring classes. Elected MP for County Cork in 1832, he founded the Northern Star at Leeds in 1837, and it became the voice of the Chartist movement. In 1845 he founded the Chartist Cooperative Land Company, which was declared illegal in 1851. Elected MP for Nottingham in 1847, he organised the Chartist meeting on Kennington Common in 1848. After striking fellow MPs in 1852 he was confined to an asylum; 40,000 people witnessed his funeral procession.

entries.name: Four Books and Five Classics
entries.desc: The Four Books and Five Classics are authoritative books associated with Confucianism, written before 300 BCE and traditionally believed to have been written, edited or commented on by Confucius or his disciples. The Five Classics, among them the Classic of Poetry, the Book of Documents, the I Ching and the Spring and Autumn Annals, became part of the state curriculum under the Western Han dynasty. The Four Books, including the Analects and the Mencius, were selected by Zhu Xi in the Song dynasty as an introduction to Confucian thought. In the Ming and Qing dynasties they formed the core of the civil service examinations.

entries.name: Poggio Bracciolini
entries.desc: Poggio Bracciolini was an Italian scholar and early Renaissance humanist who served seven popes in the Roman Curia, rising under Martin V to papal secretary. While attending the Council of Constance he searched the libraries of Swiss and Swabian abbeys, and between 1415 and 1417 recovered many lost classical Latin works, among them De rerum natura by Lucretius, De architectura by Vitruvius, Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria and orations of Cicero. He was one of the most prolific scribes of the new Humanist minuscule. In 1453 he became Chancellor of the Florentine Republic, and he died in 1459 before finishing his history of Florence.

entries.name: Pope Leo X
entries.desc: Pope Leo X, born Giovanni di Lorenzo de' Medici, was head of the Catholic Church and leader of the Papal States from 1513 until his death in 1521. The second son of Lorenzo de' Medici of Florence, he was named a cardinal in 1489 at the age of 13. As pope he oversaw the closing sessions of the Fifth Council of the Lateran and in 1517 waged a costly war to secure his nephew as Duke of Urbino. His granting of indulgences for the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica was challenged by Martin Luther, whom his bull Exsurge Domine condemned in 1520. A great patron of the arts, he saw Raphael decorate the Vatican rooms.

entries.name: Second International
entries.desc: The Second International, formally the Socialist International, was a federation of socialist and labour parties founded in Paris in 1889 and dominated by the Social Democratic Party of Germany. It established International Workers' Day on 1 May, popularised the demand for an eight-hour day, expelled the anarchists and condemned revisionism at its Amsterdam Congress of 1904. From 1905 the prevention of war became its central task, and its congresses at Stuttgart, Copenhagen and Basel called for working-class action against war. In 1914 its major parties rallied to their nations' war efforts and it collapsed, succeeded by the Communist International and the Labour and Socialist International.

entries.name: Talmud
entries.desc: The Talmud is a central text of Rabbinic Judaism and a primary source of Jewish law and theology, consisting of the Mishnah and its commentaries, the Gemara, written in a combination of Aramaic and Hebrew. In 63 tractates it records the teachings and disagreements of thousands of rabbis on law, ethics, philosophy, customs, history and folklore. The earlier Jerusalem Talmud was compiled in Galilee in the late fourth or early fifth century; the more extensive and authoritative Babylonian Talmud, traditionally compiled by Rav Ashi and Ravina II around 500 CE, more likely dates from the middle of the sixth century. In Rabbinic Judaism it is second in authority only to the Hebrew Bible.

entries.name: Brahmo Samaj
entries.desc: The Brahmo Samaj is the society of Brahmoism, a monotheistic reform movement begun in Calcutta in 1828 by Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Dwarkanath Tagore during the Bengal Renaissance. Its members denied that any scripture had authority above reason and conscience, denounced polytheism and idol-worship and opposed the caste system. The Samaj condemned sati, discouraged child marriage and polygamy and campaigned for widow remarriage. After Roy's death in 1833 Debendranath Tagore and his circle took it up in 1843; followers of Keshub Chandra Sen broke away in 1866 as the Brahmo Samaj of India, and the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1878.

entries.name: Charles Fourier
entries.desc: Charles Fourier was a French philosopher regarded as the founder of utopian socialism. Born in Besançon, he worked for years as a travelling salesman and correspondence clerk; his first book, the Theory of the Four Movements, appeared anonymously in Lyon in 1808 and sold few copies. He held that cooperation was the key to social success and proposed communities called phalanxes, housed in buildings called phalanstères, where jobs were assigned by interest and desire. He also called trade, which he associated with Jews, the source of all evil. His ideas inspired intentional communities such as Brook Farm and the North American Phalanx.

entries.name: Edward Said
entries.desc: Edward Said was a Palestinian and American academic, literary critic and political activist, born in Jerusalem under the British Mandate, who taught at Columbia University from 1963 until 2003. His book Orientalism (1978), a critique of how the Western world has represented the Orient, made him one of the founders of post-colonial studies; Culture and Imperialism followed in 1993. A member of the Palestinian National Council, he resigned in 1993 over his criticism of the Oslo Accords, and in 1999 argued that lasting peace was possible only in one Israeli–Palestinian state. That year he co-founded the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra with Barenboim. He died of leukemia in New York City in 2003.

entries.name: Egyptian Feminist Union
entries.desc: The Egyptian Feminist Union was the first nationwide feminist movement in Egypt, founded on 6 March 1923 at the home of Huda Sha'arawi, who led it until her death in 1947. Formed out of dissatisfaction with an independence movement that put women's rights second, it campaigned for women's suffrage, education for girls, an end to legalized prostitution and reform of the personal status law, publishing the periodical L'Egyptienne from 1925. Primary education became compulsory for girls in 1925, but its campaign to reform family law failed. In 1944 it convened the congress that founded the Arab Feminist Union. Women won the vote in 1956, the year the Nasser regime dissolved the union.

entries.name: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda
entries.desc: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda was a Jewish linguist, lexicographer and journalist and the primary driving force behind the revival of the Hebrew language. Born Eliezer Yitzhak Perlman in the Vilna Governorate of the Russian Empire, he studied in Paris and in 1881 joined the First Aliyah and settled in Jerusalem, then ruled by the Ottoman Empire. He raised his son Ben-Zion entirely in Hebrew, making him the first native speaker of Hebrew in modern times, and edited the newspaper HaZvi. A major figure in founding the Committee of the Hebrew Language, he began the first modern Hebrew dictionary, completed after his death by his wife Hemda. He died of tuberculosis in 1922.

entries.name: Equal Rights Amendment
entries.desc: The Equal Rights Amendment is a proposed amendment to the United States Constitution that would explicitly prohibit sex discrimination. Written by Alice Paul and Crystal Eastman, it was first introduced in Congress in December 1923 and, with the rise of the women's movement, passed the House of Representatives in 1971 and the Senate in 1972. Its ratification deadline of 1979, later extended to 1982, passed with the amendment three states short of the 38 needed, after opposition led by Phyllis Schlafly. Nevada, Illinois and Virginia ratified it between 2017 and 2020, but its status is still debated and it is not part of the Constitution.

entries.name: Eugène Delacroix
entries.desc: Eugène Delacroix was a French Romantic artist regarded as the leader of the French Romantic school. Against the Neoclassical perfectionism of his rival Ingres, he took Rubens and the painters of the Venetian Renaissance as models, stressing colour and movement over clarity of outline. His Barque of Dante was accepted by the Paris Salon of 1822, and he went on to paint the Chios Massacre and The Death of Sardanapalus. Liberty Leading the People of 1830 was bought by the French government but removed from public view by 1832. His expressive brushstrokes and study of colour shaped the work of the Impressionists.

entries.name: Ferdinand Lassalle
entries.desc: Ferdinand Lassalle was a German jurist, philosopher and socialist activist, an initiator of the social democratic movement in Germany. Born in Breslau to a prosperous Jewish family, he took part in the revolutions of 1848 and had a complex, often antagonistic relationship with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. In 1863 he founded the General German Workers' Association, the first independent German workers' party, which sought socialism through state-aided producers' co-operatives won by universal suffrage, and he negotiated secretly with Otto von Bismarck. He was killed in a duel in 1864; in 1875 his party merged into the Social Democratic Party of Germany.

entries.name: Giovanni Gentile
entries.desc: Giovanni Gentile was an Italian educator, philosopher and politician, born in Castelvetrano, and one of the primary founders of fascism. With Benedetto Croce he was a leading exponent of Italian idealism, and he devised his own system of actual idealism. Called the philosopher of fascism by himself and Benito Mussolini, he wrote the 1925 Manifesto of the Fascist Intellectuals and part of The Doctrine of Fascism of 1932. As Minister for Public Education he introduced the Gentile Reform of 1923, and he was the first editor of the Italian Encyclopedia. He followed Mussolini into the Italian Social Republic and was assassinated by partisans of the Italian resistance in 1944.

entries.name: George Orwell
entries.desc: George Orwell, the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, was an English novelist, essayist, journalist and critic whose work opposed all totalitarianism and supported democratic socialism. Born in Motihari in British India, he joined the Indian Imperial Police in Burma in 1922 and later fought for the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War, where he was wounded in the throat. The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) and Homage to Catalonia (1938) drew on such experiences. He is best known for the allegorical novella Animal Farm (1945) and the dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), whose words such as Big Brother and doublethink entered the English language.

credit.artist: Branch of the National Union of Journalists (BNUJ).

entries.name: Hannah Arendt
entries.desc: Hannah Arendt was a German and American philosopher and political theorist, one of the most influential of the twentieth century. Born to a Jewish family in Linden, she studied under Martin Heidegger and took her doctorate at Heidelberg in 1929. Briefly imprisoned by the Gestapo in 1933, she fled to Paris, escaped detention in France and reached the United States in 1941. The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) established her reputation, followed by The Human Condition (1958) and by On Revolution and Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), whose phrase the banality of evil stirred controversy. She died in 1975, leaving The Life of the Mind unfinished.

entries.name: Index Librorum Prohibitorum
entries.desc: The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, or Index of Forbidden Books, was a changing list of publications that the Catholic Church deemed heretical or contrary to morality, which Catholics were forbidden to print or read. Under Pope Paul IV a Roman Index was published in 1559, banning the entire works of some 550 authors, and from 1571 the Sacred Congregation of the Index kept it up to date. It condemned religious and secular works alike, among them Kepler's Epitome astronomiae Copernicanae and Kant's Critique of Pure Reason. The last edition, of 1948, listed 4,000 titles; in 1966 the Church declared that the Index no longer had the force of ecclesiastical law.

entries.name: Jean-François Champollion
entries.desc: Jean-François Champollion was a French philologist and orientalist, known as the decipherer of Egyptian hieroglyphs and a founding figure of Egyptology. A child prodigy in philology, as a young man he read Coptic, Ancient Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic. In 1822 he published his first breakthrough in reading the hieroglyphs of the Rosetta Stone, showing that Egyptian writing combined phonetic and ideographic signs, and in 1824 his Précis set out the values of its signs. In 1829 he travelled to Egypt and read many texts never studied before. He died in Paris in 1832, aged 41; some faulted him for not crediting the earlier work of Thomas Young.

entries.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
entries.desc: Jean-Paul Sartre was a French philosopher, political activist and writer, a key figure of existentialism and a leading figure in 20th-century French philosophy and Marxism. His principal philosophical work, Being and Nothingness (1943), centred on the conflict between bad faith and an authentic way of being, and his lecture Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946) introduced his thought. Drafted and captured during World War II, he co-founded the resistance group Socialisme et Liberté and, after the war, the journal Les Temps modernes. He supported anti-colonial movements and condemned French policies in Algeria, and in 1964 was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, which he tried to refuse.

entries.name: Haskalah
entries.desc: The Haskalah, often called the Jewish Enlightenment, was an intellectual movement among the Jews of Central and Eastern Europe that arose in the 1770s as its followers, the Maskilim, engaged with the ideas of the Age of Enlightenment. Its first centre was Berlin, around Moses Mendelssohn; it revived Hebrew as a literary language for secular purposes and pressed for educational and cultural reform and integration into the surrounding societies, clashing with both the rabbinic elite and radical assimilationists. Its last stage ended late in the 19th century, after the 1881 pogroms in Imperial Russia turned many Maskilim towards proto-Zionist groups such as Hibbat Zion.

entries.name: John Adams
entries.desc: John Adams was a Founding Father and the second president of the United States, serving from 1797 to 1801 after two terms as its first vice president. A Massachusetts lawyer, he defended British soldiers charged after the Boston Massacre, and as a delegate to the Continental Congress helped Thomas Jefferson draft the Declaration of Independence. He was a diplomat in France and the Netherlands during the Revolutionary War and the first United States ambassador to Great Britain. As president he signed the Alien and Sedition Acts and fought an undeclared naval war with France, losing the election of 1800 to Jefferson. He died in 1826, on the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration.

entries.name: Joseph Needham
entries.desc: Joseph Needham was a British biochemist, historian of science and sinologist who began the multivolume Science and Civilisation in China. He studied at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and first worked on embryology, publishing Chemical Embryology in 1931. Taught Chinese by Lu Gwei-djen, he directed the Sino-British Science Co-operation Office in Chongqing from 1942 to 1946. In 1948 he proposed to Cambridge University Press a book on science in China that grew into a long series of volumes, fifteen of them written by himself. He drew attention to what became known as the Needham Question, of why China ceded its leadership in science and technology to Western countries.

entries.name: Josiah Wedgwood
entries.desc: Josiah Wedgwood was an English potter, entrepreneur and abolitionist who founded the Wedgwood company in 1759 and led the industrialisation of European pottery manufacture. Through systematic experiment he developed improved pottery bodies, among them creamware, black basalt and jasperware, and his Etruria Works opened in 1769. A pioneer of modern marketing, he used London showrooms, direct mail, money-back guarantees and illustrated catalogues. He was elected to the Royal Society in 1783 for a pyrometer to measure kiln temperatures, and made the anti-slavery medallion Am I Not a Man and a Brother? He was the grandfather of Charles and Emma Darwin.

entries.name: July Revolution
entries.desc: The July Revolution of 1830, also called the Three Glorious Days, overthrew Charles X, the Bourbon king of France, and brought his cousin Louis Philippe, Duke of Orléans, to the throne. On 25 July 1830 Charles issued the July Ordinances, which dissolved the Chamber of Deputies, suspended the liberty of the press and excluded the commercial middle class from future elections. Parisians rose in three days of fighting from 27 July, and on 29 July they took the Hôtel de Ville. On 2 August Charles abdicated and left for Great Britain. The revolution replaced hereditary right with popular sovereignty under the July Monarchy, which fell in 1848.

entries.name: Langston Hughes
entries.desc: Langston Hughes was an American poet, social activist, novelist, playwright and columnist from Joplin, Missouri, an early innovator of jazz poetry and a leader of the Harlem Renaissance. His poem The Negro Speaks of Rivers appeared in The Crisis in 1921, and his first collection, The Weary Blues, in 1926. He also wrote plays, short stories, novels and nonfiction, and from 1943 published stories about Jesse B. Semple, an everyday black man in Harlem. From 1942 to 1962, as the civil rights movement grew, he wrote a weekly column for The Chicago Defender. He died in New York City in 1967 after surgery related to prostate cancer.

entries.name: Lin Biao
entries.desc: Lin Biao was a Chinese military commander and politician, ranked third among the Ten Marshals of the People's Republic of China. Pivotal to the Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War, he commanded the Liaoshen and Pingjin campaigns and led the People's Liberation Army into Beijing. Minister of National Defense from 1959, he directed the compilation of the Quotations from Chairman Mao Zedong, the Little Red Book, and helped build Mao Zedong's cult of personality; in 1966 he was designated Mao's sole successor. He died in 1971 when his aircraft crashed near Öndörkhaan, Mongolia, in circumstances that remain disputed, and was posthumously condemned as a traitor.

entries.name: Mikhail Bakunin
entries.desc: Mikhail Bakunin was a Russian revolutionary anarchist and political philosopher, among the most influential figures of anarchism. Born into a noble family at Pryamukhino in the Tver Governorate, he took part in the 1848 Prague and 1849 Dresden uprisings, was sentenced to death and extradited several times, and escaped from exile in Siberia via Japan and the United States to London. In 1868 he joined the International Workingmen's Association, where he led the anarchist faction against Karl Marx until his expulsion in 1872. He argued that Marxist states would be one-party dictatorships ruling over the proletariat, and his book God and the State remains in print.

entries.name: Michel Aflaq
entries.desc: Michel Aflaq was a Syrian philosopher, sociologist and Arab nationalist, considered by several Ba'athists to be the principal founder of Ba'athist thought. Born into a middle-class Orthodox Christian family in Damascus, he studied at the Sorbonne, and in 1940 founded with Salah al-Din al-Bitar the Arab Ihya Movement, which merged with Zaki al-Arsuzi's group in 1947 to form the Arab Ba'ath Party. His Ba'athism held that the Arab world must be unified into one Arab Nation, and joined Arab socialism to secularism. Ousted in the 1966 Syrian coup d'état, he went to Iraq, where he was Secretary General of the Iraqi-led Ba'ath Party from 1968 until his death in 1989, without de facto power.

entries.name: Mishneh Torah
entries.desc: The Mishneh Torah is a code of Rabbinic Jewish religious law (halakha) by Maimonides, compiled between 1170 and 1180 CE while he was living in Egypt and regarded as his magnum opus. Written in Hebrew and divided into fourteen books, it is the only medieval-era work that details all of Jewish observance, including the laws that apply only when the Temple in Jerusalem is in existence. Maimonides intended a complete statement of the Oral Law, so that a reader who had mastered the Written Torah and this code would need no other book. Early critics objected to its absence of sources and feared it would supersede study of the Talmud, but it remains an important work in Judaism.

credit.artist: Maimonides (text); Isaac (copist), Matteo di Ser Cambio (illumination)

entries.name: Muhammad Iqbal
entries.desc: Sir Muhammad Iqbal was an Islamic philosopher and poet of British India, among the most influential Muslim thinkers of the 20th century. Born in Sialkot, Punjab, he studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, qualified as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn and earned a PhD in philosophy in Munich in 1908, and he wrote in Urdu and Persian such works as Asrar-e-Khudi and Bang-e-Dara. In his Allahabad Address of 1930 to the All-India Muslim League he set out a political framework for the Muslim-majority regions of northwestern India. Pakistan, established in 1947, nine years after his death, honours him as its national poet.

entries.name: Nag Hammadi library
entries.desc: The Nag Hammadi library is a collection of early Christian and Gnostic texts discovered near the Upper Egyptian town of Nag Hammadi in 1945. Twelve leather-bound papyrus codices and a tractate from a thirteenth, buried in a sealed jar, were found by a farmer, Muhammed al-Samman, and others; they hold 52 mostly Gnostic treatises in Coptic, three works of the Corpus Hermeticum and part of Plato's Republic. The manuscripts date from the 3rd and 4th centuries, and among them is the only complete text of the Gospel of Thomas. Some scholars hold that they belonged to a nearby Pachomian monastery. The codices are now housed in the Coptic Museum in Cairo.

entries.name: Nathuram Godse
entries.desc: Nathuram Godse was a Hindu nationalist from Maharashtra who assassinated Mahatma Gandhi, shooting him in the chest three times at point blank range at a multi-faith prayer meeting in Birla House, New Delhi, on 30 January 1948. A member of the Hindu Mahasabha and of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), he popularised the works of his mentor Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, who had formulated the ideology of Hindutva. He had plotted the killing with Narayan Apte and six others, and claimed that Gandhi had favoured the political demands of Indian Muslims during the partition of India. He was sentenced to death and executed at the Ambala Central Jail on 15 November 1949.

entries.name: New Left
entries.desc: The New Left was a broad political movement of activists in the Western world that emerged from the counterculture of the 1960s and continued through the 1970s. It campaigned on social issues such as feminism, gay rights, drug policy reform and gender relations, where the traditional left had put economic goals first. The sociologist C. Wright Mills popularised the term in a 1960 open letter, and in Britain New Left Review was founded the same year. In the United States the movement centred on campus protest, above all the Students for a Democratic Society, whose 1962 Port Huron Statement called for participatory democracy, and on opposition to the Vietnam War; by 1968 it had begun to split.

entries.name: Claude McKay
entries.desc: Claude McKay was a Jamaican-American writer and poet and a central figure in the Harlem Renaissance. He moved to New York City in 1914, and in 1919 wrote the sonnet If We Must Die in response to the wave of white-on-black race riots and lynchings that followed the First World War. His poetry collection Harlem Shadows (1922) was among the first books of the Harlem Renaissance, and his novel Home to Harlem (1928) was a best-seller that won the Harmon Gold Award for Literature. A member of the Industrial Workers of the World and co-editor of The Liberator, he visited the Soviet Union in 1922–1923 but left, critical of the regime's authoritarian bent.

entries.name: Anna Walentynowicz
entries.desc: Anna Walentynowicz was a Polish trade unionist and co-founder of Solidarity, the first recognised independent trade union in the Eastern Bloc. She worked at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk from 1950, first as a welder and later as a crane operator. Her firing in August 1980 ignited the strike at the shipyard, which set off a wave of strikes across Poland; the Interfactory Strike Committee based there became Solidarity, and by September more than one million workers were on strike. Called by some the mother of independent Poland, she was awarded the Order of the White Eagle in 2006 and was killed in the 2010 Polish Air Force Tu-154 crash near Smolensk.

entries.name: Imperial Aramaic
entries.desc: Imperial Aramaic is a term coined by modern scholars for a historical variety of Aramaic, also called Egyptian Aramaic because most surviving examples were found in Egypt. In its wider sense it names the phase from the middle of the 8th century BCE to the end of the 4th century BCE, when Aramaic served as a language of public life and administration in the late Neo-Assyrian Empire, the Neo-Babylonian Empire and the Achaemenid Empire; others restrict it to the Achaemenid period. The Elephantine papyri and ostraca are its largest group of records. Its script gave rise to the Aramaic-derived alphabets of the East, among them Syriac, Palmyrene and Mandaic.

entries.name: Lucretia Mott
entries.desc: Lucretia Mott was an American Quaker, abolitionist, women's rights activist and social reformer. Excluded with other women from the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London in 1840, she formed the idea of reforming the position of women in society, and in 1848 Jane Hunt invited her to the meeting that led to the Seneca Falls Convention, where the Declaration of Sentiments was written. A Quaker preacher in her early adulthood, she advocated the vote for black people, both male and female, and her home with her husband James Mott was a stop on the Underground Railroad. She helped found the Female Medical College of Pennsylvania and Swarthmore College.

entries.name: Henri de Saint-Simon
aka: Claude Henri de Rouvroy, Comte de Saint-Simon
entries.desc: Henri de Saint-Simon was a French political, economic and socialist theorist whose thought influenced politics, economics, sociology and the philosophy of science. He fought alongside the Marquis de Lafayette in the American Revolution and was imprisoned during the Terror until 1794. His ideology, Saint-Simonianism, held that the needs of an industrial class of all productive workers, from bankers and scientists to manual labourers, must be met against an idling class, and that merit-based hierarchies of managers and scientists should lead. Marx and Engels counted him among the utopian socialists; his last work, Le Nouveau Christianisme, appeared in 1825, shortly before his death.
links: Claude Henri de Rouvroy, Comte de Saint-Simon

entries.name: Peter Kropotkin
entries.desc: Peter Kropotkin was a Russian anarchist political philosopher and geographer, a proponent of anarchist communism. Born into an aristocratic land-owning family, he attended the Page Corps and served as an officer in Siberia, where he took part in geological expeditions. Imprisoned for his activism in 1874, he escaped two years later and spent 41 years in exile in Switzerland, France and England. He argued for a decentralised communist society of voluntary associations of self-governing communities and worker-run enterprises, in The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902). He returned to Russia in 1917 but was disappointed by the Bolshevik state.

entries.name: Emma Goldman
entries.desc: Emma Goldman was a Russian-born anarchist revolutionary, political activist and writer who played a pivotal role in the development of anarchist political philosophy in North America and Europe. Born in Kaunas to a Lithuanian Jewish family, she immigrated to the United States in 1885 and lectured on anarchism, women's rights and social issues; with Alexander Berkman she planned the 1892 attempt on the life of Henry Clay Frick. She founded the journal Mother Earth in 1906, was jailed in 1917 for conspiring against the draft and was deported to Russia in December 1919. After the Kronstadt rebellion she denounced the Soviet Union, and later supported the anarchist revolution in Spain.

entries.name: Rosa Luxemburg
entries.desc: Rosa Luxemburg was a Polish and naturalised-German Marxist theorist and revolutionary, a leading theorist of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD). Born in Russian-ruled Poland to a secular Jewish family, she co-founded the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland and Lithuania and moved to Germany in 1898. In Social Reform or Revolution? (1900) she answered the reformism of Eduard Bernstein, and in The Accumulation of Capital (1913) she tied imperialism to capitalism's need to expand. Imprisoned for most of World War I for opposing it, she co-founded the Spartacus League and the Communist Party of Germany, and was killed by the Freikorps after the Spartacist uprising of 1919.

entries.name: Eduard Bernstein
entries.desc: Eduard Bernstein was a German social democratic politician and socialist theorist, known for the reformist challenge to Marxism called evolutionary socialism or revisionism. Born into a lower-middle-class Jewish family in Berlin, he lived in exile in Switzerland and London under the Anti-Socialist Laws and became a close associate of Friedrich Engels. In Evolutionary Socialism (1899) he disputed Marx's predictions of the collapse of capitalism and argued for gradual reform through democratic institutions. The SPD condemned his views but largely followed them in practice. He co-founded the anti-war Independent Social Democratic Party (USPD) during World War I, and later sat in the Reichstag.

entries.name: Karl Kautsky
entries.desc: Karl Kautsky was an Austrian-born Marxist theorist, for decades the leading theorist of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) and the Second International, often called the Pope of Marxism. Born in Prague, he founded the journal Die Neue Zeit in 1883 and edited it for 35 years, and wrote the theoretical section of the SPD's 1891 Erfurt Program. He defended orthodox Marxism against Eduard Bernstein's revisionism and opposed the revolutionary spontaneity of Rosa Luxemburg. Opposing the war, he co-founded the Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany in 1917, and he denounced the October Revolution as a premature coup. He fled to Amsterdam after the 1938 Anschluss and died there.

entries.name: Antonio Gramsci
entries.desc: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian Marxist philosopher, journalist and politician, a founding member and one-time leader of the Italian Communist Party. Born in Ales on Sardinia, he became a vocal critic of Benito Mussolini and fascism, and was imprisoned in 1926, remaining in prison until shortly before his death in 1937. There he wrote more than 30 notebooks and 3,000 pages of history and analysis, the Prison Notebooks, on subjects from the history of Italy to fascism, Fordism and popular culture. He is best known for his theory of cultural hegemony, which describes how the ruling capitalist class uses cultural institutions and ideology, rather than violence or coercion, to keep its power.

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.desc: Herbert Spencer was an English polymath active as a philosopher, psychologist, biologist, sociologist and anthropologist. Born in Derby, he worked as a civil engineer and as sub-editor of The Economist, and published his first book, Social Statics, in 1851. He coined the expression survival of the fittest in Principles of Biology (1864), after reading Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, and spent most of his later life on his System of Synthetic Philosophy, which applied evolution to biology, psychology, sociology and morality. Of great authority in his lifetime, he lost influence sharply after 1900, and his name became closely linked with Social Darwinism.

entries.name: Thomas Paine
entries.desc: Thomas Paine was an English-born American Founding Father, political philosopher and statesman whose pamphlets Common Sense (1776) and The American Crisis (1776–1783) helped inspire the colonists to declare independence from Great Britain. Born in Thetford, Norfolk, he came to the British American colonies in 1774 with the help of Benjamin Franklin. His Rights of Man (1791), a defence of the French Revolution against Edmund Burke, led to his conviction in absentia for seditious libel in 1792. Elected to the French National Convention, he was held in the Luxembourg Prison from December 1793 to November 1794, and in The Age of Reason he advocated Deism and argued against Christian doctrine.

entries.name: Friedrich Hayek
entries.desc: Friedrich Hayek was an Austrian economist and philosopher of the Austrian school of economics, known for his contributions to political economy, political philosophy and intellectual history. He earned doctorates from the University of Vienna, became a British national in 1938, and taught at the London School of Economics, the University of Chicago and later at Salzburg and Freiburg. His most popular work, The Road to Serfdom (1944), has been republished many times, and his account of how prices communicate information led to his share of the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Gunnar Myrdal. He rejected the label conservative, preferring classical liberal or libertarian.

credit.artist: The original uploader was DickClarkMises at English Wikipedia .

entries.name: The Federalist Papers
entries.desc: The Federalist Papers are a collection of 85 articles and essays written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay under the collective pseudonym Publius to promote the ratification of the Constitution of the United States. The first 77 appeared in New York newspapers between October 1787 and April 1788, and the whole was published in two volumes by J. & A. McLean in 1788. Among them, Madison's No. 10 argues against rule by a majority faction and for a large republic, his No. 51 for checks and balances, and Hamilton's No. 78 lays the groundwork for judicial review by federal courts. The Constitution was ratified by the required nine states on June 21, 1788.

credit.artist: Publius (pseudonym) [ Alexander Hamilton , John Jay , James Madison ].

entries.name: Two Treatises of Government
entries.desc: Two Treatises of Government is the principal work of political philosophy of the English philosopher John Locke, published anonymously in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution but likely drafted in 1680-81 during the Exclusion Crisis. The First Treatise refutes, sentence by sentence, Robert Filmer's Patriarcha, which argued for a divinely ordained, hereditary, absolute monarchy. The Second Treatise sets out a society based on natural rights and contract theory, in which government requires the consent of the governed and, under limited circumstances, the people may overthrow the ruler. The book is a key foundational text in the theory of liberalism.

entries.name: Das Kapital
aka: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy
entries.desc: Das Kapital, or Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, is a foundational text of Marxist theory by Karl Marx, a critical analysis of the capitalist mode of production. Only the first of its three volumes appeared in Marx's lifetime, in 1867; Friedrich Engels completed the others from his manuscripts and published them in 1885 and 1894. Its central argument is that capitalism is driven by the exploitation of labour, whose unpaid work is the ultimate source of surplus value and profit; it sets out a labour theory of value and the idea of commodity fetishism. It became foundational to the international labour movement and to socialist and communist parties, and it remains much debated.
links: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy

entries.name: On Liberty
entries.desc: On Liberty is an essay by the English philosophers Harriet Taylor Mill and John Stuart Mill, published in 1859 under the latter's name. It applies their ethical system of utilitarianism to society and the state, proposing standards for the relationship between authority and liberty. Its harm principle holds that power may rightfully be used over a member of a civilized community against his will only to prevent harm to others. The essay stresses the importance of individuality and warns that democratic ideals may result in the tyranny of the majority. Greatly influential, it has remained in print since its first publication.

credit.artist: John Stuart Mill (author), John W. Parker and Son (publisher)

entries.name: The Feminine Mystique
entries.desc: The Feminine Mystique is a book by the American author Betty Friedan, first published by W. W. Norton in 1963 and widely credited with sparking second-wave feminism in the United States. It grew from a survey Friedan made in 1957 of her former Smith College classmates, many of whom were unhappy with their lives as housewives, and from interviews with other suburban housewives and research into psychology, media and advertising. Friedan coined the phrase feminine mystique for the assumption that women would be fulfilled by housework, marriage, sexual lives and children. A bestseller, it was criticised for focusing on white, middle-class women.

credit.artist: Fred Palumbo , World Telegram staff photographer. Restored by Adam Cuerden

entries.name: Simone de Beauvoir
aka: Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir
entries.desc: Simone de Beauvoir was a French existentialist philosopher, writer, social theorist and feminist activist with a significant influence on feminist existentialism and feminist theory. In 1929 she was placed second in the agrégation in philosophy, after Jean-Paul Sartre, at 21 the youngest person to pass it. Her The Second Sex (1949), a detailed analysis of women's oppression, became a foundational tract of contemporary feminism. She also wrote the novels She Came to Stay (1943) and The Mandarins (1954), and memoirs beginning with Mémoires d'une jeune fille rangée (1958); she received the 1954 Prix Goncourt and the 1975 Jerusalem Prize.

entries.name: Betty Friedan
entries.desc: Betty Friedan was an American feminist writer and activist, born Bettye Naomi Goldstein in Peoria, Illinois, whose 1963 book The Feminine Mystique is often credited with sparking the second wave of American feminism. The book grew from a survey of college graduates she made for her 15th college reunion in 1957 and depicted the role of the full-time homemaker, which she deemed stifling. In 1966 she co-founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) and was elected its first president. In 1970 she organized the nationwide Women's Strike for Equality, and in 1971 she helped establish the National Women's Political Caucus. She died in Washington, D.C., in 2006.

credit.artist: Fred Palumbo , World Telegram staff photographer. Restored by Adam Cuerden

entries.name: Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung
entries.desc: Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung, known in English as the Little Red Book, is a compilation of quotations from the speeches and writings of Mao Zedong, published in China from 1964 to 1979 and widely distributed during the Cultural Revolution. It was first compiled by an office of the PLA Daily as an ideological handbook for the People's Liberation Army. The definitive 1965 version held 427 quotations in 33 thematic chapters, and from August 1966 the People's Publishing House printed it for the public. From the mid-1960s through the mid-1970s it was the most printed book globally. On 12 February 1979 the Chinese Communist Party ordered a halt to its publication.

entries.name: Justicialist Party
entries.desc: The Justicialist Party, also known as the Peronist Party, is a major political party in Argentina and the largest branch within Peronism. It was founded in 1946 by Juan Perón and Eva Perón, uniting the three parties that had supported Perón in the election. Its most consistent base of support has been the General Confederation of Labor, Argentina's largest trade union. All Peronist entities were banned from elections after Perón was overthrown in 1955, until his return to Argentina in 1973. Aside from Juan Perón, eleven presidents of Argentina have belonged to the party, among them Carlos Menem, Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.

entries.name: United Arab Republic
entries.desc: The United Arab Republic was a sovereign state in the Middle East from 1958 to 1971, formed as a political union of Egypt and Syria under the presidency of Gamal Abdel Nasser. It was established on 1 February 1958 at the urging of Syrian leaders, as a first step towards a larger pan-Arab state, and referendums on 21 February approved the merger and Nasser as president. Nasser demanded the dismantling of Syria's political parties, squeezed Syrians out of positions of influence and in 1961 nationalized banks and heavy industry; the backlash led to the Syrian coup of 28 September 1961 and Syria's secession. Egypt kept the name until Anwar Sadat formally dissolved it in September 1971.

entries.name: Hassan al-Banna
aka: Hassan Ahmed Abd al-Rahman Muhammed al-Banna
entries.desc: Hassan al-Banna was an Egyptian schoolteacher and imam who founded the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the largest and most influential Islamist movements. Born in Mahmudiyya in the Nile Delta, he trained at Dar al-Ulum in Cairo and taught at a primary school in Ismailia, where in March 1928 six workers of the Suez Canal Company made him their leader. He held Islam to be a comprehensive system of life and criticized Western materialism and British imperialism. By the late 1930s the Brotherhood had branches in every Egyptian province, and a decade later 500,000 active members. After the government outlawed it in December 1948, he was shot in Cairo and died on 12 February 1949.

entries.name: Sayyid Qutb
entries.desc: Sayyid Qutb was an Egyptian political theorist and revolutionary and a leading member of the Muslim Brotherhood. Raised in the village of Musha in Upper Egypt, he worked as a teacher and literary critic and spent 1948 to 1950 in the United States, whose society he came to see as materialistic. He joined the Brotherhood in the early 1950s and was jailed after an alleged plot to assassinate Gamal Abdel Nasser in 1954; in prison, where he was tortured, he wrote the 30-volume Quran commentary In the Shade of the Qur'an and the manifesto Milestones. He was executed by hanging on 29 August 1966. His ideas on Jahiliyya have highly influenced Islamist and jihadist movements.

credit.artist: The original uploader was أحمد.غامدي.24 at Arabic Wikipedia .

entries.name: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar
entries.desc: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar was an Indian politician and ideologue who developed the Hindu nationalist ideology of Hindutva in his 1923 pamphlet Essentials of Hindutva. As a student in London he was involved with India House, and in 1910 he was arrested and deported to India, where he was sentenced to 50 years of imprisonment in the Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Released in 1924 after a series of mercy petitions, he was restricted to Ratnagiri district until 1937 and then led the Hindu Mahasabha, which endorsed the idea of India as a Hindu Rashtra. In 1948 he was tried over the conspiracy to assassinate Mahatma Gandhi but was acquitted for lack of sufficient evidence.

entries.name: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh
entries.desc: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is an Indian right-wing Hindutva volunteer paramilitary organisation, founded on 27 September 1925 in Nagpur by K. B. Hedgewar, a doctor influenced by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar's Essentials of Hindutva. It set out to unite the Hindu community and establish a Hindu Rashtra, and has been accused of intolerance of minorities, particularly Muslims. It played no role in the Indian independence movement. It was banned in 1948 after Nathuram Godse, a member, assassinated Mahatma Gandhi, again during the Emergency and after the demolition of Babri Masjid in 1992. It leads the Sangh Parivar, which includes the Bharatiya Janata Party.

entries.name: Hindu Mahasabha
entries.desc: The Hindu Mahasabha is a far-right Hindutva political party in India, founded in 1915 at the Kumbh Mela in Haridwar as an umbrella body of regional Hindu Sabhas. Under Madan Mohan Malaviya it worked mainly as a pressure group for orthodox Hindus within the Indian National Congress. In the 1930s it emerged as a distinct party under Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, a fierce opponent of the secular nationalism of the Congress. During World War II it supported the British war effort and briefly formed coalition governments with the Muslim League. Nathuram Godse, who assassinated Mahatma Gandhi, was a member, and after independence the party was soon eclipsed by the Bharatiya Jana Sangh.

entries.name: Republican People's Party
entries.desc: The Republican People's Party (CHP) is the oldest political party in Turkey, founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. It grew out of the resistance groups of the Turkish War of Independence, united at the 1919 Sivas Congress, and was founded as the People's Party in 1923. In the one-party period it carried out sweeping reforms, among them strict secularism, women's suffrage and the switch of written Turkish to the Latin script, while suppressing opposition and Kurdish resistance to assimilation. Its logo, the Six Arrows, stands for the principles of Kemalism. After losing the 1950 election it handed over power peacefully; banned by the military junta of 1980, it was re-established in 1992.

entries.name: The Six Arrows
entries.desc: The Six Arrows are the symbol and flag of Kemalism, the ideology of the Turkish Republican People's Party (CHP), each arrow standing for one of its fundamental pillars: republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. The arrows are believed to have been conceived by İsmail Hakkı Tonguç, a Turkish scientist who made significant contributions to the Turkish education system. The principles of the Six Arrows were added to the Turkish Constitution on 5 February 1937, and from August 1938 the flag was hoisted at all official buildings. Republicanism, the party's main idea, holds that sovereignty belongs to the people.

entries.name: National Fascist Party
entries.desc: The National Fascist Party was the far-right party founded by Benito Mussolini in Rome in November 1921 as the political expression of Italian fascism, reorganising the earlier Italian Fasces of Combat. It ruled the Kingdom of Italy from the March on Rome in 1922, and from 1925 it was effectively the only legal party, a status formalised by a law of 1928. Its Blackshirt squads violently suppressed socialist organisations, and the Socialist leader Giacomo Matteotti was kidnapped and killed by fascist blackshirts. After the Grand Council of Fascism deposed Mussolini on 25 July 1943 the party was banned, and the Constitution of Italy forbids its re-formation.

entries.name: Falange Española de las JONS
aka: Falange Española de las Juntas de Ofensiva Nacional Sindicalista
entries.desc: Falange Española de las JONS was a national syndicalist political party founded in Spain in 1934 by the merger of the Falange Española with the Juntas de Ofensiva Nacional-Sindicalista of Onésimo Redondo and Ramiro Ledesma. Led from October 1934 by José Antonio Primo de Rivera as Jefe Nacional, it set out its programme in the Twenty-Seven Points, and in street violence with the Socialists it formed its own death squads. It won only 0.11% of the votes in the 1936 election. Primo de Rivera was executed in a Republican prison on 20 November 1936, and on 19 April 1937 Francisco Franco merged the party with the Carlists into the FET y de las JONS, the sole legal party of his regime.

entries.name: Herero and Nama genocide
entries.desc: The Herero and Nama genocide was the extermination of the Herero and Nama peoples in German South West Africa (now Namibia) by the German Empire between 1904 and 1908. After the Herero chief Samuel Maharero launched an uprising on 12 January 1904, German forces under Lothar von Trotha routed the Herero at the Battle of Waterberg and drove them into the Omaheke Desert, where a majority died of thirst and starvation; on 2 October Trotha issued an extermination order. The surviving Herero were held in concentration camps, where around half of those captured died, as did most Nama who surrendered. Around 40,000 to 80,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama died. Germany acknowledged the genocide in 2015.

entries.name: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
aka: Imperialism, the Newest Stage of Capitalism
entries.desc: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism is a book by Vladimir Lenin, written in Zürich in 1916 and published in Petrograd in 1917, originally as Imperialism, the Newest Stage of Capitalism. It argues that capitalism had moved from competition to monopoly, that the merger of bank and industrial capital produced finance capital and a financial oligarchy, and that the export of capital to undeveloped countries divided the world among the great powers. Lenin presented the First World War as a predatory war among empires. He drew on Imperialism: A Study (1902) by John A. Hobson and Finance Capital (1910) by Rudolf Hilferding, and rejected Karl Kautsky's theory of ultra-imperialism.
links: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism

entries.name: Bolsheviks
entries.desc: The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, were a radical faction of the Marxist Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) that split with the Mensheviks at the Second Party Congress in 1903, where Lenin argued for a smaller party of professional revolutionaries. Their name came from the Russian word for majority, as Lenin's faction won the votes on most important issues. The faction became a separate party in 1912, seized power in the October Revolution of 1917 and suppressed opposition during the Russian Civil War; after 1921 it was the sole legal party. Renamed the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in 1918, it became the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in 1952.

entries.name: Reflections on the Revolution in France
entries.desc: Reflections on the Revolution in France is a political pamphlet by the British statesman Edmund Burke, published in November 1790, which contrasts the French Revolution with the unwritten British Constitution. Burke wrote it as a letter to the French aristocrat Charles-Jean-François Depont, drafting it after reading Richard Price's speech A Discourse on the Love of Our Country. He argued that the Revolution would end disastrously because its abstract foundations ignored the complexities of human nature and society. Thirteen thousand copies were bought in the first five weeks. It drew replies from Mary Wollstonecraft and Thomas Paine, and it is a defining tract of modern conservatism.
links: Reflections on the Revolution in France

entries.name: Joseph de Maistre
entries.desc: Joseph de Maistre was a Savoyard lawyer, diplomat and political philosopher, remembered as one of the intellectual forefathers of modern conservatism. Born at Chambéry, a subject of the King of Piedmont-Sardinia, he was at first a liberal, but turned against the French Revolution after the August Decrees of 1789 and fled Chambéry when a French revolutionary army took it in 1792. As ambassador to the Russian Empire in Saint Petersburg he wrote his most influential works, and from 1817 he was minister of state in Turin. In Considerations on France (1796) he argued that the Revolution was divine punishment, and he defended monarchy and the ultimate authority of the Pope.

entries.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
entries.desc: Johann Gottlieb Fichte was a German philosopher and a founding figure of German idealism, which developed from the writings of Immanuel Kant. Born in Rammenau, Upper Lusatia, the son of a ribbon weaver, he first won attention with Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation (1792), published without his name and at first believed to be a new work by Kant. He taught at the University of Jena from 1794 until his dismissal for atheism in 1799, then moved to Berlin. His Addresses to the German Nation (1807–1808) gave him a reputation as one of the fathers of German nationalism. He was elected rector of the new University of Berlin and died of typhus in 1814.

entries.name: Friedrich Engels
entries.desc: Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, social and political theorist and revolutionary socialist, born in Barmen, Prussia, to a prosperous mercantile family. Sent to Manchester in 1842 to work in a cotton mill, he wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). From 1844 he worked with Karl Marx, with whom he co-authored The Communist Manifesto (1848) and developed what became known as Marxism. He fought in the Revolutions of 1848, then supported the Marx family from the family firm of Ermen & Engels. After Marx died in 1883 he completed the second and third volumes of Das Kapital; he died of cancer in London in 1895.

entries.name: Milton Friedman
entries.desc: Milton Friedman was an American economist and statistician, born in Brooklyn, New York City, who received the 1976 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. A leader of the Chicago school of economics, he introduced the permanent income hypothesis and promoted monetarism, arguing for a steady, small expansion of the money supply. With Anna Schwartz he wrote A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960 (1963), which traced the Great Depression to a severe monetary contraction. His book Capitalism and Freedom (1962) argued for free markets, school vouchers and a negative income tax, and he advised Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher.

entries.name: Pope John Paul II
entries.desc: Pope John Paul II, born Karol Józef Wojtyła in Wadowice, Poland, was head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 16 October 1978 until his death in 2005, the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI in the 16th century. Archbishop of Kraków from 1964, he visited 129 countries as pope and canonised 483 saints. His 1979 visit to Poland contributed to the formation of the Solidarity movement in 1980, and he has been credited with helping to end communist rule in Europe. He survived being shot by Mehmet Ali Ağca in 1981, and has been criticised over his response to the sexual abuse of children by priests. He was canonised in 2014.

entries.name: The Second Sex
entries.desc: The Second Sex is a 1949 book by the French existentialist philosopher Simone de Beauvoir on the treatment of women in her own society and throughout history, written in about 14 months between 1946 and 1949 and published in two volumes, Facts and Myths and Lived Experience. Beauvoir argued that man is treated as the default and woman as the Other. The first French edition sold around 22,000 copies in a week, and the Vatican placed it on its List of Prohibited Books. Translated into 40 languages, it is regarded as a groundbreaking work of feminist philosophy and a starting point of second-wave feminism.

entries.name: Isaiah Berlin
entries.desc: Sir Isaiah Berlin was a British social and political theorist, philosopher and historian of ideas, born into a Russian-Jewish family in Riga in 1909. As a boy in Petrograd he witnessed the Russian Revolution, and in 1921 his family moved to England. From 1957 to 1967 he was Chichele Professor of Social and Political Theory at Oxford; his inaugural lecture, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958), set negative liberty, the absence of interference, against positive liberty, self-mastery. He became the founding president of Wolfson College, Oxford, in 1966, and his work on liberal theory and value pluralism, and his opposition to Marxism and communism, has had a lasting influence.

entries.name: Bertrand Russell
entries.desc: Bertrand Russell, 3rd Earl Russell, was an English mathematician and philosopher and a founder of analytic philosophy, who did pioneering work in logic, set theory and the philosophy of language. A grandson of the prime minister John Russell, 1st Earl Russell, he studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, and with Alfred North Whitehead wrote Principia Mathematica (1910–1913), a major attempt to reduce the whole of mathematics to logic. He went to prison for his pacifism during the First World War, later condemned the United States' involvement in the Vietnam War and campaigned for nuclear disarmament. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950.

entries.name: Robert Peel
entries.desc: Sir Robert Peel was a British Conservative statesman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in 1834–1835 and 1841–1846 and is regarded as the father of modern British policing. As Home Secretary he reformed the criminal law and founded the Metropolitan Police, whose officers became known as bobbies and peelers, and backed the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829. His Tamworth Manifesto of 1834 laid down principles on which the modern Conservative Party is based. In his second ministry he cut tariffs and introduced a 3 per cent income tax, and after the outbreak of the Great Irish Famine he joined with Whigs and Radicals to repeal the Corn Laws, which led to his resignation in 1846.

entries.name: Weimar Constitution
entries.desc: The Weimar Constitution, formally the Constitution of the German Reich, governed Germany during the Weimar Republic. Drafted chiefly by Hugo Preuss and adopted by the National Assembly at Weimar on 31 July 1919 by 262 votes to 75, it created a federal semi-presidential republic with a Reichstag elected by universal suffrage and proportional representation, and guaranteed freedom of speech and of religion. Its Article 48 gave the president broad emergency powers; it was invoked 205 times before Adolf Hitler became chancellor and in 1933 was the basis of the Reichstag Fire Decree. Set aside in practice by the Enabling Act of 1933, the constitution was replaced in 1949.

entries.name: Ziya Gökalp
entries.desc: Ziya Gökalp was a Turkish sociologist, writer, poet and politician, born in Diyarbakır in 1876, who is considered the father of Turkish nationalism. A chief ideologist of the Committee of Union and Progress, he drew on Émile Durkheim to reject Ottomanism and Islamism in favour of Turkish nationalism, advocated the Turkification of the Ottoman Empire and regarded Greeks, Armenians, Assyrians and Jews as an undesirable foreign body in the national state; many historians have suggested that his nationalism contributed to the Armenian genocide. Exiled to Malta from 1919 to 1921, he wrote The Principles of Turkism (1923), and his ideas shaped the reforms of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

entries.name: Taha Hussein
entries.desc: Taha Hussein was an Egyptian writer, a leading figure of the Arab Renaissance and of modernism in the Arab world, known as the Dean of Arabic Literature. Blind from the age of two, he studied at Al-Azhar and the new Cairo University, then at Montpellier and the Sorbonne, which awarded him a doctorate on Ibn Khaldun in 1917. His On Pre-Islamic Poetry (1926), which doubted the authenticity of much early Arabic poetry, angered religious scholars, and he lost his post at Cairo University in 1931. An Egyptian nationalist who rejected pan-Arabism, he became Minister of Education in 1950 and called for free education; in the West he is best known for his autobiography Al-Ayyam (The Days).

entries.name: Wole Soyinka
entries.desc: Wole Soyinka is a Nigerian writer, playwright and poet, born in 1934 into an Anglican Yoruba family in Aké, Abeokuta, who in 1986 became the first African laureate of the Nobel Prize in Literature. After studying at Ibadan and Leeds, he wrote plays such as The Swamp Dwellers and The Lion and the Jewel, and many of his works reflect Nigeria's history and political struggles. During the Nigerian Civil War the federal government declared him a traitor and imprisoned him for 22 months, the subject of his prison notes The Man Died (1972). His Nobel lecture, devoted to Nelson Mandela, was an outspoken criticism of apartheid; in 2024 the National Arts Theatre was renamed after him.

entries.name: Bhagat Singh
entries.desc: Bhagat Singh was an Indian anti-colonial revolutionary, born in the Punjab in 1907, who became a martyr and folk hero in Northern India after his execution at the age of 23. A member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, in December 1928 he and Shivaram Rajguru shot dead the junior police officer John P. Saunders in Lahore, mistaking him for the superintendent James Scott, whom they held responsible for the death of Lala Lajpat Rai. In April 1929 he and Batukeshwar Dutt set off two low-intensity bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi and let themselves be arrested, and his hunger strike in jail won wide sympathy. He was convicted of murder and hanged in March 1931.

entries.name: Alain LeRoy Locke
entries.desc: Alain LeRoy Locke was an American writer, philosopher and educator, known as the philosophical architect, or Dean, of the Harlem Renaissance. Born in Philadelphia in 1885, he graduated from Harvard in 1907 and that year became the first African-American Rhodes Scholar; at Oxford several colleges refused him before Hertford College admitted him. He took his PhD in philosophy at Harvard in 1918 and chaired the department of philosophy at Howard University, where he taught the first classes on race relations. In 1925 he expanded a special issue of Survey Graphic into The New Negro, a collection of writings by African Americans that became a landmark in Black literature.

entries.name: Claude Monet
entries.desc: Claude Monet was a French painter and a founder of Impressionism, its most consistent practitioner in painting nature as he perceived it, above all in outdoor landscapes. Raised in Le Havre, he was introduced to plein air painting by Eugène Boudin and studied under Charles Gleyre alongside Auguste Renoir. The movement's name comes from his Impression, Sunrise, shown in 1874 at the First Impressionist Exhibition, which he and like-minded artists organised as an alternative to the Salon. From 1883 he lived at Giverny, where he made a water-lily pond, and he painted the same scenes many times to catch the changing light: haystacks, Rouen Cathedral and the water lilies of his last 20 years.

entries.name: Édouard Manet
entries.desc: Édouard Manet was a French painter, one of the first 19th-century artists to paint modern life and a pivotal figure in the transition from Realism to Impressionism. Born in Paris in 1832, he studied under the academic painter Thomas Couture from 1850 to 1856 and copied Velázquez and Titian in the Louvre. His Luncheon on the Grass (1863) and Olympia (1865) caused great controversy with critics and the Academy but were praised by progressive artists, and they are considered to mark the start of modern art. His last major work, A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, hung in the Salon in 1882; he died in Paris in April 1883, 11 days after his left foot was amputated because of gangrene.

entries.name: Edgar Degas
entries.desc: Edgar Degas was a French artist known for his pastels and oil paintings, more than half of his works depicting dancers. Trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and in Italy, he first meant to be a history painter, then brought its methods to contemporary subjects such as ballet dancers, bathing women, racehorses and jockeys. Regarded as a founder of Impressionism, he helped organise the eight Impressionist exhibitions of 1874–1886 and showed in all but one, yet he rejected the term and preferred to be called a realist. The Dreyfus Affair intensified his antisemitism; after 1890 his eyesight worsened, and he apparently stopped working in 1912.

entries.name: Camille Pissarro
entries.desc: Camille Pissarro was a Danish-French Impressionist and Neo-Impressionist painter, born in 1830 at Charlotte Amalie on Saint Thomas in the Danish West Indies. He learned from Gustave Courbet and Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot, and in 1873 helped establish a collective society of fifteen artists, becoming the figure who held the group together; he is the only artist who showed at all eight Paris Impressionist exhibitions, from 1874 to 1886. At 54 he took up the Neo-Impressionist style alongside Georges Seurat and Paul Signac, and he acted as a father figure to Cézanne, Seurat, Gauguin and Van Gogh. Éragny was his principal home until he died in Paris in 1903.

entries.name: Augusta Savage
entries.desc: Augusta Savage was an American sculptor of the Harlem Renaissance and a teacher of a generation of artists. Born Augusta Fells in Jacksonville, Florida, in 1892, she studied at Cooper Union in New York from 1921; in 1923 a summer school at Fontainebleau withdrew its offer when its American committee learned she was Black, the first of her many public fights for equal rights. Her Savage Studio of Arts and Crafts taught Jacob Lawrence, Norman Lewis and Gwendolyn Knight, and in 1937 she became director of the Harlem Community Art Center. Her 16-foot plaster Lift Every Voice and Sing, or The Harp, made for the 1939 New York World's Fair, was destroyed when the fair closed.

entries.name: Ten Commandments
entries.desc: The Ten Commandments, or Decalogue, are religious and ethical directives which according to the Hebrew Bible God gave to Moses. The biblical narrative tells that God revealed them to the Israelites at Mount Sinai and gave Moses two stone tablets, which he broke on seeing the worship of a golden calf, then a second set, placed in the Ark of the Covenant. The text appears in three distinct versions, at Exodus 20, Deuteronomy 5 and the Ritual Decalogue of Exodus 34, divided into ten commandments in different ways by different traditions. They are the foundational core of Jewish law, and most Christian traditions regard them as divinely authoritative.
