entries.name: Declaration of Sentiments
entries.desc: The Declaration of Sentiments, or Declaration of Rights and Sentiments, is the document signed in 1848 by 68 women and 32 men at the Seneca Falls Convention in New York, the first women's rights convention organised by women. Its principal author, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, an organiser of the convention with Lucretia Mott, modelled it on the United States Declaration of Independence, declaring that all men and women are created equal. It listed women's grievances, among them the denial of the elective franchise, of property and of education, and demanded their immediate admission to all the rights of citizens. Frederick Douglass's support helped pass the convention's resolutions.

entries.name: First Zionist Congress
entries.desc: The First Zionist Congress was the inaugural congress of the Zionist Organization, held in the Stadtcasino in Basel on August 29–31, 1897. Convened and chaired by Theodor Herzl, the founder of the modern Zionist movement, it drew 208 participants from 17 countries, over half of them from Eastern Europe; planned for Munich, it was moved to Basel because of opposition from Orthodox and Reform community leaders. The Congress founded the Zionist Organization and adopted the Basel Program, which stated that Zionism sought to establish a home for the Jewish people in Palestine secured under public law. Seventeen women attended but had no vote until the Second Zionist Congress.

entries.name: Defiance Campaign
entries.desc: The Defiance Campaign against Unjust Laws was a campaign against apartheid, presented by the African National Congress at a conference in Bloemfontein in December 1951 and launched on 26 June 1952. It was the first large-scale, multi-racial political mobilisation against apartheid laws under a common leadership: volunteers burned their pass books, entered places reserved for whites and refused to defend themselves in court. Over 2,000 people were arrested in October 1952 alone, and on 9 November police in Kimberley killed 14 protesters. The government answered with stiff penalties and the Public Safety Act, and Albert Luthuli called the campaign off in April 1953.

entries.name: Congress Alliance
entries.desc: The Congress Alliance was a multi-racial anti-apartheid coalition of the 1950s in South Africa, led by the African National Congress and committed to majority rule. Its National Action Council, of the ANC, the South African Indian Congress, the South African Congress of Trade Unions, the Coloured People's Congress, the Congress of Democrats and the Communist Party, met at Tongaat on 23 June 1955 and planned the Congress of the People at Kliptown on 26 June 1955, where the Freedom Charter was read in English, Sotho and Xhosa. In December 1956 many leaders, Nelson Mandela among them, were arrested and charged with treason; the Treason Trial ended in 1961 with the acquittal of all charged.

entries.name: Ahura Mazda
entries.desc: Ahura Mazda, also known as Ormazd and Horomazes, is the principal God and sky deity of Zoroastrianism and the spirit most often invoked in the Yasna; the words Ahura and Mazda mean lord and wisdom. Some historians hold that his worship existed before Zoroaster, who according to Zoroastrian tradition was led into his presence in a vision at the age of 30. His first notable invocation is in the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great, and until Artaxerxes II he was invoked alone in all extant royal inscriptions, then in a triad with Mithra and Anahita. Images of him from the 5th century BCE were eventually removed under an iconoclastic movement supported by the Sasanian dynasty.

entries.name: State Shinto
entries.desc: State Shinto was Imperial Japan's ideological use of the folk religion and traditions of Shinto, which emphasised the emperor as a divine being. It emerged at the start of the Meiji era in 1868: the government called Shinto a non-religious patriotic practice and defined shrines as patriotic institutions serving state purposes such as honouring the war dead. The state controlled shrine finances and priests' training; with fewer shrines funded, nearly 80,000 closed or merged; by 1940 priests risked persecution for traditionally religious ceremonies. The term was introduced by the United States in the Shinto Directive of December 1945, which banned the state's ideological use of Shinto.

credit.artist: Bank of the Empire of Japan

entries.name: Shoghi Effendi
entries.desc: Shoghi Effendi was the Guardian of the Baháʼí Faith from 1922 until his death in 1957, the grandson and successor of ʻAbdu'l-Bahá. Born Shoghí Rabbání in Acre in the Ottoman Empire in 1896 or 1897, he studied at the Syrian Protestant College and at Balliol College, Oxford, and on returning to Haifa at the end of 1921 learned that ʻAbdu'l-Bahá's will named him Guardian. As the faith's authorised interpreter he translated the writings of its central figures, built its global administration, sent more than 17,500 letters and began work on a Baháʼí World Center in Haifa; Baháʼís worldwide grew from 100,000 to 400,000 under his leadership. He died of Asian flu during a visit to London.

entries.name: Universal House of Justice
entries.desc: The Universal House of Justice is the international governing body of the Baháʼí Faith, seated in Haifa, Israel, on the slope of Mount Carmel. Envisioned by Baháʼu'lláh in the Kitáb-i-Aqdas as a body to legislate on matters his writings did not address, it was first elected in 1963 and is elected every five years by the members of the National Spiritual Assemblies, each voting for nine adult men. It guides the worldwide community through multi-year plans and annual Ridván messages and has drawn attention to the persecution of Baháʼís in Iran. Baháʼís regard its decisions as infallible, and its membership is confined to men.

entries.name: Gonur Depe
entries.desc: Gonur Depe is the site of a large early Bronze Age settlement about 60 km north of Mary, ancient Merv, in Turkmenistan, dated from 2400 to 1600 BCE and regarded as the major settlement of the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex. Viktor Sarianidi, who discovered it, excavated it from 1974 to 2013 and uncovered a palace, a fortified mud-brick enclosure and temples with fire altars, which he associated with Zoroastrianism. Its Royal Necropolis held gold, silver and bronze goods and a foal buried on a four-wheeled wagon, radiocarbon-dated to 2250 BCE, and its Large Necropolis more than three thousand graves. The site was most likely abandoned after the Murghab River shifted to the west.

entries.name: Altyndepe
entries.desc: Altyndepe (Turkmen for 'Golden Hill') is a Bronze Age archaeological site of the BMAC near Aşgabat in Turkmenistan. It was inhabited from c. 3200 to 2400 BCE and from c. 2400 to 2000 BCE, as a full urban site; in the late Chalcolithic it had grown into a centre of 25 hectares surrounded by an adobe wall with rectangular watch towers. Its remains include a monumental religious complex with a four-level tower of the Mesopotamian ziggurat type, and Indus Valley finds such as ivory objects and Harappan-type stamp seals. Models of two-wheeled carts from c. 3000 BCE found there are the earliest complete evidence of wheeled transport in Central Asia. Large-scale excavations began in 1965.

entries.name: El Mirador
entries.desc: El Mirador ('The Lookout') is a large pre-Columbian Maya settlement of the Middle and Late Preclassic period in the north of the department of El Petén, Guatemala. It flourished from about the 6th century BCE to the 1st century CE; its La Danta temple, about 72 metres tall and 2,800,000 cubic metres in volume, is one of the largest pyramids in the world. Raised causeways (sacbeob) 20 to 50 metres wide linked it with Nakbe, El Tintal and other cities of the Mirador Basin. The site was abandoned by about 150 CE, perhaps partly through soil erosion caused by deforestation, was reoccupied on a smaller scale around 700 CE and was nearly completely abandoned again by about 900 CE.

entries.name: Edict of Gülhane
entries.desc: The Edict of Gülhane (Gülhane Hatt-ı Şerifi), also called the Tanzimât Fermânı, was a proclamation by the Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid I in 1839 that launched the Tanzimât period of reform in the Ottoman Empire. Issued at the behest of the reformist Grand Vizier Mustafa Reşid Pasha and named after Gülhane Park, where it was first proclaimed, it promised security of life, honour and property, public trials, a regular system of taxation in place of tax farming and reformed conscription, to all subjects whatever their religion. It made royal promises rather than legal changes and was never fully implemented; after the Crimean War it was followed by the Imperial Reform Edict of 1856.

entries.name: Mustafa Reşid Pasha
entries.desc: Mustafa Reşid Pasha was an Ottoman statesman and diplomat, born in Constantinople, known best as the chief architect of the Tanzimat reforms. He served as ambassador to France and the United Kingdom, became minister for foreign affairs in 1837 and played a leading role in the authorship of the Edict of Gülhane of 1839, which opened the Tanzimat era. Between 1845 and 1857 he held the office of Grand Vizier six times, setting up commercial courts and codes on French models, a committee of education meant to reduce the influence of the ulema, and an Academy of Sciences in 1852. He died of a heart attack in 1858, and his protégés Fuad Pasha and Mehmed Emin Âli Pasha carried the reforms on.

entries.name: Ganden Phodrang
entries.desc: The Ganden Phodrang was the Tibetan system of government established by the 5th Dalai Lama in 1642, after the Oirat lord Güshi Khan, founder of the Khoshut Khanate, conferred all spiritual and political power in Tibet on him at a ceremony in Shigatse. It took its name from the Dalai Lamas' residence at Drepung Monastery: Ganden is the Tibetan name for the Tushita heaven and Phodrang means a palace. Lhasa became the capital and the Gelug school held authority. From 1720 Tibet was a protectorate of the Qing, who created the governing council, the Kashag, in 1721. The Ganden Phodrang operated in Lhasa until 1959, when the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India during the Tibetan uprising.

entries.name: Hamza ibn Ali
entries.desc: Hamza ibn Ali ibn Ahmed was an 11th-century Persian Isma'ili missionary and the founding leader of the Druze. Born in Zuzan in Greater Khorasan, he preached a heterodox strand of Isma'ilism in Cairo under the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, teaching from a mosque on the Raydan Canal that God had become incarnate in al-Hakim. Despite opposition from the Isma'ili clergy he set up a parallel hierarchy of missionaries in Egypt and Syria. After al-Hakim's disappearance, most likely his assassination, in February 1021, Hamza's followers were persecuted and he disappeared; his disciple Baha al-Din al-Muqtana resumed the mission in 1027–1042 and finalized the doctrines of the Druze faith.

entries.name: Tawûsî Melek
entries.desc: Tawûsî Melek, the Peacock Angel, is one of the central figures of Yazidism. In Yazidi creation stories God, before creating this world, created seven Divine Beings, also called the Seven Angels, and appointed Tawûsî Melek as their leader; as Lord of this World he is responsible for all that happens in it, good and bad. Yazidis hold him to be an emanation of God and not a fallen angel, and believe that Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir was his incarnation; the peacock is his symbol and a sacred bird. Muslims and followers of other Abrahamic religions have erroneously identified him with Satan, a misconception that incited centuries of violent persecution of the Yazidis as devil-worshippers.

entries.name: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir
aka: Sharaf al-Din Abu al-Fadl Adi ibn Musafir
entries.desc: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir was a 12th-century mystic, ascetic and theologian who is the central saint of the Yazidi religion, regarded as its reformer, renewer or founder. Born in the 1070s at Bait Far near Baalbek, in present-day Lebanon, he studied in Baghdad and settled in the Hakkari mountains before 1111, gathering followers at Lalish. Islamic literature and Western scholarship traditionally describe him as a Sufi mystic of Islamic background, a framing Yazidis reject; in Yazidi belief he is an earthly incarnation of God. The caste structure of Sheikhs, Pirs and Murids is conventionally traced to his reforms. He died in 1162, and his tomb at Lalish is the holiest site in Yazidism.

entries.name: Iolo Morganwg
entries.desc: Edward Williams, better known by his bardic name Iolo Morganwg ('Iolo of Glamorgan'), was a Welsh antiquarian, poet and collector, born near Llancarfan in the Vale of Glamorgan. He was seen as an expert collector of medieval Welsh literature, but after his death it emerged that he had forged several manuscripts, among them poems he attributed to Dafydd ap Gwilym in 1789 and the third series of Welsh Triads in The Myvyrian Archaiology of Wales (1801–1807). In 1792 he founded the Gorsedd, a community of Welsh bards, at Primrose Hill in London, through which he co-opted the Eisteddfod revival. The philosophy of his forgeries has had an enormous impact on neo-Druidism.

entries.name: Mortimer Wheeler
entries.desc: Sir Mortimer Wheeler was a British archaeologist and army officer who directed the National Museum of Wales and the London Museum and in 1934 established the Institute of Archaeology in London. He argued for a scientific and methodical approach to excavation and the recording of stratigraphic context, developing the 'Wheeler method', and excavated Verulamium and the Iron Age hill fort of Maiden Castle. As director-general of the Archaeological Survey of India from 1944 he oversaw excavations at Harappa, Arikamedu and Brahmagiri. His books and broadcasts brought archaeology to a mass audience, though many of his interpretations have since been discredited or reinterpreted.

entries.name: Colin Renfrew
entries.desc: Colin Renfrew, Baron Renfrew of Kaimsthorn, was a British archaeologist, paleolinguist and Conservative peer noted for his work on radiocarbon dating, the prehistory of languages, archaeogenetics, neuroarchaeology and the prevention of looting. In Before Civilisation (1973) he challenged the assumption that prehistoric cultural innovation originated in the Near East and spread to Europe. His Anatolian hypothesis, set out in Archaeology and Language (1987), held that Proto-Indo-European originated about 9,000 years ago in Anatolia and spread with farming, against Marija Gimbutas's Kurgan hypothesis. He was Disney Professor of Archaeology at Cambridge from 1981 to 2004.

credit.artist: Portable Antiquities Scheme from London, England

entries.name: Bhagavata Purana
entries.desc: The Bhagavata Purana, also known as the Srimad Bhagavatam, is one of the eighteen major Puranas (Mahapuranas) of Hinduism and a central text of Vaishnavism. Composed in Sanskrit and traditionally attributed to Veda Vyasa, it promotes bhakti, devotion, towards Krishna, and treats cosmology, genealogy, legend and yoga. Its twelve books hold 335 chapters and 18,000 verses; the tenth, with about 4,000 verses, has been the most popular and widely studied. Scholars date it variously, many placing much of it in the Gupta period and others its final redaction in the 9th or early 10th century. It was the first Purana translated into a European language, in a French version of a Tamil text in 1788.

entries.name: Book of Rites
entries.desc: The Book of Rites, or Liji, is a collection of texts describing the social forms, administrative structures and ceremonial rites of the Zhou dynasty as interpreted in the Warring States period and the early Han dynasty. With the Rites of Zhou and the Book of Etiquette and Rites it forms the Three Li, the ritual part of the Five Classics of the Confucian tradition. Its chapters are of uncertain origin and date, and a copy of its 'Black Robes' chapter was found in a Guodian tomb sealed around 300 BCE. Zheng Xuan's annotated edition of 49 books remains the standard text, and its chapters were the foundation of the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean.

entries.name: Book of Han
entries.desc: The Book of Han is a Chinese history of the Western, or Former, Han dynasty from the first emperor in 206 BCE to the fall of Wang Mang in 23 CE, and one of the Twenty-Four Histories. Begun by Ban Biao as a continuation of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian and recast by his son Ban Gu, it was finished in 111 CE by Ban Gu's sister Ban Zhao, 19 years after he died in prison. In 100 fascicles of annals, tables, treatises and biographies, it was the first history in the annals-biography form to cover a single dynasty and set the model for the official histories until modern times. Its treatise on geography holds the first unambiguous mention of the people of Japan.

credit.source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:前漢書宋福唐郡庠刻宋元遞修本.jpg

entries.name: Great Purge
entries.desc: The Great Purge, or Great Terror, also called the Yezhovshchina, was a political purge in the Soviet Union from 1936 to 1939. After the assassination of Sergei Kirov in 1934, Joseph Stalin launched the show trials known as the Moscow trials, and the NKVD removed Old Bolsheviks such as Nikolai Bukharin, Lev Kamenev and Grigory Zinoviev, officials, party bosses and the Red Army high command. At its peak, from September 1936 to August 1938 under NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov, hundreds of thousands were accused of political crimes and shot or sent to Gulag labour camps, and minorities such as the Volga Germans were deported. Scholars estimate the death toll at 700,000 to 1.2 million.

entries.name: Great Migration
entries.desc: The Great Migration was the movement of six million Black Americans out of the rural Southern United States to the urban Northeast, Midwest and West between 1910 and 1970. It was driven by racial segregation and discrimination under the Jim Crow laws and by lynchings, and drawn by labor shortages in Northern factories during World War I. Historians divide it into a first migration (1910–1940) of about 1.6 million people and a second (1940–1970) of at least five million. Most migrants settled in the largest cities, among them New York City, Chicago, Detroit and Los Angeles, where they built culturally influential communities; by 1970 more than 80% of Black Americans lived in cities.

credit.artist: undetermined; published in The Chicago Defender on September 4, 1920

entries.name: Assembly of Experts
entries.desc: The Assembly of Experts is the deliberative body of Iran empowered to appoint, supervise and dismiss the Supreme Leader of Iran. Its 88 members, all mujtahids, are directly elected for eight-year terms from candidates vetted by the Guardian Council, half of whose members the Supreme Leader appoints, so that many reformist and opposition candidates are excluded. First elected in December 1982 and convened in 1983, it chose Ali Khamenei to succeed Ruhollah Khomeini after his death in 1989. It has never dismissed or questioned the Supreme Leader, and many analysts call it a ceremonial body. In March 2026, after the assassination of Ali Khamenei, it chose his son Mojtaba Khamenei.

entries.name: Peking University
entries.desc: Peking University is a public university in Haidian, Beijing, founded in 1898 as the Imperial University of Peking by royal charter of the Guangxu Emperor during the Hundred Days' Reform; it is the second-oldest university in China after Tianjin University. Renamed in 1912, it was transformed under Cai Yuanpei, president from 1917, into the country's largest institution of higher learning, with a faculty that included Hu Shih, Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and Lu Xun. Its students helped lead the protest of 4 May 1919 against the Treaty of Versailles. In 1952 it merged with Yenching University.

entries.name: Cai Yuanpei
entries.desc: Cai Yuanpei was a Chinese philosopher and politician, born in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, who was an influential figure in the history of modern Chinese education. A founder of the Guangfuhui in 1904 and a member of the Tongmenghui, he studied at Leipzig and became Minister of Education of the new Republic of China in 1912. As president of Peking University from 1917 he recruited Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao and Hu Shih as well as conservative scholars, defended academic freedom and admitted the first women in 1920; in 1919 he resigned in protest when the May Fourth student leaders were jailed. In April 1928 he helped found the Academia Sinica and became its first president. He died in Hong Kong in 1940.

entries.name: Hu Shih
entries.desc: Hu Shih was a Chinese academic, writer, diplomat and politician who contributed to Chinese liberalism and was a leading advocate of written vernacular Chinese. Born in Shanghai, he studied at Cornell and at Columbia under John Dewey, whose translator he became, then lectured at Peking University and became one of the leading intellectuals of the May Fourth and New Culture Movements. He promoted vernacular Chinese in literature in place of Classical Chinese. He was the Republic of China's ambassador to the United States from 1938 to 1942 and, from 1957 until his death, president of the Academia Sinica in Taipei; in the 1950s the Chinese Communist Party campaigned against his thought.

entries.name: Paulette Nardal
entries.desc: Paulette Nardal was a French writer and journalist from Martinique and one of the drivers of the development of black literary consciousness and of the creation of the Négritude genre. In 1920 she was the first black person to study at the Sorbonne, and with her sisters held a salon that brought together black intellectuals from Africa, the Caribbean and the United States; her translations introduced French intellectuals to writers of the Harlem Renaissance. In 1931 she co-founded La Revue du Monde Noir. Injured when her ship was torpedoed in 1939, she returned to Martinique, founded Le Rassemblement féminin in 1944 and later worked at the United Nations.

entries.name: Amy Ashwood Garvey
entries.desc: Amy Ashwood Garvey was a Jamaican Pan-Africanist activist, born in Port Antonio, who with Marcus Garvey founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in 1914 and organized its women's section. In the United States she was secretary of the UNIA's New York branch and in 1919 became one of the first directors of the Black Star Line; she married Garvey that year, and he divorced her in 1922. In London she opened the Florence Mills Social Club with Sam Manning in 1934, and in 1945 she helped organize the 5th Pan-African Congress in Manchester. After the 1958 Notting Hill race riots she co-founded the Association for the Advancement of Coloured People.

entries.name: William Lovett
entries.desc: William Lovett was a British activist and a leader of the Chartist movement, one of the leading London-based artisan radicals of his generation. Born in Newlyn in Cornwall, he worked in London as a cabinet maker, helped form the National Union of the Working Classes in 1831 and in June 1836 founded the London Working Men's Association. In 1838 he and Francis Place drafted the parliamentary bill that was the foundation of the People's Charter. Elected secretary of the first Chartist Convention in 1839, he was convicted of seditious libel over placards condemning the police and held in Warwick Gaol until July 1840. A moral-force Chartist who rejected violence, he then turned to education.

entries.name: Lord Protector
entries.desc: Lord Protector is a title used for a royal prince or noble who protected and defended the realm and governed for a monarch unable to do so, and later for the head of state of the Commonwealth. In England the dukes of Bedford and Gloucester were jointly Lords Protector for Henry VI from 1422, and Richard, Duke of Gloucester held the title in 1483 before taking the throne as Richard III. Under the Instrument of Government of 1653 Oliver Cromwell became Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland for life; his son Richard succeeded him in September 1658 and resigned in May 1659. Since the Restoration the title has not been used in these ways.

entries.name: Seymour Martin Lipset
entries.desc: Seymour Martin Lipset was an American sociologist and political scientist whose work covered political sociology, trade unions, social stratification, public opinion and the conditions for democracy. Born in Harlem to Russian Jewish immigrants, he took a PhD at Columbia University in 1949 and taught at Stanford and Harvard, among others. His 1959 article Some Social Requisites of Democracy set out the Lipset hypothesis that economic development leads to democracy, and Political Man (1960) sold more than 400,000 copies. He alone presided over both the American Political Science Association and the American Sociological Association. A socialist when young, he later moved to the right.

entries.name: Juan José Linz
aka: Juan José Linz Storch de Gracia
entries.desc: Juan José Linz was a German-born Spanish sociologist and political scientist of comparative politics, best known for his work on authoritarian regimes and democratization. Born in Bonn, he went with his mother to Spain in 1932 and took a doctorate at Columbia University in 1959; he taught at Columbia from 1961 and at Yale from 1969 for the rest of his life. His study of Francisco Franco's Spain classed it as an authoritarian regime, when regimes tended to be called either democratic or totalitarian. His works include Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes (1975), The Perils of Presidentialism (1990) and, with Alfred Stepan, Problems of Democratic Transition and Consolidation (1996).

entries.name: Chinvat Bridge
entries.desc: The Chinvat Bridge, or Bridge of the Requiter, is in Zoroastrianism the sifting bridge that separates the world of the living from the world of the dead, which all souls must cross upon death. According to the Bundahishn, it appears narrow to the wicked, whom the demon Chinnaphapast drags into the House of Lies, a place of eternal punishment, while for those whose good thoughts, words and deeds were many it is wide enough to cross, and the Daena leads the soul into the House of Song. Two four-eyed dogs guard it, as the Videvdat describes. It appears in the Yasna and the Vendidad, and bridges on early medieval Sogdian funerary couches have been identified with it.

entries.name: Warrior of Hirschlanden
entries.desc: The Warrior of Hirschlanden is a sandstone statue of a warrior, the oldest known Iron Age life-size anthropomorphic statue north of the Alps. A work of the Hallstatt culture, probably of the 6th century BCE, it was found in 1963 beside a low barrow with 16 burials at Hirschlanden, now part of Ditzingen in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, and is supposed to have stood on its top. Its preserved height is 1.50 m, the feet having been broken off. The figure wears a torc, a belt with a late Hallstatt dagger and a pointed hat, and its sketchy face has led to speculation that it wears a mask. It is now in the Württembergisches Landesmuseum in Stuttgart, with a copy at the site.

entries.name: Mont Lassois
entries.desc: Mont Lassois is a hill in the commune of Vix, near Châtillon-sur-Seine in the Côte-d'Or, France, that rises about 100 m above the upper Seine valley and is known for its remains of the Hallstatt culture. At the end of the Hallstatt period it was an oppidum that seems to have controlled the circulation of tin from Great Britain to Italy; its people, ruled in the 6th century BCE by a female aristocracy, taxed the passing convoys. A rich tumulus at Vix holds a woman, probably a queen or a priestess, and excavations since 2002 have revealed the Vix Palace, a very large building. The city of Latiscum later stood on the hill, which is crowned by the church of Saint-Marcel.

entries.name: Irk Bitig
entries.desc: The Irk Bitig, or Book of Omens, is a manuscript book on divination in Old Turkic, the only known complete manuscript text in the Old Turkic script. Aurel Stein found it in 1907 in the Library Cave of the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang, China, and it is now in the British Library in London. Its colophon says an anonymous monk wrote it in a year of the tiger at a Manichaean monastery; the manuscript is dated to the 9th or 10th century, and Marcel Erdal dated the original work to the 8th and 9th centuries. Each of its 65 sections gives an omen, thought to come from throws of a four-sided die, with a short story and a verdict of good or bad. It is an important source for early Turkic mythology.

entries.name: Edward Hincks
entries.desc: Edward Hincks was an Irish Church of Ireland clergyman, Egyptologist and Assyriologist, known for the decipherment of cuneiform. Born in Cork, he became a Fellow of Trinity College Dublin in 1813 and from 1826 was rector of Killyleagh, County Down, until his death. Working independently of Henry Creswicke Rawlinson, he deduced the essentially syllabic nature of Old Persian cuneiform, and by 1850 he had concluded that Akkadian cuneiform was syllabic and its signs polyphonic, each with several readings. In 1857 he, Rawlinson, Jules Oppert and William Henry Fox Talbot each translated a new inscription of Tiglath-Pileser I, and the close agreement of their versions settled the decipherment.

entries.name: Max Uhle
entries.desc: Max Uhle was a German archaeologist whose work in Peru, Chile, Ecuador and Bolivia at the turn of the 20th century had a significant impact on the practice of South American archaeology. Born in Dresden and trained as a philologist, he took his doctorate at the University of Leipzig in 1880, and in 1892 published, with B. von Grumbkow, the first in-depth scientific account of Tiwanaku. From 1896 he excavated Pachacamac and Mochica and Chimu sites, recovering about 9,000 artifacts, and built a chronology from their styles that Alfred Kroeber later advanced and that remains key to the dating of pre-Inca Peru. In 1917 he was the first to describe the Chinchorro mummies scientifically.

entries.name: Bernard Fagg
entries.desc: Bernard Fagg was a British archaeologist and museum curator who worked extensively in Nigeria before and after the Second World War. After studying at Downing College, Cambridge, he joined the British colonial administration in Jos in 1939 and in 1944 excavated the Rop rock shelter on the Jos Plateau. He first encountered the finds of what became known as the Nok culture, and his controlled excavation at Taruga yielded terracotta figurines and iron slag with radiocarbon dates of about the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. In 1952 he founded the National Museum in Jos, the first public museum in Nigeria, and from 1963 he was curator of the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford.

entries.name: Castellet de Banyoles
entries.desc: The Castellet de Banyoles is an ancient Iberian city and archaeological site near the River Ebro in Tivissa, in the Ribera d'Ebre region of Catalonia. Built around the first half of the 4th century BCE on a headland reached only through a narrow entrance, it is known for the pentagonal towers flanking that entrance, unique among the protohistoric fortifications of the Iberian Peninsula, and for a treasure of decorated silver and gold vessels found in 1927. It was destroyed in a Roman siege, possibly during the revolts of Indibil and Mandonius (206–205 BCE) or, most likely, during the campaign of Cato the Elder in 195 BCE, and traces of the Roman camp lie outside its walls.

entries.name: ʿAin Mallaha
entries.desc: ʿAin Mallaha, or Eynan, was an Epipalaeolithic settlement of the Natufian culture in the Hula Valley of northern Israel, 25 kilometres north of the Sea of Galilee. Its people were sedentary hunter-gatherers, a crucial step in the transition from foraging to farming: they ground wild nuts and grain, cut wild cereals with stone sickles, hunted gazelle, deer and wild boar, and fished in the lake. Kathleen Kenyon describes the village as 50 circular, semi-subterranean huts with stone walls. Families were probably buried in their own houses, and a woman buried with her hand on a puppy is among the earliest archaeological evidence of dog domestication. The site was discovered in 1954.

entries.name: Blackwater Draw
entries.desc: Blackwater Draw is an intermittent stream channel about 140 km long that runs from Roosevelt County, New Mexico, south-eastward across the Llano Estacado towards Lubbock, Texas, and holds Blackwater Locality No. 1, the type site of the Clovis culture. Ridgley Whiteman first recognized the site in 1929, and the first large excavation came in 1932. Its stratified levels, from Clovis and Folsom to the historic period, hold fluted Clovis points and other tools with the remains of extinct Late Pleistocene animals such as mammoth, camel, bison and dire wolf. Two of its points were used in the 1930s to define Clovis technology, and its Clovis layers date to around 11,290 years before the present.

entries.name: Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
entries.desc: Hopewell Culture National Historical Park is a United States national historical park in Ross County, Ohio, that preserves earthworks and burial mounds of the Hopewell culture, which flourished from about 200 BCE to 500 CE. It began as the Mound City Group, much of it destroyed by an army training camp built on the site in World War I, which was declared a National Monument in 1923; in 1992 it was renamed and expanded to include other earthwork and mound groups, among them the Hopewell Mound Group, the culture's type site, and the geometric Seip and Hopeton Earthworks. It is run by the National Park Service and became part of the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks World Heritage Site in 2023.

entries.name: Havana Hopewell culture
entries.desc: The Havana Hopewell culture was a Hopewellian people who lived in the Illinois River and Mississippi River valleys in Iowa, Illinois and Missouri from 200 BCE to 400 CE. It was one complex within the Hopewell exchange system, which began in the Ohio and Illinois River valleys around 300 BCE and carried obsidian from the Yellowstone area, copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf Coast. Its sites include the Toolesboro Mound Group in Louisa County, Iowa, whose conical burial mounds were built between 100 BCE and 200 CE beside a large octagonal earthen enclosure, and the Ogden-Fettie Site in Illinois, with thirty-five mounds in a crescent-shaped enclosure.

entries.name: Coles Creek culture
entries.desc: The Coles Creek culture was a Late Woodland archaeological culture of the Lower Mississippi valley, in present-day Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, which followed the Troyville culture and is considered ancestral to the Plaquemine culture. Its population grew dramatically, and by 1000 CE simple elite polities had begun to form. From roughly 800 CE its people built flat-topped platform mounds, usually two or three around a central plaza, to carry temples and other civic buildings, often over earlier burial mounds. They lived on acorns and other wild plants and on hunting rather than maize, which only began to increase by 1000–1200 CE, and the bow and arrow came into use.

entries.name: Edict of Expulsion
entries.desc: The Edict of Expulsion was a royal decree issued by Edward I on 18 July 1290 that expelled all Jews from the Kingdom of England, the first time a European state is known to have permanently banned their presence. It followed punitive taxation, the Statute of the Jewry of 1275, which outlawed lending at interest, and the death sentences on over 300 Jews in the coin-clipping crisis of the late 1270s. The Jews, perhaps as few as 2,000, could take cash and personal possessions, but their debts, homes, synagogues and cemeteries were forfeited to the king, and some died through piracy or drowned in the Channel. It stood until 1656, when Oliver Cromwell informally permitted their resettlement.

entries.name: Peace and Truce of God
entries.desc: The Peace and Truce of God was a movement led by the Catholic Church in the Middle Ages that sought, with the threat of spiritual sanctions, to limit feuding in the western half of the former Carolingian Empire, and that drew popular support. The Peace of God, first proclaimed at the Council of Charroux in 989, protected clergy, peasants, church property and other noncombatants. The Truce of God, first proclaimed at the Council of Toulouges in 1027, forbade fighting on certain days and seasons; by the middle of the 12th century about eighty days were left for fighting. The Third Lateran Council of 1179 extended the Truce to the whole Church, and the movement lasted until the 13th century.

entries.name: Hildegard of Bingen
entries.desc: Hildegard of Bingen was a German Benedictine abbess and polymath of the High Middle Ages, active as a writer, composer, philosopher, mystic, visionary and medical writer. Enclosed young at Disibodenberg, she was elected magistra of its women in 1136 and founded the monasteries of Rupertsberg in 1150 and Eibingen in 1165. Her three volumes of visionary theology began with Scivias; she also wrote on medicine, left nearly 400 letters, invented a constructed language, the Lingua Ignota, and left more surviving chants than any other medieval composer, among them the Ordo Virtutum, arguably the oldest surviving morality play. In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI named her a Doctor of the Church.

entries.name: Rashi
entries.desc: Rashi, Shlomo Yitzchaki, was a French rabbi of Troyes who wrote comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and the Hebrew Bible and is generally considered a leading biblical exegete of the Middle Ages. He studied in Worms under Yaakov ben Yakar and Isaac ben Eliezer Halevi, then returned to Troyes, where he joined and later led the rabbinical court and around 1070 founded a yeshiva. His commentary on nearly all of the Babylonian Talmud has been printed in every edition since Daniel Bomberg's of the 1520s, and his commentary on the Five Books of Moses is the basis of more than 300 supercommentaries. He mourned the victims of the People's Crusade of 1096 in penitential poems, and died in 1105.

entries.name: Thomas Becket
entries.desc: Thomas Becket was an English cleric and statesman who served as Lord Chancellor from 1155 to 1162 and as Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 until his murder in 1170. Born in London to a Norman family, he rose in the household of Archbishop Theobald of Bec, who recommended him to Henry II. As archbishop he resisted the king's attempt to reassert royal prerogatives over the Church; convicted in 1164 of contempt of royal authority, he spent six years in exile under the protection of Louis VII of France. Soon after his return in 1170 four knights loyal to Henry killed him in Canterbury Cathedral. Pope Alexander III canonized him in 1173, and he is venerated as a saint and martyr.

entries.name: Anna Komnene
entries.desc: Anna Komnene was a Byzantine Greek princess and historian, author of the Alexiad, an account of the reign of her father, Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, and the most important primary source for Byzantine history of the late 11th and early 12th centuries and for the early Crusades. Born in 1083 in the Porphyra Chamber of the palace in Constantinople, she was betrothed to Constantine Doukas, with whom she was next in line to the throne until her brother John II Komnenos became heir in 1092. After 1118 she is commonly believed to have plotted against John in favour of her husband, Nikephoros Bryennios, though no contemporary evidence shows it; she ended her life in the Kecharitomene convent.

entries.name: Michael Psellos
entries.desc: Michael Psellos was a Byzantine monk, writer, philosopher, historian and imperial courtier who advised several 11th-century emperors. Born Constantine, probably in Constantinople, in 1017 or 1018, he rose from the imperial chancellery to advise Constantine IX Monomachos and to be the leading professor at the University of Constantinople, and he played a decisive part in the changes of ruler of 1057, 1059 and 1071. His Chronographia, biographies of 14 emperors and empresses from Basil II to Michael VII Doukas, is a valuable source on the 11th-century empire, and his revival of classical studies later influenced the Italian Renaissance. Most scholars believe he died soon after 1078.

entries.name: Book of the Prefect
entries.desc: The Book of the Prefect, or Book of the Eparch, is a Byzantine commercial manual addressed to the eparch, the governor of Constantinople. It is traditionally dated to the reign of Leo VI the Wise (886–912), but it seems to have grown gradually, and its references to tetartera coins show that its final form is no earlier than the reign of Nikephoros II Phokas (963–69). Its twenty-two chapters regulate the city's guilds, from notaries, bankers and silk merchants to butchers, bakers and inn-holders, setting entrance fees, prices, profit margins and areas of work. Lost until 1891, when Jules Nicole found its only surviving manuscript in Geneva, it is a unique source for the Byzantine economy.

entries.name: East–West Schism
entries.desc: The East–West Schism, also called the Great Schism or the Schism of 1054, is the break of communion between the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church. It followed long disputes between the Greek East and the Latin West over the Filioque clause of the Nicene Creed, the bread of the Eucharist and the pope's claim to universal jurisdiction. In 1054 Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, legate of Pope Leo IX, excommunicated Patriarch Michael I Cerularius of Constantinople, who excommunicated the legates in turn. The breach deepened with the sack of Constantinople in 1204 and has never healed, though Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I nullified the anathemas of 1054 in 1965.

entries.name: Leo VI the Wise
entries.desc: Leo VI the Wise was Byzantine emperor from 886 to 912 and the second ruler of the Macedonian dynasty, though his parentage is unclear: he was the son either of Michael III or of Basil I. Reportedly very well read, he completed the Basilika, a Greek code in 60 books that translated and arranged the laws of Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis, and issued new laws, the Novels, which removed obsolete Roman institutions such as the Senate and the consulate. His reign saw defeat by Simeon I of Bulgaria at Boulgarophygon in 896 and the loss of Taormina, the last Byzantine outpost in Sicily, in 902. His fourth marriage, to Zoe Karbonopsina, caused a scandal; their son became Constantine VII.

entries.name: Ban Zhao
entries.desc: Ban Zhao was a Chinese historian, philosopher and politician of the Han dynasty and the first known female Chinese historian. Daughter of the historian Ban Biao and sister of the historian Ban Gu and the general Ban Chao, she was widowed young and devoted her life to scholarship. After Ban Gu died in prison in 92, she completed his Book of Han, the history of the Western Han, supplying the missing Eight Tables. She also wrote Lessons for Women, a guide to women's conduct that was popular for centuries. She taught Empress Deng Sui and the court, advised the empress during her regency, and as a court librarian enlarged the Biographies of Eminent Women by Liu Xiang.

entries.name: Lessons for Women
entries.desc: Lessons for Women, also translated as Admonitions for Women, Women's Precepts or Warnings for Women, is a work by Ban Zhao, the Han dynasty female intellectual who lived from 45 or 49 to 117 or 120 CE, written for her daughters. The small book, of only seven chapters, describes the status and position of women in society and sets out the four virtues a woman must keep: womanly virtue, speech, manner and merit. Each is defined by restraint, so that a woman should not distinguish herself in talent and intelligence nor outdo others in skill. As one of the Four Books for Women it had wide circulation in the late Ming and Qing dynasties, and many women had its sections memorised.

entries.name: Gongsun Hong
entries.desc: Gongsun Hong was a senior official of the Western Han dynasty under Emperor Wu and, with Dong Zhongshu, one of the earliest proponents of Confucianism at the Han court. Born in Zichuan in present-day Shandong, a former prison officer who had made his living tending pigs, he began his political career at sixty and rose from commoner to grand secretary in 126 and chancellor in 124 BCE, the first commoner and first Confucian chancellor and the first chancellor made a marquis. His support brought into being the national academy and the imperial examination, a precedent that lasted into the twentieth century. Sima Qian and Dong Zhongshu called him a flatterer and a hypocrite.

entries.name: Sang Hongyang
entries.desc: Sang Hongyang was an official of the Han dynasty who served Emperor Wu and Emperor Zhao, known for his economic policies. Born to a merchant family in Luoyang and noted for his skill in mathematics, he became a Palace Attendant at 13. When the campaigns against the Xiongnu had drained the treasury, he helped plan the state monopolies over iron and salt proposed in 120 BCE, systems later imitated by other dynasties, and as Assistant Minister of Agriculture introduced an asset tax on artisans, bankers and merchants. He became Imperial Secretary in 87 BCE and took part in the debate on Salt and Iron of 81 BCE, but was executed in 80 BCE by the regent Huo Guang on charges of treason.

entries.name: Chao Cuo
entries.desc: Chao Cuo was a Chinese philosopher, politician and writer who served as an adviser and official under Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing of the Han dynasty. In a memorandum of 169 BCE he compared Han and Xiongnu tactics and proposed settling government-supported migrants in walled towns on the northern frontier, to farm and train as militia; Emperor Wen approved it. He helped revive the Classic of History, taught by the daughter of the aged scholar Fu Sheng, though later Eastern Han scholars called him a Legalist. Made Imperial Secretary in 155 BCE, he urged cutting down the princely kingdoms, and when seven kings rebelled his rivals persuaded Emperor Jing to have him executed in 154 BCE.

entries.name: Rebellion of the Seven States
entries.desc: The Rebellion of the Seven States was a revolt in 154 BCE by the semi-autonomous regional kings of the Western Han dynasty against Emperor Jing, who sought to centralise the government further. On the advice of Chao Cuo the emperor had cut commanderies from the principalities of Chu, Zhao, Jiaoxi and Wu; Liu Pi, Prince of Wu, then led seven princes in revolt, demanding Chao's execution. While Wu and Chu besieged Suiyang, the capital of Liang, the imperial commander Zhou Yafu cut their supply lines until their armies starved and collapsed. The rebellion was crushed within three months, and the powers of the princes were gradually reduced under Emperor Jing and Emperor Wu.

entries.name: Wei Zifu
entries.desc: Wei Zifu was an empress consort of the Han dynasty, the second wife of Emperor Wu, his spouse for 49 years and his empress for 38, the second longest tenure in Chinese history. Born to a serf family in the household of Princess Pingyang, where she was trained as a singer and dancer, she caught the emperor's eye in 139 BCE and was made empress after bearing his first son, Liu Ju. Her half-brother Wei Qing and nephew Huo Qubing became leading generals. In 91 BCE, amid the witchcraft persecutions, the official Jiang Chong accused the crown prince; Liu Ju rose against the conspirators with her support and was defeated, and when the emperor had her seal seized she took her own life.

entries.name: Jin Midi
entries.desc: Jin Midi was a Xiongnu prince of Xiutu who became a general and co-regent of the Western Han dynasty. Heir of the Prince of Xiutu, he was taken into imperial service in the stables after his father was killed in 121 BCE by the Prince of Hunye, who surrendered to the Han. Emperor Wu, impressed by his propriety, made him director of the imperial stables and gave him the surname Jin, gold, after the golden statues his father had used to worship heaven. In 88 BCE he wrestled down Ma Heluo, who was entering the emperor's bedchamber with a knife. Named a secondary regent for the young Emperor Zhao in 87 BCE, beside Huo Guang and Shangguan Jie, he died the following year.

entries.name: Manusmriti
entries.desc: The Manusmriti, also known as the Manava Dharmashastra or the Laws of Manu, is a major legal text among the Dharmashastras of Hinduism, a Sanskrit work in verse that most scholars date to between 200 BCE and 200 CE. It presents itself as a discourse by Manu and Bhrigu on duties, laws, conduct, gender norms and virtues, and is best known for its different rules for the four varnas. Its influence reached Hindu kingdoms in what are now Cambodia and Indonesia, and it was used to construct the Hindu law code of the East India Company's enclaves. In modern times it is controversial for its treatment of women and lower castes: B. R. Ambedkar burned copies in 1927 to protest caste discrimination.

entries.name: Indica
entries.desc: The Indica is an account of Mauryan India by the Greek writer Megasthenes, who died around 290 BCE. The original is lost, but fragments survive in later Greek and Latin works, the earliest by Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Pliny and Arrian; E. A. Schwanbeck collected them in 1846, and John Watson McCrindle published a reconstruction in 1877 that is not universally accepted. It described India's land, peoples and customs, and divided its society into seven castes, where Indian texts name four varnas. Strabo called Megasthenes a liar for his tales of mouthless tribes and gold-digging ants, but some authors consider the work an important source on the society and administration of its time.

entries.name: Vakataka dynasty
entries.desc: The Vakataka dynasty was an ancient Indian dynasty that arose in the Deccan in the mid-3rd century CE and became the most important successor of the Satavahanas there, contemporary with the Guptas in the north. Little is known of its founder, Vindhyashakti (r. 250–270); expansion began under his son Pravarasena I, after whom the family is thought to have divided into branches, two of them known. The Gupta emperor Chandragupta II married his daughter into the dynasty. The Vakatakas were patrons of art and literature: the Buddhist caves of Ajanta were built under King Harishena (c. 475–500). The end of the dynasty is unknown, and the Chalukyas of Badami later filled the vacuum.

entries.name: Sanghamitta
entries.desc: Sanghamitta was an Indian Buddhist nun who, according to Sri Lankan tradition, was the eldest daughter of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. With her brother Mahinda she entered the Buddhist order, and at the request of King Devanampiya Tissa of Sri Lanka she was sent there with other nuns to ordain Anula and the women of the court at Anuradhapura, founding the Bhikkhuni Sangha, the order of nuns. She brought a sapling of the Bodhi tree, which was planted at Anuradhapura and still survives. Tradition holds that she died in 203 BCE at the age of 79. Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka mark her arrival every year on the full moon of December, Unduvapa Poya or Sanghamitta Day.

entries.name: Deir el-Medina
entries.desc: Deir el-Medina is an ancient Egyptian village on the west bank of the Nile, across from modern Luxor, that housed the artisans who built the tombs in the Valley of the Kings during the 18th to 20th Dynasties of the New Kingdom. Its ancient name was Set maat, Place of Truth, and at its peak it had around 68 houses. Excavated from 1922 to 1951 by a French team under Bernard Bruyère, it yielded thousands of ostraca and papyri recording letters, sales, prayers and work, making it one of the best-documented communities of the ancient world. Around 1170 BCE, under Ramesses III, its workmen staged what may have been the first recorded strike. It was abandoned c. 1110–1080 BCE under Ramesses XI.

entries.name: Valley of the Kings
aka: Valley of the Gates of the Kings
entries.desc: The Valley of the Kings is a wadi on the west bank of the Nile, opposite Thebes (modern Luxor), where rock-cut tombs were excavated for pharaohs and powerful nobles of the New Kingdom for nearly 500 years, from the Eighteenth to the Twentieth Dynasty. It holds 65 known tombs and chambers, from the simple pit KV54 to KV5, with over 120 chambers for the sons of Ramesses II; only about twenty contain the remains of kings. Almost all were robbed in antiquity, and during the civil war under Ramesses XI the mummies were gathered into caches. The discovery of the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922 drew wide attention to the valley, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

entries.name: The Satire of the Trades
entries.desc: The Satire of the Trades, also called the Instruction of Kheti, is a didactic work of ancient Egyptian literature written during the Middle Kingdom. In it a scribe from Sile named Kheti tells his son Pepi that the scribe's career is greater than any other, describing in exaggerated terms the toil of smiths, masons, potters and other workers. Copied widely as a schoolboy text, it was among the most copied texts in Theban scribal schools in the Twentieth Dynasty (1189–1077 BCE); the whole text survives on the Papyrus Sallier II in the British Museum. Egyptologists disagree on whether it is satire: Miriam Lichtheim held that it is, while Chris Rollston reads it as scribal propaganda.

entries.name: Wilbour Papyrus
entries.desc: The Wilbour Papyrus is the largest known non-funerary papyrus from ancient Egypt, an administrative survey of cultivatable land made in the 4th year of Ramesses V, around 1145 BCE, in the late Ramesside Period. Ten metres long, it covers about 140 kilometres from the Faiyum to near Tihna: Text A lists the holders of plots, among them priests, soldiers, ladies, herdsmen, stable-masters and farmers, and Text B the crown lands of the pharaoh. It suggests that temples held 13 to 18 percent of Egypt's farmland, though whether the grain it records was tax or rent is unknown. Charles Edwin Wilbour bought it at Elephantine in 1893; it is in the Brooklyn Museum.

entries.name: Tutankhamun
entries.desc: Tutankhamun was a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of ancient Egypt who ruled c. 1332–1323 BCE and died at about the age of 19. Born Tutankhaten in the reign of Akhenaten, he restored the traditional religion after Atenism, restoring the cult of Amun at Thebes, changing his name and moving the court from Amarna back to Memphis. DNA testing identified his father as the mummy from tomb KV55, thought to be Akhenaten or Smenkhkare. As his royal tomb was unfinished, he was buried in a small non-royal tomb, which excavators led by Howard Carter found in 1922 with much of its contents, over 5,000 artifacts and the king's undisturbed mummy; the discovery renewed public interest in ancient Egypt.

entries.name: Horemheb
entries.desc: Horemheb was the last pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty of Egypt, ruling for at least 14 years between 1319 and 1292 BCE. Believed to have been of common birth, he rose to be commander-in-chief of the army under Tutankhamun and Ay, and was linked to the royal family only by marriage to Mutnedjmet, thought, though this is disputed, to be Ay's daughter. As king he restabilised Egypt after the Amarna Period: he demolished Akhenaten's monuments, usurped those of Tutankhamun and Ay, and issued the Edict of Horemheb against corruption. Having no surviving son, he named his vizier Paramessu as his successor, who reigned as Ramesses I. His tomb, KV57, was discovered in 1908.

entries.name: Nefertari
entries.desc: Nefertari, also Nefertari Meritmut, was an Egyptian queen and the first of the Great Royal Wives of Ramesses the Great, whom she married before he became king. She bore at least four sons and two daughters, among them the crown prince Amun-her-khepeshef. Able to read and write hieroglyphs, a rare skill, she corresponded with other royals: tablets from the Hittite capital Hattusas preserve her letters, as Naptera, to King Hattusili III and Queen Puduhepa. Ramesses built a temple for her at Abu Simbel beside his own. She was buried in QV66, one of the largest tombs of the Valley of the Queens, robbed in antiquity and excavated by Ernesto Schiaparelli in 1904.

entries.name: Tiye
entries.desc: Tiye was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian pharaoh Amenhotep III, mother of Akhenaten and grandmother of Tutankhamun. Her parents, Yuya and Thuya, were non-royal and came from Akhmim, where Yuya was a wealthy landowner and priest. Married to Amenhotep III by the second year of his reign, she wielded great power during his reign and her son's: in the Amarna letters Tushratta, king of Mitanni, wrote to her directly. She outlived her husband by as many as twelve years; if she died soon after Akhenaten's 12th year (1338 BCE), she was born around 1398 BCE. In 2010 DNA analysis identified her as the Elder Lady, a mummy found in the tomb of Amenhotep II (KV35) in 1898.

entries.name: Rekhmire
entries.desc: Rekhmire was an ancient Egyptian noble and official of the 18th Dynasty who served as Governor of the Town, the mayor of Thebes, and as vizier under Thutmosis III and Amenhotep II, around 1400 BCE. The nephew of the vizier User, he was also High Priest of Heliopolis. He built a richly decorated tomb, TT100, at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna in the Theban Necropolis, whose lively and well-preserved scenes of daily life illustrate the New Kingdom; it also holds a full copy of the text on the duties of the vizier known as the Installation of the Vizier. The cause of his downfall is unclear: he is suspected to have fallen into disgrace and been deposed.

entries.name: Ahmose, son of Ebana
entries.desc: Ahmose, son of Ebana, was an Egyptian soldier, born in the city of Nekheb, the modern El Kab, who served under the pharaohs Ahmose I, Amenhotep I and Thutmose I. His father Baba had enlisted in the navy during the war to expel the Hyksos under Seqenenre Tao. Ahmose fought at Avaris, the Hyksos capital in the Delta, where he killed two Hyksos and was twice awarded the gold of valor, took part in the three-year siege of Sharuhen in southern Canaan, and fought the Nubians. Under Thutmose I he was appointed admiral and followed the king against Naharin as far as the Euphrates. The autobiography inscribed on the wall of his tomb is a valuable source for the late 17th and early 18th Dynasties.

entries.name: Tausret
entries.desc: Tausret, also spelled Tawosret or Twosret, was the last known ruler of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Probably the second royal wife of Seti II, and not a king's daughter, she became regent with Chancellor Bay for his heir Siptah after Seti's death; Bay was executed on Siptah's orders in his Year 5, a move Aidan Dodson believes Tausret engineered. When Siptah died she took the throne as pharaoh, counting his nearly six years as her own; inscriptions of her Year 8 on her mortuary temple at Gournah suggest perhaps three years of sole rule. Her reign ended in a civil war, most likely with her overthrow by Setnakhte, founder of the Twentieth Dynasty, who usurped her tomb KV14.

entries.name: Athenian democracy
entries.desc: Athenian democracy was the system of government that developed from around the 6th century BCE in the Greek city-state of Athens and its territory of Attica, open only to free adult male citizens, probably no more than 30 percent of adults. Its development is credited to Solon in 594 BCE, Cleisthenes in 508–507 BCE, who organised citizens into ten groups by where they lived, and Ephialtes in 462 BCE. It was direct rather than representative: citizens attended the assembly by right, and most officials and large juries were chosen by lot. Twice interrupted by oligarchic revolutions, in 411 and 404 BCE, its forms persisted until Philip II of Macedon conquered Athens in 338 BCE.

entries.name: Ecclesia
entries.desc: The ecclesia, or ekklesia, was the assembly of the citizens in the city-states of ancient Greece, best known from Athens, where it was open to all male citizens; in 594 BCE Solon allowed all Athenian citizens to take part regardless of class. The Athenian assembly declared war, elected the strategoi and other officials, had the final say on legislation and called magistrates to account after their year of office. Its agenda was set by the Boule, and it voted by show of hands, counting of stones and broken pottery. A typical meeting probably held around 6,000 of 30,000–60,000 citizens; it met on the Pnyx, and around 300 BCE its meetings moved to the Theatre of Dionysus.

entries.name: Boule
entries.desc: The boule was a council that ran the daily affairs of a city in ancient Greece; originally a council of nobles advising a king, it was hereditary in some oligarchies and chosen by lot for one year in democracies. Athens is the best documented: under Solon it had 400 members, 100 from each of the four tribes, and after 508 BCE Cleisthenes made it a council of 500, 50 from each of his ten new tribes, chosen by lot from male citizens aged 30 or more. It set the agenda of the Assembly and carried out its decisions, and after the reforms of Ephialtes and Pericles it took over many functions of the Areopagus. The name survives as the Vouli, the Parliament of modern Greece.

entries.name: Solonian constitution
entries.desc: The Solonian constitution was the body of laws and reforms given to Athens by Solon in the early 6th century BCE, when the state was close to falling apart through quarrels between its parties. Chosen archon by a compromise, Solon cancelled all debts, freed debt-slaves and abolished the status of the hectemoroi, measures known as the Seisachtheia, and of Draco's laws kept only those on homicide. He made wealth rather than birth the measure for office, dividing citizens by the yield of their land into four classes: pentacosiomedimnoi, hippeis, zeugitae and thetes. The code was written as poetry, and Solon went into self-imposed exile for ten years lest he be tempted to rule as a tyrant.

entries.name: Battle of Arginusae
entries.desc: The Battle of Arginusae was a naval battle of the Peloponnesian War, fought in 406 BCE near Canae in the Arginusae Islands, east of Lesbos, in which an Athenian fleet under eight strategoi defeated a Spartan fleet under Callicratidas. Athens had built and manned the fleet in haste to relieve Conon, blockaded at Mytilene, enlisting slaves and metics; facing more experienced crews, the generals fought in eight divisions and a double line. Callicratidas was killed, and the Spartans lost some 70 ships to the Athenians' 25. A storm kept the ships from rescuing the survivors of the disabled triremes, many sailors drowned, and the Athenian assembly tried and executed six of the generals as a group.

entries.name: Thesmophoria
entries.desc: The Thesmophoria was an ancient Greek religious festival in honour of the goddess Demeter and her daughter Persephone, held each year, mostly around the sowing of seed in late autumn, to promote human and agricultural fertility. Among the most widely celebrated Greek festivals, it was restricted to adult women, and its rites were kept secret. In Athens it lasted three days, the 11th to the 13th of Pyanepsion; the second, the nesteia, was a day of fasting imitating Demeter's mourning. Pigs were sacrificed and put into pits called megara, and their rotten remains were later retrieved and scattered on the fields with the seed. Aristophanes parodied the festival in his Thesmophoriazusae.

entries.name: Lysias
entries.desc: Lysias was an Athenian logographer, a writer of speeches for the law courts, and one of the ten Attic orators. His father Cephalus, a native of Syracuse, had settled at Athens at the invitation of Pericles; Lysias went to the colony of Thurii and was driven out in 412 BCE, returning to Athens, where he and his brother Polemarchus owned a shield factory with 120 skilled slaves. In 404 BCE the Thirty Tyrants made Polemarchus drink hemlock, and Lysias escaped to Megara with the help of a bribe. Afterwards he wrote speeches for litigants, thirty-four of which survive, and became the model of the plain style; in 403 he accused Eratosthenes, one of the Thirty.

entries.name: Pasion
entries.desc: Pasion was a slave in ancient Athens who rose to become a banker and an Athenian citizen in the early 4th century BCE. His origin is unknown, though he is widely presumed to have come from Syria and the Levant. Owned by the bankers Antisthenes and Archestratus, who had a bank at the Piraeus, he rose to chief clerk at a money-changing table and by 394 BCE had been freed and made a resident alien. He inherited the bank when his owners retired, set up a shield factory, gave Athens one thousand shields and a trireme, and was granted citizenship. When he died in 370 BCE his widow Archippe, who knew the bank's business, married Phormion, the slave who ran it, to keep the bank in the family.

entries.name: Nicias
entries.desc: Nicias was an Athenian politician and general prominent in the Peloponnesian War, a wealthy aristocrat with interests in the silver mines of Laurion, where Xenophon says he owned a thousand men. After the death of Pericles in 429 BCE he led the aristocrats as the principal rival of Cleon, opposing the aggressive imperialism of Cleon and Alcibiades, and served as strategos with a reputation for over-caution. He was largely responsible for the Peace of Nicias with Sparta in 421. Appointed in 415 BCE to command the Sicilian Expedition, he delayed the withdrawal after a lunar eclipse, surrendered to Gylippus at the Assinaros river and was executed by the Syracusans in 413.

credit.artist: William Jennings Bryan, Francis Whiting Halsey

entries.name: Gerousia
entries.desc: The Gerousia, also called the Spartan Senate, was the council of elders of the ancient Greek city-state of Sparta. In the Archaic and Classical periods it consisted of the two kings and twenty-eight citizens, the gerontes, who had to be at least sixty, were elected by the shouts of the Assembly and held office for life. It was the highest court, judging capital cases, even of kings, and it prepared the measures put to the Assembly. Aristotle called their election childish, and they were likely drawn from a few aristocratic families. In 227 BCE Cleomenes III probably made the office annual, and by the reign of Augustus the council had been reduced to twenty-three members.

entries.name: Agoge
entries.desc: The agoge was the training programme required for Spartiate, or citizen, status in ancient Sparta. Boys entered at seven and were divided into the paides, paidiskoi and hēbōntes, living in packs called agelai under an older youth and the official paidonomos. It deliberately deprived them of food, sleep and shelter, made them steal food and beat those caught, and trained them in endurance, hunting, dancing, singing and brief, witty speech; violent by the standards of the day, it was sometimes fatal. Xenophon credited it to the lawgiver Lycurgus, while modern scholars date its beginning to the 7th or 6th century BCE; in the Roman period it became a tourist attraction.

entries.name: Crypteia
entries.desc: The Crypteia was an institution of the ancient Spartan state, made up of young upper-class men, probably aged between 21 and 30, who had passed through the agoge with distinction. Ancient accounts differ on its purpose: Plutarch and Heraclides Lembus, possibly following a lost work by Aristotle, describe kryptai sent into the countryside with daggers to kill helots, after the ephors declared war on the helots each autumn, while others saw it as military training or an initiation ordeal. Aristotle credited it to the lawgiver Lycurgus, but Plutarch thought it was introduced, if at all, after the helot revolt of the mid-460s BCE. Modern historians often translate the name as secret police.

entries.name: Syssitia
entries.desc: The syssitia were the common meals of men and youths in social or religious groups in ancient Greece, above all in Crete and Sparta, but also in Megara in the sixth century BCE and Corinth in the seventh. Tradition attributed their origin to Rhadamanthus, the legendary lawgiver of Knossos. In Sparta, where they were called pheiditia, the daily meal was obligatory even for the two kings; men were admitted from the age of twenty by a vote with balls of bread, a single flattened ball rejecting the candidate. Each member contributed a monthly share of barley, wine, cheese, figs and money, and those who could not pay were excluded. The main dish was the black soup.

entries.name: Gorgo
entries.desc: Gorgo was a Spartan woman, the only known child of King Cleomenes I, wife of King Leonidas I and mother of King Pleistarchus, and one of the few women named by Herodotus. Herodotus tells that as a girl of eight or nine she warned her father to leave lest the bribes of Aristagoras corrupt him. Before the Persian invasion of 480 BCE, when a warning from the exiled Demaratus arrived on a wooden tablet covered with wax, she advised the Spartans to clear off the wax, and David Kahn counts her among the first named female cryptanalysts. Though daughter and wife of kings, she could not be considered a queen: the title was not used of Greek women until the late Hellenistic period.

entries.name: Cynisca
entries.desc: Cynisca was a Spartan princess of the Eurypontid dynasty, daughter of King Archidamus II and sister of Agesilaus II, and the first woman to win at the Olympic Games. Born probably around 440 BCE, she bred horses, and in 396 BCE her team, driven by charioteers she employed, won the four-horse chariot race; it won again in 392 BCE. Xenophon and Plutarch say Agesilaus encouraged her to show that the sport proved only wealth, while modern scholars suspect he used her fame for his own career. She dedicated bronze statues of herself, her charioteer, chariot and horses at the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, and a hero-shrine was raised for her in Sparta, an honour previously given only to kings.

entries.name: Copán
entries.desc: Copán is an archaeological site of the Maya civilization in the Copán Department of western Honduras, near the border with Guatemala. Occupied for more than two thousand years, it was the capital of a major Classic period kingdom from the 5th to the 9th century CE, refounded in 426 by a dynasty with its origins at Tikal; at its Late Classic peak the kingdom had at least 20,000 people. In 738 its king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil was captured and beheaded by his former vassal, the king of Quiriguá. The population later declined and the city was abandoned in the early 10th century. Known for its sculpture and Hieroglyphic Stairway, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

entries.name: Palenque
entries.desc: Palenque, anciently known as Lakamha, is the site of a Maya city-state near the Usumacinta River in the Mexican state of Chiapas; its ruins date from about 226 BCE to about 799 CE. A medium-sized site, smaller than Tikal or Copán, it holds some of the finest architecture, sculpture and bas-relief carving the Maya produced. Sacked by Calakmul in 599 and 611, the city was rebuilt under K'inich Janaab' Pakal, who ruled from 615 to 683 and whose tomb Alberto Ruz Lhuillier found in the Temple of the Inscriptions in 1952. Elite construction in the ceremonial centre ceased sometime after 800, and the site was later abandoned and overgrown by forest.

entries.name: Calakmul
entries.desc: Calakmul is a Maya archaeological site in the Mexican state of Campeche, 35 kilometres from the Guatemalan border, and was one of the largest and most powerful Maya cities. It was the seat of the Kaan dynasty, the Kingdom of the Snake, whose emblem glyph is more widely distributed than that of any other Maya city; at its Late Classic height the city had an estimated 50,000 people. Throughout the Classic period it was a rival of Tikal, and under Yuknoom Che'en II, crowned in 636, it held a wide network of vassals. Its alliances collapsed after Tikal defeated El Peru in 743 and Naranjo in 744, and the city was finally abandoned after the early 10th century.

entries.name: Naranjo
entries.desc: Naranjo, called Wak Kab'nal in Mayan, is a Maya city in the Petén Basin of Guatemala, about 50 kilometres east of Tikal, occupied from about 500 BCE to 950 CE and at its height in the Late Classic period; its rulers were the Holy Lords of Sa'aal. In 546 it came under the control of Calakmul, which in 682 sent Lady Six Sky, a daughter of the Dos Pilas ruler, to re-establish its dynasty; acting as ruler, possibly as regent for her son, she oversaw attacks that defeated Tikal in 695. Tikal defeated Naranjo in 744 and took its ruler captive. Its final abandonment may have followed political turmoil and a severe drought of 810, and the site has been severely looted.

entries.name: Dos Pilas
entries.desc: Dos Pilas is a Maya site in the Petexbatún region of Petén, Guatemala, founded by an offshoot of the Tikal dynasty in 629 CE to control trade along the Pasión River. In 648 its ruler B'alaj Chan K'awiil, who claimed the Tikal throne, broke away and became a vassal of Calakmul; Tikal captured the city in 672, but Dos Pilas defeated Tikal in 679, conquered neighbouring cities and ruled with Aguateca as twin capitals of the Petexbatún kingdom. After Calakmul's defeat, Tamarindito and other centres rebelled, and in 761 the city was abandoned. Refugees threw up walls of stone stripped from its temples and palaces, but their village was overrun early in the 9th century.

entries.name: Quiriguá
entries.desc: Quiriguá is an ancient Maya archaeological site on the lower Motagua River in the department of Izabal, south-eastern Guatemala, where several Classic period trade routes met. Occupied by 200 CE, it was long a vassal of nearby Copán, with which it shares its architectural and sculptural styles. In 738 its king K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat captured Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil of Copán and had him sacrificed, and the city kept its independence and expanded rapidly. Its modest architecture is outweighed by its sculpture in hard red sandstone, including Stela E of 771, the tallest stela of the Maya world. Construction had halted by about 850; the site joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1981.

entries.name: Joya de Cerén
entries.desc: Joya de Cerén is an archaeological site in La Libertad Department, El Salvador, holding the remains of a pre-Columbian Maya farming village about 36 kilometres north-west of San Salvador. Thought to have been occupied between 200 and 600 CE, the village of an estimated 200 people was buried by ash from an eruption of the Loma Caldera around 600, apparently after its people had fled, for no human remains have been found. The ash preserved its houses, ceremonial buildings, stored food and fields, among them a manioc field, the earliest known evidence of manioc cultivation in the New World. Found by a bulldozer driver in 1976, it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993.

entries.name: Capacocha
entries.desc: Capacocha (Qhapaq hucha) was a sacrificial rite of the Inca that typically involved the sacrifice of children, sent as tribute by communities from across the empire and offered at important shrines known as huacas. Ceremonies marked events in the life of the Sapa Inca, such as his accession, illness or death, or were held to stop natural disasters; Pachacuti was the first Sapa Inca to order one. The children were paraded at Cuzco, then taken to the shrines, often on high Andean peaks, where they were killed or died of cold. Mummies found on Llullaillaco in 1999 and on Ampato, among them the girl called Juanita, preserve the rite's victims and offerings.

entries.name: Mitma
entries.desc: Mitma was a policy of forced resettlement used by the Incas, in which extended families or whole ethnic groups were moved from their home territory, often hundreds of kilometres, to lands recently conquered, forming enclaves of settlers called mitmaqkuna. People of loyal provinces were sent to new or hostile territories and rebellious villages to consolidated regions, carrying loyalty to the state and Inca language and technology with them. Settlers had to keep their own dress and practices; one who tried to return home was tortured, and executed on a second attempt. Modern studies suggest that about a quarter to a third of the empire's population was resettled.

entries.name: Yanakuna
entries.desc: The yanakuna were people in the Inca Empire who left the ayllu system and worked full-time for the Inca, the quya (queen) or the religious establishment, herding, fishing, making pottery, building and serving in households. The status was often hereditary, and a few yanakuna held high office and owned property. After the Spanish conquest the name passed to Indians in Spanish service, as auxiliaries or in encomiendas, and yanakuna became skilled artisans and free wage labourers, rising from less than 10% of tribute-paying subjects in the late 16th century to about 40% in the late 17th. In Chile, yanacona is now an insult for Mapuche considered to have betrayed their people.

entries.name: Calpulli
entries.desc: In Aztec society a calpulli (Classical Nahuatl calpōlli, 'large houses') was a unit of commoner housing within a Nahua city-state or altepetl, organised as a kin-based or other land-holding group; Spanish sources call them parcialidades or barrios. A calpul could rest on an extended family, a shared ethnic background or similar skills and tribute demands. Its members coordinated land use, food production and the making of tribute, paid in goods or labour, and shared organisational and religious tasks. The calpul also educated the young, running the Tēlpochcalli schools where young men learned to be warriors, and its men went to war for their calpul.

entries.name: Calmecac
entries.desc: The calmecac was a school for the sons of the Aztec nobility (pīpiltin) in the Late Postclassic period, where pupils entering at five to seven years of age lived and were trained in history, calendars, astronomy, religion, economy, law, ethics and warfare. Run by priests, it prepared students for the priesthood and for posts in government; Sahagún records that commoners were at times admitted to train as priests, and Moctezuma II graduated from it. The calmecac of Tenochtitlan stood in the ceremonial centre near the Templo Mayor and was dedicated to Quetzalcoatl; archaeologists of INAH uncovered seven successive buildings there in the mid-2000s.

credit.artist: Codex_Mendoza_folio_61r.jpg : Francisco Gualpuyohualcal? derivative work: El Comandante Hasta ∞

entries.name: Tēlpochcalli
entries.desc: The Tēlpochcalli (Nahuatl, 'house of the young men') were schools in each district or calpulli of the Aztec world, where youths were educated from the age of 15 to serve their community and to fight. They were attended by commoners, the macehualtin, and a few noble boys, while the sons of nobles went to the calmecac. Life there was hard: the day began with a cold bath and a frugal meal, and students memorised songs of praise to the gods, trained with the sling and the macuahuitl, carried materials to repair the temples and worked the fields together for their keep.

entries.name: Cihuacōātl
entries.desc: Cihuacōātl, sometimes known as Quilaztli, was one of a number of motherhood and fertility goddesses in Aztec mythology, associated especially with midwives and the sweat lodges where they worked, and patroness of the city of Culhuacan.
