In tradition she helped Quetzalcoatl create the present humanity by grinding the bones of earlier ages and mixing them with his blood; she was usually shown as a fierce skull-faced old woman bearing a warrior's spears and shield. Her name was also the title of a high official of Tenochtitlan, second to the tlatoani, who supervised internal affairs; Tlacaelel held it under four emperors in the 15th century.

entries.name: Idia
entries.desc: Idia was the mother of Esigie, Oba of Benin from 1504 to 1550, and the first Iyoba (queen mother) of Benin. When Oba Ozolua died she raised an army that defeated Esigie's brother Arhuaran, the heir by tradition, and secured the throne for her son; she was alive during the Idah war of 1515–1516, in which she helped Benin to victory. Esigie gave her the title of Iyoba with a palace of her own and ended the custom of killing the king's mother, and after her death he commissioned brass heads of her. Several images of her were looted in 1897, and an ivory mask of her in the British Museum became the symbol of the FESTAC festival in Nigeria in 1977.

entries.name: Emotan
entries.desc: Emotan, born Uwaraye in Eyaen, was a market woman who sold foodstuffs around the Oba Market in the Benin kingdom. After her husband's death she built a hut where she cared for children, the first day-care centre in Benin City. Oral history holds that she warned the exiled Prince Ogun of a murder plot by Oba Uwaifiokun and some chiefs, helping him take the throne as Ewuare the Great, who made her Iyeki, charged with enforcing the market rules. After her death Ewuare deified her and had a sacred Uruhe tree planted where she had traded; a bronze statue of her was unveiled at the Oba Market in 1954.

entries.name: Kapu
entries.desc: Kapu was the ancient Hawaiian code of conduct, a system of laws and prohibitions reaching into daily life, gender roles, politics and religion; the word, related to the Polynesian tapu that gave English 'taboo', means forbidden but also sacred, and its opposite is noa. Breaking a kapu, even by accident, often meant immediate death. Commoners could not touch a chief's hair or nail clippings, look directly at him or hold their heads higher than his, and under the ʻai kapu men and women could not eat together and women were barred from pork, most bananas and coconuts. Kamehameha II abolished the system in 1819 by sharing a meal of forbidden foods with the women of his court.

entries.name: Kahuna
entries.desc: Kahuna is a Hawaiian word for an expert in any field, used historically for doctors, surgeons and dentists as well as priests, ministers and sorcerers, and for masters of crafts such as canoe building, navigation and carving; it is glossed as 'keeper of hidden knowledge', from kahu, 'caretaker', and huna, 'secret'. According to Fornander the priesthood had ten branches, and a master of all ten could become kahuna nui, high priest, as Hewahewa was to Kamehameha I. Some kahuna practices were outlawed from 1831 to 1863 and from 1887 to 1919; since then all have been legal except sorcery, which was decriminalised in 1972.

entries.name: Ahupuaʻa
entries.desc: An ahupuaʻa is a traditional Hawaiian division of land, usually a slice of an island running from the mountains to the sea and taking in one or more whole watersheds with their marine resources, so that each held a cross section of the island's resources. It ranked below the island and the moku and was divided into ʻili and kuleana farmed by commoners, who paid labour taxes to support the chief. Each was ruled by an aliʻi and run by a konohiki; the name joins ahu, 'heap', and puaʻa, 'pig', for the stone cairns on its boundary where offerings, often a pig, were left for the chief. After the Great Mahele of 1848 most were split up, but many towns keep their names.

entries.name: Heiau
entries.desc: A heiau is a Hawaiian temple, ranging from simple earth terraces to elaborate stone platforms, built for purposes from healing the sick and offering first fruits to bringing rain, success in voyaging and success in war. Only the war temples, the luakini, were dedicated through human sacrifice, and only the ruling chief of an island or moku could use one. The largest known, Hale O Piʻilani on Maui, is a three-acre platform dating to the 13th century. After Kamehameha II abolished the kapu in October 1819 the heiau ceased to be places of worship and most were destroyed over the years, though some have been restored and many are still considered sacred.

entries.name: Makahiki
entries.desc: Makahiki was the ancient Hawaiian New Year festival in honour of the god Lono, lasting four lunar months from about October or November to February or March; on Hawaiʻi island it began with the crescent moon after the Pleiades, Makaliʻi, rose shortly after sunset. Work and war were forbidden; the konohiki collected offerings of pigs, taro, kapa and other goods for Lono's altars, while priests carried his image, the Akua Loa, around each island. Sports, hula and feasting followed, and at the end a canoe loaded with offerings was set adrift for Lono. Captain James Cook arrived at Kealakekua Bay during Makahiki in 1778.

entries.name: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park
aka: City of Refuge National Historical Park
entries.desc: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park, on the west coast of the island of Hawaiʻi, preserves a puʻuhonua, a place of refuge where until the early 19th century Hawaiians who had broken a kapu could escape death, be absolved by a priest and go free; defeated warriors and non-combatants could also shelter there in war. Its Hale o Keawe heiau, built about 1650 as the burial place of the ruler Keaweʻīkekahialiʻiokamoku, held 23 remains; the last bones were removed in 1829 and the temple destroyed, then reconstructed in the 1960s. Established in 1955 as City of Refuge National Historical Park, the 420-acre site took its Hawaiian spelling in 2000.
links: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park

entries.name: Kaʻahumanu
entries.desc: Kaʻahumanu was the favourite and most politically powerful wife of Kamehameha I and, as kuhina nui, co-ruler of the Hawaiian Kingdom under his first two successors. Born at Hāna on Maui, she married Kamehameha at thirteen. After his death in 1819 she shared power with Kamehameha II and, with Keōpūolani and the high priest Hewahewa, brought about the end of the kapu. In 1821 she and Kamehameha II had Kaumualiʻi of Kauaʻi kidnapped, and she married him by force. She converted to Protestant Christianity in 1824, ordered the first Catholic missionaries to leave in 1827, banned the hula in 1830, and died near Honolulu in 1832.

credit.artist: Louis Choris / Jean-Pierre Norblin de La Gourdaine

entries.name: Keōpūolani
entries.desc: Keōpūolani was the highest-ranking wife of Kamehameha I, a chiefess of naha rank, born of a royal half-brother and half-sister marriage, whose kapu required commoners to fall prostrate before her. Daughter of Kīwalaʻō, king of Hawaiʻi island, she was caught with her grandmother Kalola after Kamehameha's victory at Kepaniwai on Maui in 1790, and married him in 1795, linking his house to the ruling houses of Maui and Hawaiʻi. She bore Kamehameha II, Kamehameha III and Princess Nāhiʻenaʻena. In 1819 she joined Kaʻahumanu and Hewahewa in sharing a meal of forbidden foods to break the kapu, and she was baptised a Christian just before her death in 1823.

entries.name: Kānāwai Māmalahoe
entries.desc: The Kānāwai Māmalahoe, or Law of the Splintered Paddle, is a precept of Hawaiian law proclaimed by Kamehameha I in 1797, ordering that the old, women and children be free to lie by the roadside without fear of harm. It arose from an incident in Puna, where a fisherman, Kaleleiki, struck Kamehameha on the head with a paddle that broke, yet spared him; years later Kamehameha ruled that the man had only defended his land and family. Drawn from older Hawaiian ideas of legitimate rule, the law is written into Article 9, Section 10 of the state constitution and has become a model for modern human rights law on the treatment of civilians in war.

entries.name: Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site
entries.desc: Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site, at Kawaihae on the northwestern coast of the island of Hawaiʻi, preserves the ruins of the last major ancient Hawaiian temple. Kamehameha I built the luakini, the 'Temple on the Hill of the Whale', on the advice of the priest Kapoukahi to win the favour of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku; thousands of people raised it by hand without mortar, passing stones along a human chain about 14 miles long, and it was finished in the summer of 1791. His rival Keōua Kuahuʻula, invited there for peace, was killed on landing and his body offered to dedicate it. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1962.

entries.name: Abna al-dawla
entries.desc: The abna al-dawla, Arabic for sons of the regime or dynasty, were the Khurasani Arabs who took part in the Abbasid Revolution of 749–750 and their descendants who settled in Baghdad and Iraq. They became the ruling elite of the Abbasid Caliphate and formed the mainstay of the caliphal army. The term rarely appears in the sources until the Fourth Fitna of the 810s, when it was applied to the Khurasanis of Baghdad, who overwhelmingly supported Caliph al-Amin against his brother al-Ma'mun. After al-Ma'mun's victory they were largely replaced by his Persian followers, and under his successor al-Mu'tasim the Turkish slave-soldiers began their rise to power.

entries.name: Abu Hanifa
entries.desc: Abu Hanifa was a Muslim scholar, jurist and theologian, the founder and eponym of the Hanafi school of Sunni jurisprudence. After studying in Mecca and Medina he succeeded his teacher Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman as the leading authority on Islamic law in Kufa, and his school was distinguished by its use of analogy (qiyas), juristic preference (istihsan) and personal judgement (ra'y). He refused the post of chief judge offered by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur in 763, was imprisoned and tortured, and died in prison in Baghdad in 767. Through his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani his school spread, and it remains the most widely practised of the Sunni schools.

entries.name: Abu Yusuf
entries.desc: Abu Yusuf, born Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Ansari, was a Muslim jurist of Kufa and Baghdad and one of the foremost authorities of the early Hanafi school of Islamic law. The leading student of Abu Hanifa, he also studied under Malik ibn Anas in Medina. The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid made him Grand Qadi (qadi al-qudat), the first time the title had been conferred in Islamic history, with the power to appoint other judges, and through this office Hanafi law spread in the courts of the state. His Kitab al-Kharaj, written at the caliph's request, is one of the earliest systematic treatises on taxation and public finance in Islamic law.

entries.name: Affranchi
entries.desc: Affranchi was a French legal term for a freedman or emancipated slave, also used pejoratively for free people of color; in English it names the class of freedmen in Saint-Domingue and other slave-holding French territories, whose legal rights stood between those of free whites and enslaved Africans. Affranchis could get some education and own land, and many owned slaves: the indigo planter Julien Raimond claimed they held a third of the colony's slaves. Colonial laws barred them from voting, administrative posts and careers as doctors or lawyers. A 1791 court decision in their favour provoked a backlash from white planters that helped bring on the Haitian Revolution.

entries.name: Ahmad ibn Hanbal
entries.desc: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was an Arab jurist and hadith scholar of Baghdad, the founder of the Hanbali school of Sunni law and the compiler of al-Musnad, the largest hadith collection. He studied jurisprudence under Abu Yusuf and later under al-Shafi'i, and travelled through Arabia collecting narrations of the Prophet Muhammad. In the Mihna, the inquisition by which the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun imposed the Mu'tazili doctrine that the Quran was created, he refused to accept it: he was imprisoned, flogged to unconsciousness under al-Mu'tasim and banished under al-Wathiq, until al-Mutawakkil welcomed him back. He died in Baghdad in 855; his school is now dominant in Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

entries.name: Al-Hajj Salim Suwari
entries.desc: Al-Hajj Salim Suwari was a Soninke Islamic scholar (karamogo) of West Africa whose teaching centred on the town of Jagha; his dates are disputed, Ivor Wilks placing him in the late 15th century and Lamin Sanneh two centuries earlier. He formulated the Suwarian tradition, a rationale for Muslim minorities living under non-Muslim rulers: unbelievers are ignorant rather than wicked, God and not people decides the timing of conversion, and military jihad is a resort only in self-defence. His followers carried the tradition to the Voltaic region in the 16th and 17th centuries, and it survives today; the Jakhanke people also trace their spiritual ancestry to him.

entries.name: Al-Khayzuran
entries.desc: Al-Khayzuran bint Atta was the wife of the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi and the mother of the caliphs al-Hadi and Harun al-Rashid, and she exercised great influence over the state from 775 to 789. Kidnapped from her home near modern Bisha and sold as a slave to al-Mahdi, she persuaded him on his accession in 775 to free and marry her and to name her sons his heirs. She held audiences with officials and petitioners and amassed great wealth, and on al-Mahdi's death in 785 she secured the army's allegiance for al-Hadi. Al-Hadi tried to exclude her from state affairs, and she was rumoured to have had him murdered; Harun al-Rashid governed with her advice until her death in 789.

entries.name: Al-Nasir Hasan
entries.desc: Al-Nasir Hasan was a Mamluk sultan of Egypt, a son of al-Nasir Muhammad, who reigned twice, in 1347–1351 and 1354–1361. Installed at the age of 12, he was at first a ceremonial ruler under the senior emirs and was deposed in 1351 when he tried to assert his authority. Restored by a coup of the emirs Shaykhu and Sirghitmish, he purged the leading emirs through imprisonment, exile and execution and gave high ranks to the awlad al-nas, the descendants of mamluks, on a scale unprecedented in the sultanate. He was killed in 1361 by one of his own mamluks, Yalbugha al-Umari; the Sultan Hasan Mosque-Madrasa in Cairo, begun in 1357, was completed in 1363.

entries.name: Al-Qalqashandi
entries.desc: Al-Qalqashandi was a medieval Arab Egyptian encyclopedist and mathematician, a native of the Nile Delta who became a Scribe of the Scroll (katib al-darj), a clerk of the Mamluk chancery in Cairo. His major work, the Subh al-A'sha, a fourteen-volume encyclopedia completed in 1412, is an administrative manual covering geography, political history, natural history, cosmography and time measurement, based on the Masalik al-absar of Shihab al-Umari. David Kahn cited it as the first published discussion of substitution and transposition ciphers and of a polyalphabetic cipher; its section on cryptology quotes the work of Ibn al-Durayhim (1312–1361).

entries.name: Al-Shafi'i
entries.desc: Al-Shafi'i was a Muslim jurist and theologian, the founder and eponym of the Shafi'i school of Sunni jurisprudence, regarded as the founder of the principles of Islamic jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Born in Gaza into the Banu Muttalib clan of the Quraysh and raised in Mecca, he studied under Malik ibn Anas in Medina and later under the Hanafi jurist al-Shaybani in Baghdad. His al-Risala, among the earliest works on legal theory, set the order of the sources of law: the Quran, the hadith of the Prophet, consensus and analogy. He left for Egypt in 814, where he taught and dictated his major works, and died in al-Fustat in 820; his mausoleum remains an important site.

entries.name: Ali al-Rida
entries.desc: Ali al-Rida was the eighth Imam of Twelver Shia Islam, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad born in Medina, who succeeded his father Musa al-Kazim in 799. Departing from the anti-Shia policy of his predecessors, the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun invited him to Merv in Khorasan and in 817 named him heir apparent, changing the official colour from Abbasid black to green. The appointment provoked an Abbasid revolt in Baghdad, and as the court travelled back to Iraq al-Rida died at Tus in 818, probably poisoned; many historians hold al-Ma'mun responsible. The city of Mashhad grew up around his grave, the holiest site in Iran, visited by millions of Shia pilgrims every year.

entries.name: Ali ibn Isa ibn al-Jarrah
entries.desc: Ali ibn Isa ibn al-Jarrah was an official of the Abbasid Caliphate, born in Dayr Qunna into a family with a long history of government service, who served as vizier in 913–917 and 927–928 and in effect also during the vizierate of Hamid ibn al-Abbas in 918–923. His career, which coincided with the terminal decline of the Abbasid state, was marked by a power struggle with his rival Abu'l-Hasan Ali ibn al-Furat and by frequent exile. Austere and a determined opponent of corruption, he made many enemies, but he was later remembered as the good vizier for his administrative talent and honesty. He died in 946 during the sack of Baghdad by the Daylamites under Mu'izz al-Dawla.

entries.name: Allelengyon
entries.desc: The allelengyon was a Byzantine tax established in 1002 by Emperor Basil II, which obliged the wealthiest landowners, the dynatoi, to pay the tax arrears of their poorer neighbours. It rested on an old principle of Hellenistic and Byzantine law: the word allelengye, mutual guarantee, is first attested in papyri from Oxyrhynchus, and by the 9th and 10th centuries it described the collective tax obligation of rural communities. The law was unpopular with the wealthy, and pressure from the Church led Romanos III Argyros to abolish it in 1028, though around the turn of the 12th century Nicholas Mouzalon accused tax collectors of still applying it.

entries.name: Amat-Mamu
entries.desc: Amat-Mamu was a Babylonian nadītu priestess of the god Shamash who lived in the walled nadītu quarter, the gagûm, of Sippar and worked there as a scribe. Her name means woman servant of Mamu, the daughter of Shamash; as a nadītu she could own land but not marry or have children. Because the nadītu rarely dealt with men, several women of the community were taught to read and write, and the tablets she signed date from the reigns of three kings, Hammurabi, Samsu-iluna and Abi-Eshuh, showing that she worked as a scribe for at least 40 years. She is the only female scribe with a surviving work from the time of Abi-Eshuh.

entries.name: Ana Afonso de Leão
entries.desc: Ana Afonso de Leão was the queen regnant of Nkondo in the Kingdom of Kongo from 1673 and a decisive figure in the Kongolese civil war. A sister of King Garcia II Afonso and widow of Afonso II, she was regarded as the matriarch of the House of Kinlaza and built a quasi-independent principality, the Land of the Queen, that included Nkondo, Mpemba and the Duchy of Mbamba. She fought King Manuel I from 1682 to 1693 and took part in the negotiations to reunite the kingdom, finally backing Pedro IV, who was crowned in São Salvador in 1696. Pope Clement XI wrote to her in 1707, and she is believed to have died in 1710.

entries.name: Anne Robert Jacques Turgot
entries.desc: Anne Robert Jacques Turgot, Baron de l'Aulne, was a French economist and statesman, sometimes considered a physiocrat and best remembered as an early advocate of economic liberalism. As intendant of Limoges in 1761–1774 he sought a fairer assessment of the taille and replaced the corvée with a money tax, and in 1766 he wrote his Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth. Appointed Controller-General of Finance by Louis XVI in 1774, he freed the grain trade and in 1776 presented the Six Edicts, which suppressed the corvées and the privileges of the craft guilds. Opposition at court forced his resignation in May 1776, and he spent his last years in scientific and literary study.

entries.name: António I of Kongo
entries.desc: António I Vita a Nkanga was mwenekongo of the Kingdom of Kongo from 1661 until his death at the Battle of Mbwila in 1665. Elected after the death of Garcia II, he sought to remove the Portuguese from the region, sending envoys to Spain in vain and turning to Kongo's Mbundu allies in Matamba and the kingdoms of Dembos and Mbwila. When Alfonso VI of Portugal ordered the seizure of Kongo's copper mines in 1663, António denied that the mines existed. A succession dispute in Mbwila brought both sides to battle, where he was killed leading 400 swordsmen; his death without an heir opened a civil war between the houses of Kinlaza and Kimpanzu, and the kingdom took forty years to be reunited.

entries.name: Arib al-Ma'muniyya
entries.desc: Arib al-Ma'muniyya was a qayna, a slave trained in the arts of entertainment, of the early Abbasid period, characterised as the most famous slave singer ever to reside at the Baghdad court. Born in 797, she claimed to be the daughter of the Barmakid Ja'far ibn Yahya, a parentage modern scholars have questioned; she was bought by al-Amin and then by al-Ma'mun, and was freed by al-Mu'tasim. A poet, singer, composer and oud player, she left songs said to number around 1,000, and the Kitab al-Aghani of Abu'l-Faraj al-Isfahani places her singing without rival among her peers. Her career spanned the courts of five caliphs, and she died at Samarra in 890, aged 96.

entries.name: Askeri
entries.desc: The askeri were the ruling class of military administrators of the Ottoman Empire, made up of three main groups: the military, the court officials and the clergy. Although the word literally means of the military, it covered all the higher levels of imperial administration, and anyone holding a political office in the empire's service, Muslim or non-Muslim, could rank as askeri. They stood apart from the reaya, the tax-paying lower class, and from the kul, the slave class that included the Janissaries. After Napoleon invaded Ottoman Egypt in 1798, a reform movement under Sultan Selim III sought to reduce their numbers.

entries.name: Atossa
entries.desc: Atossa was an Achaemenid queen of Persia, the daughter of Cyrus the Great, wife first of her brother Cambyses II and then of Darius the Great, and mother of Xerxes I. After Darius overthrew the usurper Gaumata, he married her and her sister Artystone, and the union with the line of Cyrus reinforced his claim to the throne; Atossa became his primary consort. Herodotus credits her with urging Darius to send an expedition against the Greeks, and around 487 BCE she secured the succession of her son Xerxes, though he was not Darius's eldest son. Nothing is known of her death; Aeschylus' tragedy The Persians shows her still alive when Xerxes invaded Greece.

entries.name: Aud the Deep-Minded
entries.desc: Aud the Deep-Minded was a 9th-century settler of Iceland, the daughter of the Norwegian hersir Ketill Flatnose and wife of Olaf the White, King of Dublin. After her son Thorstein the Red was killed in battle in northern Scotland, she had a knarr built in secret at Caithness and sailed with her kin by way of Orkney and the Faroes to Breiðafjörður in Iceland, where she claimed land in Dalasýsla and freed the thralls aboard, giving them land to farm. Landnámabók describes her as a baptised Christian who raised crosses at Krosshólar, while Laxdæla saga, which calls her Unn, makes her a heathen given a ship burial. Many medieval Icelanders, among them the Sturlungs, descended from her.

entries.name: Balla Fasséké
entries.desc: Balla Fasséké is, in the oral tradition of the Epic of Sundiata, the jeli (griot) of Sundiata Keita and the ancestor of the Kouyate line of Malinke griots. Griots were the aristocratic oral historians who attended kings, recording and recalling the legacies of kings and kingdoms. In the epic, the dying king Naré Maghann Konaté gives Balla Fasséké, the son of his own jeli, to the young Sundiata as a gift, honouring a prophecy that Sundiata would be Mali's greatest king. When Sassouma Berete takes control of the throne for her son Dankaran Touman, she sends Balla Fasséké and Sundiata's half-sister Nana to the sorcerer king Soumaoro Kante of the Sosso.

entries.name: Basil Lekapenos
entries.desc: Basil Lekapenos, called the Parakoimomenos or the Nothos (the Bastard), was an illegitimate son of the Byzantine emperor Romanos I Lekapenos, a eunuch who served as grand chamberlain and chief minister for most of the period from 947 to 985. He served Constantine VII, helped bring Nikephoros II Phokas to the throne in 963 with some 3,000 armed attendants, and ran the fiscal administration under John I Tzimiskes, amassing vast estates in southeastern Anatolia. In 985 his great-nephew Basil II removed him, confiscated his possessions and annulled his laws, and he died in exile soon after. A lavish patron, he commissioned the enamelled cross reliquary now at Limburg Cathedral.

entries.name: Basilika
entries.desc: The Basilika, the imperial laws, was a Byzantine collection of law in sixty books completed around 892 in Constantinople by order of Emperor Leo VI the Wise, continuing the work of his father Basil I to simplify and adapt the Corpus Juris Civilis issued by Justinian I between 529 and 534. Justinian's code was in Latin, by then obsolete in the empire, and many of its laws no longer applied; the Basilika gave the law in Greek, added newer law such as the Procheiron and the Epanagoge, and carried commentaries (scholia). Its influence was limited to the East, but after the Greek War of Independence it was adopted in Greece until the present Civil Code.

entries.name: Battle of Keresztes
entries.desc: The Battle of Keresztes was fought on 24–26 October 1596 near the village of Mezőkeresztes in northern Hungary between a Habsburg-Transylvanian army and the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed III, which had just taken the fortress of Eger. The Christian army of about 55,000 men held fortified trenches and on the second day broke into the Ottoman camp, but its soldiers turned to plunder, and a counterattack by grooms, cooks and tent makers, followed by the Ottoman cavalry, routed it. Both sides lost heavily, so the Ottomans could not exploit their victory; 30,000 sipahis found absent were stripped of their timars, which contributed to the Celali rebellions.

entries.name: Birka grave Bj 581
entries.desc: Birka grave Bj 581 is a 10th-century chamber grave at the Viking Age site of Birka on the island of Björkö in Lake Mälaren, Sweden, which held the remains of a woman over the age of 30 buried with a sword, an axe, spears, arrows, two shields, a gaming set and two horses. Excavated by Hjalmar Stolpe in the 1870s, it was long held to be the grave of a high-status male warrior, until osteological analysis and a 2017 DNA study showed that the skeleton was female. The 2017 study, led by Charlotte Hedenstierna-Jonson, interpreted her as a high-ranking professional warrior; critics argue that grave goods do not establish a person's role, and the authors have defended their conclusion.

entries.name: Bois Caïman
entries.desc: Bois Caïman, Gator Wood, near Le Cap in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, was the site of the meeting of enslaved Africans in August 1791 at which the first major slave insurrection of the Haitian Revolution was planned. The Vodou ceremony, attended by 200 enslaved Africans according to a witness, was presided over by the houngan Dutty Boukman and the mambo Cécile Fatiman, and is remembered above all for the sacrifice of a black Creole pig. Within days the Northern Plain was in flames; the French later captured and beheaded Boukman. No first-hand written account survives and some scholars doubt that it took place, but it became a symbol of resistance to oppression.

entries.name: Bourgeoisie
entries.desc: The bourgeoisie is a social class of business owners, merchants and wealthy people that emerged in the Late Middle Ages as a middle class between the peasantry and the aristocracy. The word comes from the Old French borgeis, 'town dweller', from bourg, 'market town': the medieval bourgeois were the craftsmen, artisans and merchants of the towns, which grew into cities of commerce and crafts from the 11th century. The English Civil War, the American War of Independence and the French Revolution were partly motivated by their wish to be rid of feudal and royal limits on property and trade. In Marxist theory it owns the means of production and exploits the labour of the proletariat.

entries.name: Bóndi
entries.desc: Bóndi (plural bændr) was the Old Norse name for the free farmers and craftsmen who formed the core of society in Scandinavia in the Viking Age, a widespread middle class. They were free men with rights such as bearing weapons and, as farm-owning landlords, joining the Thing. The poem Rígsthula tells how the god Ríg fathered three classes, the thralls, the karls (or bændr) and the jarls. Besides farming, bændr were sailors, merchants and Vikings, and further north hunters and fishermen. In the Icelandic Commonwealth a bóndi was the formal follower of a goði, whose will influenced his vote at the Althing, under laws collected in the Grágás.

entries.name: Cacicazgo
entries.desc: A cacicazgo (anglicised as caciquedom) was an Indigenous chiefdom of the Caribbean ruled by a cacique and, in colonial Mexico, Peru and other parts of Spanish America, the entailed estate of an Indigenous noble, modelled on the Spanish mayorazgo. Spanish chronicles placed the cacique at the head of Caribbean society, and Bartolomé de las Casas called the cacicazgos kingdoms. In colonial Mexico entailment proved a successful means of keeping noble Indigenous resources as the situation of commoners declined. By law a cacique was the single heir of the estate, which always included land and often a subject labour force; cacicazgos survived into the 19th century.

entries.name: Cacique
entries.desc: A cacique (feminine cacica) was a chief of certain Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean and Latin America, such as the Kalinago and the Taíno; the word comes from the Kalinago kassiquan, 'to keep house'. Among the Taíno the rank was hereditary. The Spanish used the word for the leader of almost any Indigenous group: early Caribbean caciques such as Hatuey and Enriquillo eventually revolted, while those of Central Mexico became loyal intermediaries of colonial rule, styled don and doña, and some held entailed estates. Mexican independence in 1821 abolished their last privileges; the word later also came to mean a local political boss.

entries.name: Callicratidas
entries.desc: Callicratidas was a Spartan navarch, or fleet commander, in the Peloponnesian War, who rose to prominence although he belonged to the non-citizen mothax class. In 406 BCE he was sent to the Aegean to take over the Spartan fleet from Lysander, who had apparently returned the money meant to pay it to the Persian prince Cyrus. As a traditionalist Spartan he was loath to ask a Persian for funds, and the city of Miletus eventually paid instead. After a first victory over the Athenian admiral Conon at Mytilene, he was defeated and killed at the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE. He opposed alliance with Persia and said he would seek peace with Athens, and was well regarded after his death.

entries.name: Castizo
entries.desc: Castizo (feminine castiza) was a racial category of colonial Spanish America for people of three-quarters Spanish and one-quarter Amerindian ancestry, the child of a Spaniard and a mestiza. The category was widely recognised in colonial Mexico by the 18th century and was a standard subject of the century's casta paintings. Censuses kept records of castizos, in the hope of regulating entry into the coveted español category. Most scholars do not regard the labels as a rigid system of castes, since people could be classified differently at different points in their lives. In the 1778 census of what is now Argentina, castizos were counted as whites.

entries.name: Celali rebellions
entries.desc: The Celali rebellions were a series of risings in Anatolia against the Ottoman Empire in the late 16th and early to mid-17th centuries, by irregular troops led by bandit chiefs and provincial officials, named after Bozoklu Celal, who had rebelled in 1519. Historians link them to inflation, famine and unemployed soldiers; they never had a unified command and sought local power. Karayazıcı rose with 20,000 men in 1599. Kuyucu Murad Pasha crushed them from 1606 to 1608, throwing the heads of tens of thousands into wells, while the stronger leaders were taken into the government. Peasants fled their lands in the Great Flight, and thousands of Armenians left their homeland.

entries.name: Chandala
entries.desc: Chandala is a Sanskrit word for a person who deals with the disposal of corpses, and the name of a Hindu lower caste traditionally held to be untouchable. Vedic literature names the Chandala among groups outside the four varnas, the 'fifth' or panchama, and the Yajur-Veda describes them as an untouchable class born of the union of a Shudra man and a Brahmin woman. The Chinese traveller Faxian, crossing India in the 4th–5th centuries CE, wrote that they lived apart from others and that only the Chandalas were fishermen and hunters and sold meat. In many parts of India the word Chandal is still used as an insult.

entries.name: Charter to the Gentry
aka: Charter for the Rights, Freedoms, and Privileges of the Noble Russian Gentry
entries.desc: The Charter to the Gentry, in full the Charter for the Rights, Freedoms, and Privileges of the Noble Russian Gentry, was issued in 1785 by the Russian empress Catherine II. It recognised that the gentry owned their landed estates outright and guaranteed them civil rights, among them freedom from taxation and from corporal punishment, the right of assembly and trial in their own courts. It made the nobles of each province a legal corporate body, with assemblies of the nobility and books of genealogy. Though it mentioned only land, Richard Pipes argues that it turned the serfs, tied to the land and about half of the country's population, into the private property of their landlords.

entries.name: Cheng Yi
entries.desc: Cheng Yi was a Chinese classicist, philosopher and politician of the Song dynasty who, with his older brother Cheng Hao and later Zhu Xi, gave his name to the Cheng–Zhu, or Rationalistic, school of neo-Confucianism. He gained the 'presented scholar' degree in 1059, taught in Luoyang and declined many high offices. He campaigned against the reforms of Wang Anshi and in 1086 was appointed to lecture the emperor, but his enemies, among them Su Shi, had his teachings banned and him banished in 1097. He was pardoned in 1106, a year before his death. He is widely believed responsible for the rise of the cult of widow chastity, though he insisted on it only for scholar-officials.

entries.name: Cécile Fatiman
entries.desc: Cécile Fatiman was a Haitian Vodou priestess (manbo) and revolutionary who, with Dutty Boukman, led the ceremony at Bois Caïman that marked the beginning of the Haitian Revolution. The daughter of an enslaved African woman and a Corsican prince, she and her mother were bought and sold as slaves, and she gained her freedom before or during the rising of 1791. On the night of 21–22 August 1791 she presided over the ceremony, which gathered 200 enslaved people: a black pig was sacrificed, and those present swore to kill the white slavers and to obey Boukman as their commander. She later married the general Jean-Louis Pierrot and reportedly died at the age of 112.

entries.name: Danielis
entries.desc: Danielis was a widowed Byzantine noblewoman and landowner of Patras in the 9th century. According to the written tradition continuing that of Theophanes, she owned a large part of the Peloponnese and a flourishing carpet and textile industry, and gave lavish gifts and land to the future emperor Basil I the Macedonian when he visited Patras. After he became emperor she travelled to Constantinople and was given the title of Emperor's Mother (Basileomētōr). She outlived Basil and left her estate, with 80 domains and over 3,000 slaves, to his son Leo VI, who sent the slaves to settle in southern Italy. The historian Ilias Anagnostakis has argued that the story is largely fictional.

entries.name: Danjong of Joseon
entries.desc: Danjong (personal name Yi Hong-wi) was the sixth king of Joseon, who came to the throne at the age of 11 on the death of his father, King Munjong, in 1452. As he was too young to rule, the state was governed by the councillors Hwangbo In and Kim Chongsŏ, until his uncle, Grand Prince Suyang, overthrew them in a coup in 1453. Danjong was forced to abdicate in 1455; after a plot by six officials to restore him failed the next year, he was demoted to Prince Nosan and exiled to Yeongwol, and in November 1457 he was put to death on the orders of Suyang, now King Sejo, though the records conflict on how he died. He was restored to his title, with the temple name Danjong, only in 1698.

entries.name: Danka system
entries.desc: The danka system is the long-term affiliation of Japanese households with Buddhist temples, in use since the Heian period: the households (danka) support a temple, which in return provides for their spiritual needs. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637–38 the Tokugawa shogunate made it compulsory, so that every household had to join the nearest temple and obtain each year its certificate (terauke) that it was not Christian. The certificate was needed to marry, travel or take certain jobs, and those without one were recorded as hinin (non-persons) or executed as Christians. The compulsory system was abolished in the Meiji period, but it survives as a voluntary association.

entries.name: Darughachi
entries.desc: A darughachi (in Turkic basqaq or baskak) was an official of the Mongol Empire responsible for taxes and administration in a province, a division called a darugha. The title was established under Genghis Khan from 1211, and after the conquest of the Kipchaks and the Russian principalities in 1237–1240 Ögödei placed darughachi over peoples whose cities included Bolghar and Kiev. In Russia, where they were called baskaki, they supervised the collection of tribute, but were withdrawn by 1328, when the grand prince of Vladimir gathered it for the Golden Horde. In Goryeo the darughachi stationed after the invasion of 1231 were all killed in the summer of 1232.

entries.name: David Malo
entries.desc: David Malo (Davida Malo) was a Native Hawaiian historian, educator, politician and minister of the Kingdom of Hawaii. Born in Keauhou on the Island of Hawaiʻi, he grew up as Kamehameha I united the islands and probably served the chief Kuakini as oral historian and court genealogist. In 1823 he moved to Lahaina on Maui, learned to read and write from the Reverend William Richards, became a Christian and joined the first class of the Lahainaluna School. He composed a lament for Queen Kaʻahumanu in 1832, was elected to the kingdom's first House of Representatives in 1841 and was ordained a minister in 1852. His history, Ka Moʻolelo Hawaiʻi, appeared in English in 1898.

credit.artist: Alfred Thomas Agate of the United States Exploring Expedition, 1838-1842

entries.name: Demaratus
entries.desc: Demaratus was a king of Sparta from around 515 to 491 BCE, the 15th ruler of the Eurypontid dynasty and the firstborn son of King Ariston. He is best known for opposing his co-ruler, Cleomenes I of the Agiad dynasty. When Demaratus hindered him from punishing Aegina for submitting to Persia, Cleomenes backed Leotychidas' claim that Demaratus was not Ariston's son and bribed the Delphic oracle, and Demaratus was deposed in 491 BCE. He fled to the Persian court, received the cities of Teuthrania and Halisarna near Pergamum, and went with Xerxes I on his invasion of Greece in 480 BCE, where according to Herodotus he warned the king not to underestimate the Spartans.

entries.name: Demosioi
entries.desc: The demosioi (singular demosios, 'of the state') were the public slaves of ancient Athens, bought and owned by the state itself. The most numerous were the toxotai or Scythians, a police force armed with bows that kept order in the assembly, the courts and public places; 300 were bought in 480 BCE, and their number later rose to 1,200. Others served as clerks, executioners and torturers, worked in the treasury, the mint and the mines, or did tasks thought unsuitable for free citizens, such as waste disposal and the removal of the dead. Some historians argue that the demosioi were public appointees rather than slaves, but 'public slaves' remains the usual translation.

entries.name: Di Qing
entries.desc: Di Qing was a Chinese general of the Northern Song dynasty who led campaigns against the Western Xia and against the rebellion of Nong Zhigao in Guangxi. Born to a poor family in Xihe, Fenzhou, he was made commander of Yanzhou in 1038 and fought in the war with the Western Xia, going into battle in a bronze mask. On the advice of Fan Zhongyan he read the Zuo Zhuan and became a versed strategist, rising to Assistant Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs. Of the 25 battles he fought, he was best known for a night raid on Kunlun Pass in 1053. Folklore held him to be an incarnation of the God of Military Arts, and three Qing novels, the Romance of Di Qing, tell his story.

entries.name: Dream Pool Essays
aka: Brush Talks from a Dream Brook
entries.desc: The Dream Pool Essays (Meng Xi Bi Tan, in full Brush Talks from a Dream Brook) is an encyclopedic book by the Chinese polymath and statesman Shen Kuo, published in 1088 during the Song dynasty. Shen compiled it in forced retirement on his estate near modern Zhenjiang and named it after the estate. Its observations range over medicine, mathematics, astronomy, optics, engineering, metallurgy, early archaeology and fossils, from which Shen reasoned that climates had changed. It holds the first record of a compass used for navigation and the first description of Bi Sheng's movable type printing. Originally 30 chapters, it was reorganised into 26 in an edition of 1166.

entries.name: Dutty Boukman
entries.desc: Dutty Boukman was a leader of the Haitian Revolution, born to a Muslim family in Senegambia in about 1767 and enslaved first in Jamaica and then in Saint-Domingue. Sold for trying to teach other enslaved people to read, he became a slave driver and later a coach driver, which let him travel between plantations, carry news and encourage resistance. According to some contemporary accounts, he and the priestess Cécile Fatiman presided over the ceremony at Bois Caïman in August 1791, and on 22 August he led the rising at the Noé sugar refinery, usually taken as the start of the revolt. He was killed by French soldiers in November 1791 defending a rebel base.

entries.name: Ebussuud Efendi
entries.desc: Ebussuud Efendi was an Ottoman Hanafi jurist and Quran exegete who served as qadi of Istanbul from 1533 to 1537 and as Shaykh al-Islām, the empire's supreme judge, from 1545 until his death. Working closely with Suleiman the Magnificent, he built a legal framework joining sharia with the sultan's administrative law (qānūn), under which judges derived their power from the sultan and had to follow his law-letters. He systematised the issuing of fatwās and wrote thousands of them: some legitimised Suleiman's killings of Yazidis and declared the killing of the Qizilbash praiseworthy, others allowed coffee and Karagöz plays. He completed a commentary on the whole Quran in 1566.

entries.name: Eduba
entries.desc: An eduba (Sumerian for 'house where tablets are passed out') was a scribal school for the Sumerian language, which trained young scribes in ancient Mesopotamia in the late third or early second millennium BCE. Most of what is known of it comes from cuneiform texts of the Old Babylonian period (ca. 2000–1600 BCE), among them school stories such as 'Schooldays'. Archaeology suggests that training was small-scale and took place in private houses, such as House F at Nippur, where nearly one and a half thousand tablet fragments, mostly students' exercises, were found. Some scholars hold that the literary accounts are idealised or describe an earlier institution of the Ur III period.

entries.name: Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès
entries.desc: Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, usually known as the Abbé Sieyès, was a French Catholic priest and political writer, one of the leading theorists of the French Revolution. Born in Fréjus, he was educated for the priesthood but drawn to the Enlightenment thinkers, and rose to be vicar general of Chartres. His pamphlet What Is the Third Estate? of January 1789 became the Revolution's political manifesto and helped turn the Estates-General into the National Assembly in June 1789. He voted for the death of Louis XVI, lived through the Terror, became a director in 1799 and was among the instigators of the Coup of 18 Brumaire, which brought Napoleon Bonaparte to power. He also coined the term sociologie.

entries.name: Emperor Zhezong
entries.desc: Emperor Zhezong of Song (personal name Zhao Xu) was the seventh emperor of the Song dynasty of China, reigning from 1085 until his death in 1100. A son of Emperor Shenzong, he came to the throne as a child under his grandmother, Grand Empress Dowager Gao, whose conservative ministers reversed Wang Anshi's New Policies. After her death in 1093 he restored the reforms, named Zhang Dun grand chancellor and in 1094 renamed the era Shaosheng; the conservatives were purged and exiled, and the factional fighting intensified. His renewed war against the Western Xia expanded the Song to its greatest extent. He died in Kaifeng at 23 and was succeeded by his half-brother Huizong.

entries.name: Empress Gi
entries.desc: Empress Gi was a Goryeo-born empress of the Yuan dynasty, consort of Toghon Temür and mother of Biligtü Khan, later an emperor of the Northern Yuan. Sent to the Yuan court in 1333 among the concubines Goryeo had to supply, she became the emperor's favourite and, after the birth of her son in 1339, secondary empress in 1340, despite opposition at court to raising a Goryeo woman so high. As the emperor lost interest in governing she came to control the state economically and politically, and her brother Ki Ch'ŏl became in effect the ruler of Goryeo until King Gongmin destroyed the Gi family in 1356. She became primary empress in 1365, fled when the Yuan collapsed in 1368 and died in 1369.

entries.name: Enderun School
entries.desc: The Enderun School (Enderûn Mektebi) was a palace and boarding school in the Topkapi Palace, run by the Inner Service (Enderûn) of the Ottoman palace, chiefly for princes of the court and the Janissaries. Its students were mostly recruited through the devşirme, the Islamization of abducted Christian slave children for service in the Ottoman government and army. Mehmet II improved the palace school founded by his father, Murat II, to select the best youths of the empire and train them for government. Three preparatory schools outside the palace held some 1,000–2,000 students and the palace school about 300, who studied Islamic and positive sciences, languages, law, music and arms.

entries.name: Erling Skjalgsson
entries.desc: Erling Skjalgsson was a Norwegian political leader of the late 10th and early 11th centuries, a chieftain of Rogaland who lived on the farm Sola in Nord-Jæren and is commonly seen as the foremost defender of the traditional small kingdoms and the þing system against the Fairhair line. Baptised and married to Astrid, sister of King Olav Tryggvason, in 996, he was given the land between the Sognefjord and Lindesnes to rule. He fought Olav Haraldsson at the Battle of Nesjar in 1016, and in 1022 raised a 1,000-man army to free his nephew from the king. Trapped by Olav's fleet in the Battle of Boknafjorden in 1028, he was captured and killed by Aslak Fitjaskalle.

entries.name: Esnaf
entries.desc: Esnaf is a Turkish word meaning 'corporation', used for the guilds of craftsmen and traders of the Ottoman Empire. In the early modern period guilds were an urban phenomenon: membership gave people a voice and was an important part of their identity, and their economic activity was controlled by political authorities. In the Istanbul uprising of 1651 people made their voices heard as a group within their guilds, marched on the palace and, with a powerful religious leader on their side, forced the vizier to step down. Unlike European guilds, which marginalised Jews, Ottoman guilds mixed many religions, and many young women in the empire were hired to unwind cocoons, spin silk and weave.

entries.name: Esther Handali
entries.desc: Esther Handali was a Jewish Ottoman businesswoman, reportedly a Sephardic Jew from Jerez de la Frontera in Spain, who served as kira, or business agent, to the women of the Imperial Harem in Istanbul. Married to the merchant Eliya Handali, who sold jewellery, clothing and cosmetics to the harem, she acted as his agent and took over the business when widowed. She was the kira of Nurbanu Sultan from at least 1566, and while Nurbanu was valide sultan (1574–1583) carried her political and diplomatic correspondence, with Catherine de' Medici and, from 1578 to 1588, with Venice. Her fortune made her a benefactor of Istanbul's Jews, remembered for her relief after the great fire of 1569.

entries.name: Fan Zhongyan
entries.desc: Fan Zhongyan was a statesman, writer, scholar and reformer of the Northern Song dynasty in China. Born in Wu County, he passed the imperial examination as a jinshi in 1015 and served in regional posts and at court for over two decades, building a 150 kilometre coastal dyke and reorganising the defence of Shaanxi against the Tangut leader Li Yuanhao from 1040. As vice chancellor under Emperor Renzong he led the Qingli reforms, proposed with Fu Bi in 1043 and rescinded in 1045, which later inspired Wang Anshi. His essay 'On Yueyang Tower' (1046) holds his often-quoted ideal that scholar-officials should be the first to worry the worries of all-under-Heaven and the last to enjoy its joys.

entries.name: Fief
entries.desc: A fief (Latin feudum) was a central element of medieval contracts under feudal law: property or rights granted by an overlord to a vassal, who held it in fealty in return for allegiance, services or payments. It was usually land or revenue-producing property, but could also be an office, hunting or fishing rights, a trade monopoly or a tax farm. The term feudum, first attested in 984, replaced the older beneficium, and by the middle of the 10th century fiefs had largely become hereditary, an heir doing homage and paying a relief. By the 12th century English and French kings and barons commuted military service for cash payments (scutages); feudal fiefs still exist by law in Guernsey.

entries.name: Flour War
entries.desc: The Flour War was a wave of riots from April to May 1775 in the northern, eastern and western parts of the Kingdom of France, set off by a rise in the price of grain and bread. Turgot, Louis XVI's Controller-General of Finances, had abolished police regulation of the grain trade on 13 September 1774, and after poor harvests merchants' speculation spread shortages across the country. Rioters seized grain and paid what they held to be a just price, a practice known as popular taxation, and stood before Versailles on 2 and 3 May. Order returned with 25,000 soldiers, 162 arrests, two hangings and price controls; recent analyses treat the riots as a prelude to the French Revolution.

entries.name: François Mackandal
entries.desc: François Mackandal was a maroon and spiritual leader in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (present-day Haiti), sometimes described as a vodou priest (houngan). Born in Central or Western Africa and enslaved young, he is thought to have lost his right arm in a sugarcane press, and from around 1748 he lived as a maroon, making protective charms and holding rituals among the enslaved. Amid a panic among enslavers over poisoning, he was captured in 1758, accused of joining the maroons to kill slave owners, and burned at the stake without ever confessing; recent scholarship disputes that he ever used poison to kill. His case was seen as a precursor to the Haitian Revolution.

entries.name: Gabelle
entries.desc: The gabelle was the French state monopoly of the salt trade, in some regions a salt tax, and one of the most hated and unequal forms of revenue in the country's history. It grew from a duty on salt producers at Aigues-Mortes under Louis IX, and on 16 March 1341 Philip VI established the first permanent royal tax on salt; everyone over the age of eight had to buy a minimum amount each year. Rates differed widely between six groups of provinces: in 1784 Jacques Necker reported that a minot of salt cost 31 sous in Brittany but 611 in Berry, and smugglers (faux-sauniers) risked the galleys or death. Abolished in the French Revolution, it was reinstated by Napoleon and finally abolished in 1945.

entries.name: Gaspar Yanga
entries.desc: Gaspar Yanga was a Central African man who led a maroon colony of enslaved Africans in the highlands near Veracruz, New Spain, under early Spanish colonial rule. Thought to be of Bantu descent, he was kidnapped and sold into slavery, and around 1570 escaped a sugar plantation with others to the highlands near Mt. Orizaba, where their palenque grew to about 500 people and raided caravans on the Camino Real. In 1609 the maroons held off a Spanish force of about 550, and the stalemate ended in a treaty granting them freedom and self-rule, achieved sometime between 1618 and 1641. Their town, San Lorenzo de los Negros, was the first free town in the Americas and was renamed Yanga in 1932.

entries.name: General Indian Court
entries.desc: The General Indian Court (Juzgado General de Indios) was a judicial body the Spanish crown established in New Spain between 1585 and 1607 to settle disputes between indigenous communities and individuals. It followed the almost complete destruction of the indigenous peoples of the Caribbean and the steep fall in those of Central Mexico in the 16th century, and the failure of efforts to give Indians redress through the Spanish courts. Resting on the crown's duty to protect miserables such as widows and orphans, it offered swift, inexpensive justice, with legal aides paid by a tax of a half real. Vested Spanish interests opposed it, as complaints of exploitation could block their practices.

entries.name: Guan Daosheng
entries.desc: Guan Daosheng was a Chinese painter, calligrapher and poet of the early Yuan dynasty, credited as the most famous female painter and calligrapher in Chinese history and a prominent figure in bamboo painting. Born into a landed family in Huzhou, she married the scholar-official and artist Zhao Mengfu in 1286 and travelled with him between Dadu and the south. Her ink bamboo, unusual for a woman because the plant carried masculine associations, set bamboo within misty landscapes; the Yuan court collected her work and in 1317 gave her the title Madam of the Wei Kingdom. She died in 1319, and a handscroll of 1308 in the National Palace Museum in Taipei has a plausible claim to be hers.

entries.name: Gwageo
entries.desc: The gwageo were the national civil service examinations of Korea under the Goryeo (918–1392) and Joseon (1392–1910) periods, testing candidates' writing and knowledge of the Chinese classics, with technical examinations for medicine, interpretation, law and other fields. Based on imperial China's examinations, they first arose in Silla in 788 and were set up in Goryeo after the Hanlin scholar Shuang Ji visited in 958. Under Joseon they had literary, military and miscellaneous branches and became virtually the only path to a position of rank; in theory any man who was not a nobi could sit them, but in practice the yangban monopolised them. They were abolished in the Gabo Reforms of 1894.

entries.name: Hatamoto
entries.desc: A hatamoto ('guardian of the banner', often translated 'bannerman') was a high-ranking samurai in the direct service of the Tokugawa shogunate of Japan. The term arose in the Sengoku period for a lord's direct retainers, and after the Tokugawa clan's ascendancy in 1600 its hatamoto system was institutionalised; unlike the lower gokenin, a hatamoto of high enough rank had the right to an audience with the shogun. A 1722 study counted about 5,000, and at the start of the 18th century over two thirds earned less than 400 koku; they served as magistrates, inspectors and tax collectors. They lost their status with all other samurai on the abolition of the domains in 1871.

entries.name: Hellespontine Phrygia
entries.desc: Hellespontine Phrygia, or Lesser Phrygia, was a Persian satrapy (province) in northwestern Anatolia, directly southeast of the Hellespont, with its capital at Dascylium. Its first Achaemenid ruler was Mitrobates, appointed by Cyrus the Great, and from about 479 BCE the satrap Artabazus and his heirs, the hereditary Pharnacid dynasty, ruled it for most of its existence. In 334 BCE Alexander the Great gave it to his general Calas, who held the Persian title of satrap and collected the tribute once paid to Darius III. It then passed to Leonnatus and Lysimachus, joined the Seleucid Empire after the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BCE and was finally integrated into the kingdom of Bithynia.

entries.name: Hersir
entries.desc: A hersir was a local Viking military commander of a hundred, a county subdivision of about 100 men, who owed allegiance to a jarl or king. The term first meant a wealthy farmer who owned land and had the status of a leader, and during the Viking Age came to mean one who organised and led raids. From the 10th century the hersirs' influence declined as effective national monarchies developed in Scandinavia, and their independence as military leaders gave way to the title of a royal representative. Known hersirs include the Norwegian Ketill Flatnose of the 9th century and the Swede Jarlabanke Ingefastsson, who raised about 20 runestones with his relatives.

entries.name: Hewahewa
entries.desc: Hewahewa was a Hawaiian religious leader who served as kahuna nui (high priest) to King Kamehameha I and his successor Kamehameha II. A descendant of Paʻao and of the priestly order of the war god Kū, he was granted the Waimea Valley on Oahu and by the 1810s enforced the kapu code for Kamehameha. After Kamehameha I died in 1819 he joined Kaʻahumanu and other reformers in abolishing the kapu, ordering the burning of idols and the destruction of heiaus; a revolt against the change led by Keaoua Kekuaokalani was defeated at the Battle of Kuamo'o that December. He later converted to Christianity, brought by missionaries from 1820, and by contemporary reports died at Waimea in 1837.

entries.name: Hieratic
entries.desc: Hieratic (from the Greek for 'priestly') was a cursive writing system for Ancient Egyptian and the principal script of that language from its development in the third millennium BCE until the rise of Demotic in the mid-first millennium BCE. It developed from hieroglyphic script in the Naqada III period, roughly 3200–3000 BCE, and was mostly written in ink with a reed brush on papyrus, reading from right to left. Far more used than hieroglyphs, it served for administrative documents, accounts, letters and mathematical, medical, literary and religious texts. Demotic developed from it around 650 BCE, and priests kept hieratic for religious texts and literature into the third century CE.

entries.name: Hillersjö stone
entries.desc: The Hillersjö stone (U 29) is a runestone at Hillersjö on Färingsö in Uppland, Sweden, whose Old Norse inscription in the Younger Futhark tells the family history of Gerlög and her daughter Inga. The longest runic inscription in Uppland and the second longest in Sweden after the Rök runestone, it is carved in the Urnes style on an intertwined serpent, on a stone 2.8 by 1.0 metres, and signed by the runemaster Þorbjôrn Skald. It records how Gerlög's husbands and children died one after another, so that Inga's estate of Snottsta passed to her mother, a chain of inheritance consistent with rules later codified in the 1296 Uppland Law. It was carved sometime between 1060 and 1100.

entries.name: Hippeis
entries.desc: Hippeis (singular hippeus) is the Greek term for cavalry, and in Athens after the reforms of Solon the name of the second highest of the four social classes: men with a yearly income of at least 300 medimnoi, enough to buy and keep a war horse. The Athenian cavalry, formed after the Greco-Persian War in the 5th century BCE, grew from 300 men to 1,200 and was commanded by two hipparchs, while the boule examined its members and their equipment. In Sparta the hippeis were the royal guard of honour, 300 youths under thirty who served as heavy infantry in the king's bodyguard. Their counterparts were the Roman equites and medieval knights.

entries.name: Hird
entries.desc: The hird was, in Scandinavian history, at first an informal retinue of armed companions, the hirdmen or housecarls, and later the core of the royal army and a formal royal court household. The word comes from Old Norse hirð, from Old English hir(e)d, 'household, retinue', or perhaps a German cognate. By the reign of Håkon IV (1204–1263) the Norwegian hird had subdivisions on continental patterns, squires, men-at-arms and knights, its law code, the Hirdskraa, was read when the whole hird assembled at Christmas and Easter, and its upper ranks supplied royal officials. Under Håkon V (1299–1319) its Norse titles gave way to continental ones, and the king was technically first among equals.

entries.name: Hopae
entries.desc: Hopae were identification tags carried by Koreans in the Joseon period, recording the bearer's name, birthdate, place of birth, status and residence, which helped the government collect taxes and recover runaway slaves. After certain military officials were required to wear them in 1391, King Taejong made them compulsory for all males in 1413 to control migration, but the law was dropped in 1416 once a new household registry was complete. The system was abolished and restored several times, revived by Sejo in 1458 and by Prince Gwanghae in the early 17th century. The tags marked class: yellow for the yangban, ivory or deer horn for officials, and wood for commoners and slaves.

entries.name: Housecarl
entries.desc: A housecarl (Old Norse húskarl, 'house man'; Old English huscarl) was a non-servile manservant or household bodyguard in medieval Northern Europe. In Scandinavia the word first meant any free manservant and came to mean a lord's retainer; the institution was brought to Anglo-Saxon England by the Danish conquest in the 11th century, where a special tax paid the royal housecarls in coin. They also served as royal agents: in 1041 two of Harthacnut's housecarls, collecting a heavy levy, were killed in a revolt at Worcester. Historians debate whether they formed a standing elite army; under Harold Godwinson they were the backbone of the English army at Hastings and fought on after his death.

entries.name: Huang Daopo
entries.desc: Huang Daopo was a Chinese textile artist of the Yuan dynasty who rose from poverty to become one of the best-known women of the early Chinese textile industry. Sold into marriage by her family, she ran away from Songjiang, near Shanghai, and sailed to Yazhou on Hainan, where she learnt spinning and weaving from the local Li people. Around 1295 she returned to Songjiang and taught local women cotton spinning and weaving, improving the tools for ginning, fluffing, spinning and weaving, among them a three-spindle treadle-powered machine. Her methods made her hometown a centre of textile manufacturing and had a large economic impact on the Yangtze River Delta.

entries.name: Hunayn ibn Ishaq
entries.desc: Hunayn ibn Ishaq al-Ibadi, known in Latin as Johannitius, was an Arab Nestorian Christian translator and physician of the Abbasid period, his era's most productive translator of Greek medical and scientific works. Born in al-Hirah to the ʿIbad, an Arab community of the Church of the East, he studied medicine in Baghdad and mastered Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Persian. Called the Sheikh of the Translators, he translated 129 works of Galen and works of Plato and Aristotle into Syriac and Arabic, and his Ten Treatises of the Eye is the first known systematic treatment of ophthalmology. Caliph al-Mutawakkil made him his physician, but imprisoned him for a year for refusing to make a poison.

entries.name: Hundi
entries.desc: A hundi is a financial instrument developed in medieval India for trade and credit, used to send money from place to place, to borrow money as a form of IOU, and as a bill of exchange between merchants. Written records show its use at least as far back as the 12th century; the Jain merchant Banarasi Das, born in 1586, received a hundi for 200 rupees from his father to borrow money and start trading. There were many kinds, among them the sahyog hundi passed from merchant to merchant, the darshani hundi payable on sight and the muddati hundi payable after a set time. In the colonial era the British regarded the system as indigenous but not informal and sought to tax its transactions.

entries.name: Hwang Jini
entries.desc: Hwang Jini was one of the best-known kisaeng of Korea's Joseon period, who lived during the reign of King Jungjong and was also known by her kisaeng name Myŏngwŏl. Born around 1506, the illegitimate daughter of Hwang Chinsa, a politician's son from a noble family of Kaesong, and of a woman who was either a kisaeng or of cheonmin status, she became a kisaeng, according to legend, after losing a lover at the age of 15. That life let her learn music, dance, art, literature and poetry, subjects not normally taught to young women. Only a handful of her sijo verses and geomungo pieces survive, many about Kaesong and lost love, and she has become an almost mythic figure in modern Korea.

entries.name: Hydarnes the Elder
entries.desc: Hydarnes, also known as Hydarnes the Elder, was a Persian nobleman and one of the seven conspirators who overthrew the Pseudo-Smerdis, a plot led by the Achaemenid prince Darius. His name is the Greek form of the Old Persian Vidṛna, which may have meant 'he who knows the guilt'. According to some Persepolis tablets he served as satrap of Media under Darius, and for his services he was seemingly given the satrapy of Armenia as a semi-hereditary fief, which his descendants governed until the Hellenistic period; Orontes I, ancestor of the Orontid dynasty, descended from him. His sons Hydarnes the Younger and Sisamnes served as commanders under Xerxes I.

entries.name: Hürrem Sultan
entries.desc: Hürrem Sultan, known in Europe as Roxelana, was the chief consort and legal wife of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, the mother of his successor Selim II and the first haseki sultan. Presumably born in Ruthenia to an Orthodox family, she was captured by Crimean Tatars in a slave raid, taken to Constantinople and became Suleiman's favourite concubine around his accession in 1520. Breaking with custom, he freed and married her, and she became his most trusted adviser, influencing appointments and diplomacy, the first in a series of powerful women of the Sultanate of Women. She founded the Haseki Sultan Complex and died in 1558.

entries.name: Ibn Taghribirdi
entries.desc: Ibn Taghribirdi, Abu al-Mahasin Yusuf, was a historian of Mamluk Egypt who studied under al-Ayni and al-Maqrizi, two of the leading Cairene historians of the day. His best-known work, al-Nujum al-zahira fi muluk Misr wa'l-Qahira, is a multi-volume chronicle of Egypt from the Islamic conquest of 641 to 1468, written year by year with precise dates that suggest privileged access to the sultans and their records. He also compiled al-Manhal al-safi, a biographical dictionary of about 3,000 entries on sultans, amirs, scholars and others, and a continuation of al-Maqrizi's history of Egypt. His father's Turkic name, Taghribirdi, means god-given.

entries.name: Ibn Taymiyya
entries.desc: Ibn Taymiyya was a Sunni Muslim scholar, jurist and theologian of the Hanbali school, born in Harran in 1263, whose family fled the Mongol invasion to Damascus in 1269. He issued fatwas declaring the Mongol Ilkhanids unbelievers and calling for jihad against them, fought at the Battle of Marj al-Saffar, and wrote polemics against Shia Islam, Ash'arism and philosophy and against the veneration of saints at their tombs. Accused of anthropomorphism and censured for his rulings, he was imprisoned several times and died in the Citadel of Damascus in 1328. His writings later influenced Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and modern Salafi and militant Islamist movements.

entries.name: Imperial Preceptor
entries.desc: The Imperial Preceptor, or Dishi, 'Teacher of the Emperor', was a high title and powerful post of the Yuan dynasty, created by Kublai Khan as part of the Mongol patronage of Tibetan Buddhism and Yuan rule over Tibet. In 1260 Kublai named the Sakya lama Drogön Chögyal Phagpa State Preceptor (Guoshi) and put him in charge of all Buddhist clergy; when the title was renamed in 1270, Phagpa became Imperial Preceptor. A Sakya monk residing in China held the post, supervising the clergy of the empire and advising on appointments in Tibet. After the Ming overthrew the Yuan in 1368, the title was revoked and replaced by titles of lesser status.

entries.name: Irdabama
entries.desc: Irdabama was a Persian businesswoman in the reign of Darius the Great, the wealthiest businesswoman attested in the Achaemenid records at Persepolis. Who she was is unclear: she has been suggested to be of aristocratic or royal birth, perhaps from a family of Elamite dynasts centred at Susa, and the records may even concern two different women. She had her own workforce, including 480 labourers based mainly around present-day Shiraz, dealt chiefly in wine and grain and managed estates and production centres. Seals record her transactions and the rations she gave her staff, and she travelled widely in Iran and Mesopotamia with her own servants.

entries.name: Itakh
entries.desc: Itakh al-Khazari was a leading commander of the Turkic army of the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim, a Khazar said to have worked as a slave cook before al-Mu'tasim bought him as a ghulam in 815. He rose to command the caliph's personal guard, took part in the Sack of Amorium and under al-Wathiq was named governor of the Yemen and of Egypt. In 847 he helped choose al-Mutawakkil as caliph and on his orders arrested the vizier Ibn al-Zayyat, who was tortured to death, becoming chamberlain and head of the barid, the post and intelligence service. Sent on pilgrimage in 848, he was arrested on his return and died of thirst in prison in 849.

entries.name: Jacques Necker
entries.desc: Jacques Necker was a Genevan banker and statesman who served as finance minister of France under Louis XVI. Born in Geneva in 1732, he grew rich as a banker in Paris and in 1777 was made director-general of the royal treasury, as his Protestant faith barred him from the post of Controller-General. In 1781 he published the Compte rendu, making the royal budget public, and was dismissed within months. Recalled in 1788 amid fiscal crisis, he doubled the representation of the Third Estate at the Estates-General; his dismissal on 11 July 1789 helped bring about the Storming of the Bastille. Recalled within two days, he resigned in September 1790 and died in 1804.

entries.name: Jahanara Begum
entries.desc: Jahanara Begum was a Mughal princess, the eldest surviving child of the emperor Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal. After her mother's death in 1631, the 17-year-old was given the royal seal and the title Padshah Begum, first lady of the empire, and she wielded great political influence in her father's reign. In the war of succession after Shah Jahan's illness in 1657 she backed her brother Dara Shikoh, then cared for her father under Aurangzeb's house arrest in Agra Fort until his death in 1666, later reconciling with Aurangzeb. She wrote a biography of the Sufi saint Mu'in al-Din Chishti, funded the Jami Masjid of Agra and is buried at the Nizamuddin Dargah in Delhi.

entries.name: Jakhanke
entries.desc: The Jakhanke are a Manding-speaking people of the Senegambia region, often classed as a subgroup of the Soninke, who historically formed an endogamous caste of Muslim clerics and teachers. Centred in Guinea, with smaller communities in The Gambia, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau and Mali, they have been part of the region since the 15th century and helped spread Islam among the Manding peoples. Their tradition stressed learning, the teaching of the young, the rejection of jihad and keeping out of politics; when threatened, they moved their villages. From at least the 17th century they also traded in rice, salt, cloth, gold and slaves, and their farms relied on slave labour.

entries.name: Jiaochao
entries.desc: Jiaochao is the Chinese word for the banknotes of the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty and later of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Wanyan Liang issued them in 1154, three years before the Jin minted coins of their own, in ten denominations from 100 wen to 10 guan; overprinting brought runaway inflation, and in 1215 they were replaced by a new paper currency. Kublai Khan issued jiaochao in 1260, the October issue on the silver standard, and they became the first paper currency to serve as China's main circulating medium, described by Marco Polo, William of Rubruck and Ibn Battuta. They too lost their value, and the last series, a fiat currency of 1350, was widely rejected.

entries.name: John Axouch
entries.desc: John Axouch was a Byzantine commander of Seljuk Turkish birth who served as megas domestikos, commander-in-chief of the army, under John II Komnenos and early in the reign of Manuel I Komnenos. Captured as a child at the Siege of Nicaea in 1097 and given to Alexios I Komnenos, he was raised in the imperial household as the companion of the future John II, who made him megas domestikos on his accession in 1118. He conducted the siege of Laodicea in 1119 and fought in the Balkans, Cilicia and Syria, and on John's death in 1143 secured Constantinople for Manuel. He led the forces that drove the Normans from Corfu in 1149 and died soon after, possibly in 1150.

entries.name: John Papa ʻĪʻī
entries.desc: John Papa ʻĪʻī was a Hawaiian politician and historian, born on Oʻahu in 1800 into a family of hereditary kahu, caretakers of the chiefs. Raised under the kapu system, he was taken to Honolulu at the age of ten to be companion and attendant to Prince Liholiho, the future Kamehameha II. Among the first Hawaiians to learn reading and writing from the missionaries, he later sat on the Privy Council, in the House of Nobles from 1841 to 1870 and on the Supreme Court as an associate justice from 1852 to 1864. His articles in the newspaper Ka Nupepa Ku'oko'a, published in English in 1959 as Fragments of Hawaiian History, give a first-hand account of life under Kamehameha.

credit.artist: Henry L. Chase derivative work: Yjenith ( talk )

entries.name: Julien Raimond
entries.desc: Julien Raimond was an indigo planter of the French colony of Saint-Domingue, a free man of colour who became a leader in the Haitian Revolution and the formation of Haiti. A slaveholder with over 100 slaves by the 1780s, he moved to France in 1785 to campaign against the colony's racially discriminatory laws, and from 1789 pressed the National Assembly, working with Vincent Ogé, Henri Grégoire and the Society of the Friends of the Blacks. On 15 May 1791 the legislature gave wealthy free-born men of colour the vote, and white colonists' resistance led to civil war. Raimond later returned to Saint-Domingue, helped write the 1801 Constitution under Toussaint L'Ouverture and died soon after.

entries.name: Kalanimoku
entries.desc: Kalanimoku, who took the name William Pitt, was a Hawaiian high chief who served much like a prime minister under Kamehameha I, Kamehameha II and early in the reign of Kamehameha III. Born on Maui around 1768, a grandson of Kekaulike of Maui, he was captured by Kamehameha's forces at the Battle of Mokuohai but spared, and became his chief minister and treasurer. In 1819 he was baptised a Roman Catholic aboard the French ship Uranie, and in December that year he led the army that defeated Kekuaokalani's revolt at Kuamoʻo. He was regent with Kaʻahumanu from 1823 and died at Kailua Kona in 1827; for his abilities he was called the Iron Cable of Hawaiʻi.

credit.artist: Kalanimoku.jpg : Attributed to Louis Choris, German Russian painter 1795-1828 derivative work: PawełMM ( talk )

entries.name: Kamehameha II
entries.desc: Kamehameha II, born Liholiho, was the second king of the Kingdom of Hawaii, from the death of his father Kamehameha I in 1819 until his own in 1824. Young and inexperienced, he was held to a largely ceremonial role by his father's wife Kaʻahumanu, who became the first Kuhina Nui. Six months into his reign he ate a meal with Kaʻahumanu and his mother Keōpūolani, breaking the kapu system of religious laws in the 'Ai Noa; the priesthood was disbanded, temples and images were destroyed and his forces defeated the defenders of the old religion at the Battle of Kuamoʻo. He sailed to London in 1823, where he and Queen Kamāmalu died of measles in 1824.

credit.artist: not given, probably from Hawaii State Archives

entries.name: Keʻeaumoku Pāpaʻiahiahi
entries.desc: Keʻeaumoku Pāpaʻiahiahi was a high chief of the Kona district of Hawaiʻi island, the father of Kaʻahumanu and the principal agent in raising Kamehameha I to the throne. One of the first five Kona chiefs to back Kamehameha against his cousin Kīwalaʻō, he led Kamehameha's warriors to victory at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai in 1782, where Kīwalaʻō was killed. He commanded Kamehameha's forces in most of his campaigns and served as his counsellor and prime minister, and he persuaded George Vancouver to trust Kamehameha, which led to an alliance with the British. He died in 1804 in an epidemic, likely cholera, that struck Kamehameha's army as it prepared to invade Kauaʻi.

entries.name: Khopesh
entries.desc: The khopesh was an Egyptian sickle-like sword that developed from crescent-shaped battle axes. The type originated in Western Asia in the Bronze Age: the Stele of the Vultures shows King Eannatum of Lagash wielding one, dating it to at least 2500 BCE, and it was introduced to Egypt in the Second Intermediate Period, when the Hyksos ruled Lower Egypt. Typically 50–60 cm long and sharpened only on the outside of its curved end, it became more common in the New Kingdom, when it changed from bronze to iron. Kings were often shown with it as a symbol of power and conquest, and dull-edged examples from high-status graves were probably ceremonial; two were found with Tutankhamun.

entries.name: Kletorologion
entries.desc: The Kletorologion of Philotheos is the longest and most important of the Byzantine lists of offices and court precedence, published in September 899 in the reign of Leo VI the Wise by Philotheos, a protospatharios and atriklines otherwise unknown. As atriklines he received the guests at imperial banquets and seated them by their place in the hierarchy, and he compiled the work from older kletorologia as a guide to the order of the banquets and the name and value of each title.
