It survives only as an appendix in the De Ceremoniis of Constantine Porphyrogennetos. Its four sections survey the ranks and offices of the empire, set the order of precedence and advise on the year's banquets.

entries.name: Kongo Civil War
entries.desc: The Kongo Civil War was a war of succession in the Kingdom of Kongo between the rival houses of Kinlaza and Kimpanzu, joined by other factions such as the Água Rosada of Kibangu and the da Silva of Soyo. It began after the Battle of Mbwila in 1665, where the Portuguese of Angola defeated Kongo and killed King António I and many Kinlaza nobles. Soyo then made and unmade kings, and in 1678 the capital, São Salvador, was burnt, leaving rival claimants to rule from mountain fortresses. Pedro IV retook São Salvador in 1709 and set a rotating succession between the two houses, but many Bakongo captured in the fighting had been sold into the Atlantic slave trade.

entries.name: Konohiki
entries.desc: A konohiki was the headman of an ahupuaʻa, a land division of the Kingdom of Hawaii, who administered the land on behalf of the aliʻi chief who ruled it. The islands were split into districts, or moku, running from the mountain tops down to the sea, and these into ahupuaʻa, named after the boundary altars where taxes were collected during the Makahiki. Usually a relative of the chief and of aliʻi rank, the konohiki oversaw water rights, the distribution and farming of land and its upkeep, and saw that gifts and tributes reached the chief at the right times. As capitalism entered the kingdom, the konohiki became tax collectors, landlords and wardens of the fisheries.

entries.name: Kuge
entries.desc: The kuge were the Japanese aristocratic class that dominated the imperial court in Kyoto. Leaders and patrons of the arts in the Heian period, from the late 8th century, they were eclipsed by the warrior class, the bushi, with the rise of the Kamakura shogunate in the 12th century, but kept a weak court around the emperor. Only the higher dōjō, about 130 families in the Edo period, could hold the highest court offices, and the regents came from the Fujiwara. Having lost most of their income after the Sengoku period, they lived partly by teaching arts such as waka poetry and the biwa. In 1869 they merged with the daimyō into the kazoku peerage, abolished by the 1947 constitution.

entries.name: Kuhina Nui
entries.desc: The Kuhina Nui was a powerful office of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi from 1819 to 1864, usually held by a relative of the king and roughly equivalent to a prime minister or regent. It was created for Queen Kaʻahumanu, Kamehameha I's favourite wife, when Kamehameha II came to the throne in 1819, and she ruled as regent for the young Kamehameha III from 1824; later female holders took the title Kaʻahumanu with a number. The constitutions of 1840 and 1852 made the Kuhina Nui share power with the king, neither acting without the other's knowledge. Kamehameha V, who favoured a more autocratic monarchy, abolished the office in his constitution of 1864.

entries.name: Kuttab
entries.desc: A kuttab, or maktab, is a type of elementary school of the Muslim world, where a sheikh teaches a group of children seated before him on the ground. It taught reading, writing, grammar and Islamic studies, above all memorising and reciting the Qur'an, and often other subjects. Known since at least the 10th century and often attached to a mosque, it was described in the 11th century by Ibn Sina, who held that children should start at six and learn better in classes than with private tutors. In Cairo kuttabs were often built above public water kiosks as sabil-kuttabs, and until modern schools spread in the 20th century they were the main means of mass education in much of the Islamic world.

entries.name: Leysingi
entries.desc: In Norse law, a leysingr (plural leysingi) was a freed slave, or freed thrall. A slave whose freedom had been given but not made public was a frjálsgjafar, the lowest rank of freedman, who became a leysingi by giving a freedom ale; manumission had to be confirmed by oath and announced at an assembly or in church. Freedmen stayed inferior in the law codes: the former master controlled where they lived and whom they married, they could not leave his property without permission, and their children's inheritance was restricted. Slavery, most widespread in the Viking Age, was small-scale and household-based, and it had disappeared in most of Scandinavia by the 14th century.

entries.name: Li Qingzhao
entries.desc: Li Qingzhao was a Chinese poet and essayist of the Song dynasty, considered one of the greatest poets in Chinese history. Born in 1084 in present-day Shandong to a family of scholar-officials, she was known in elite circles by 1101, when she married Zhao Mingcheng, with whom she collected books, inscriptions and calligraphy. In the Jin–Song wars the couple fled south after the fall of Kaifeng in 1127; Zhao died in 1129, and Li settled in Hangzhou, completing his Catalogue of Inscriptions on Metal and Stone and writing an afterword on their life. Only about a hundred of her poems survive, mostly in the ci form, her later work marked by loss and nostalgia.

entries.name: Logothete
entries.desc: Logothete was an administrative title of the eastern Roman Empire that rose in the middle and late Byzantine Empire to a senior post equivalent to a minister or secretary of state. Logothetes succeeded the fiscal officials of Late Antiquity; under Justinian I they gathered revenue in the provinces, and in the 7th century the old financial departments gave way to smaller ones, some headed by a logothete, such as the genikon for taxation and the dromos for the imperial post, diplomacy and intelligence. Alexios I Komnenos created a logothete over all the departments, later the Grand Logothete. The title spread to Bulgaria, Sicily, Serbia and the Danubian Principalities.

entries.name: Léger-Félicité Sonthonax
entries.desc: Léger-Félicité Sonthonax was a French politician and colonial administrator who, as Civil Commissioner in Saint-Domingue during the Haitian Revolution, proclaimed the freedom of all slaves in its north province on 29 August 1793. A lawyer from Oyonnax and a member of the Society of the Friends of the Blacks, he was sent to the colony in 1792 with Étienne Polverel to enforce equal rights for free people of colour, not to end slavery. The National Convention ratified emancipation on 4 February 1794, applying it to all French colonies. Acquitted in France in 1795, he returned to Saint-Domingue, but Toussaint Louverture sent him back to France in 1797; he died in Oyonnax in 1813.

entries.name: Madame de Pompadour
entries.desc: Jeanne Antoinette Poisson, Marquise de Pompadour, was a member of the French court who was the official chief mistress of King Louis XV from 1745 to 1751 and remained influential as court favourite until her death. Born in Paris in 1721, she moved in the salons of the Enlightenment, and the king gave her the marquisate of Pompadour in 1745; she was made a duchess in 1752 and lady-in-waiting to the queen in 1756. She shaped appointments and domestic and foreign policy, patronised the philosophes, among them Voltaire, and bought the porcelain factory at Sèvres in 1759. She died of tuberculosis in 1764 at the age of 42.

entries.name: Magi
entries.desc: The magi (singular magus) were priests in Zoroastrianism and earlier Iranian religions. The earliest known use of the word is in the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great, of about 520 BCE, and in the mid-5th century BCE Herodotus described the magi both as a tribe of the Medes and as a priestly caste who interpreted omens and dreams. Through Greek the word came to mean a practitioner of magic, the source of the modern words magic and magician. In the Gospel of Matthew, magi from the east pay homage to the infant Jesus, a use rendered in English as kings or wise men. A hereditary Zoroastrian priesthood survives in India and Iran.

entries.name: Mana
entries.desc: Mana is, in Melanesian and Polynesian cultures, a supernatural force that permeates the universe that anyone or anything can have. The reconstructed Proto-Oceanic word *mana is thought to have referred to powerful forces of nature such as thunder and storm winds, and came to mean unseen supernatural power as Oceanic-speaking peoples spread eastward. In Polynesia, to have mana implies influence, authority and efficacy; in Māori culture it underlies leadership and authority over a territory. The missionary Robert Henry Codrington gave the first detailed English description in 1891; later theories of mana as a universal origin of religion are now viewed as inaccurate.

entries.name: Manorialism
entries.desc: Manorialism, also called seigneurialism or the manor system, was the method of land tenure in parts of Europe, notably France and later England, during the Middle Ages. A lord and his dependents lived in a manor house or castle and administered a rural estate worked by labourers or serfs who owed labour, produce and later cash. It originated in the Roman villa system of the Late Roman Empire, where coloni were bound to the land, and was an essential element of feudal society. It faded slowly with the rise of a money-based market economy: the last feudal dues in France were abolished at the French Revolution, and Junker manors in parts of eastern Germany remained until World War II.

entries.name: Megabyzus
entries.desc: Megabyzus (Old Persian Bagabuxša) was an Achaemenid Persian general, son of Zopyrus, satrap of Babylonia, and grandson of Megabyzus I, one of the seven conspirators who put Darius I on the throne. After his father was killed in the Babylonian revolt of 484 BCE, he led the forces that recaptured the city, and he took part in the Second Persian invasion of Greece (480–479 BCE). As satrap of Syria he commanded the army that put down the revolt of Inarus in Egypt from 456 BCE, besieging the Athenians on the island of Prosopitis for 18 months until he drained the river around it. He later revolted against Artaxerxes I, was pardoned, and died at the age of 76.

entries.name: Mehmed III
entries.desc: Mehmed III was sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1595 until his death in 1603. Born at Manisa in 1566 to the future Murad III and his concubine Safiye, he had all nineteen of his brothers executed on his accession, while his mother Safiye Sultan held such power as valide sultan that ministers regarded her as a co-ruler. In the Long Turkish War he took personal command of the army, the first sultan to do so since Suleiman I, conquering Eger in 1596 and winning the Battle of Keresztes, though Győr was later lost. He had his son Mahmud strangled in 1603 and died that December at 37, succeeded by his 13-year-old son Ahmed I.

entries.name: Mestizo
entries.desc: Mestizo, Spanish for mixed person, is an ethno-cultural category used mainly in the Hispanic world for people whose identity derives mostly from mixing between Spanish and Native heritage. It began as one of the castas of the Spanish Empire's colonies, a formal label in censuses, parish registers and Inquisition trials; mestizos were the first group set apart from Spaniards and enslaved Africans, and stood above other castas, since they paid no tribute and their men could be ordained priests. With the Bourbon reforms and independence the caste system disappeared, legal racial categories ending in Mexico in 1824, and in modern Latin America the word has become largely a cultural term.

entries.name: Micaela Bastidas
entries.desc: Micaela Bastidas Puyucahua was an Indigenous leader who, with her husband Túpac Amaru II, led a rebellion against Spanish rule in Peru, and is regarded as a martyr for Peruvian independence. Born in Pampamarca in the province of Canas in 1744, she married José Gabriel Condorcanqui in 1760 and was a full partner in his enterprises. When the rebellion began in November 1780 she supplied the troops with money, food, clothing and weapons, became acting chief after the victory at Sangarará, and urged a swift march on Cuzco. Captured when the revolt failed, she was executed in the Plaza de Armas of Cuzco in May 1781, after her son Hipólito.

entries.name: Mihna
entries.desc: The Mihna, the ordeal of Quranic createdness, was a period of religious persecution instituted by the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun in 833, in which Sunni scholars were punished, imprisoned or even killed unless they conformed to the Mu'tazilite doctrine that the Quran was created. It tested officials such as judges rather than commoners, and continued under al-Mu'tasim, who had Ahmad ibn Hanbal imprisoned and flogged until he was unconscious, and under al-Wathiq. Al-Mutawakkil abandoned it in 847 and banned it around 851. Its end marked the end of the caliphs' claim to decide matters of religious orthodoxy, which passed to the scholars.

entries.name: Mu'nis al-Muzaffar
entries.desc: Mu'nis al-Muzaffar, also called al-Khadim, the Eunuch, was commander-in-chief of the Abbasid army from 908 until his death in 933 and virtual dictator and king-maker of the Caliphate from 928. A Byzantine Greek eunuch slave, he served the future caliph al-Mu'tadid from the 880s, was banished to Mecca in 901, and was recalled in 908 by al-Muqtadir, whom he saved from a palace coup that December. He raided the Byzantine Empire, defeated Fatimid invasions of Egypt in 915 and 920 and saved Baghdad from the Qarmatians in 927. After a confrontation in 931–932 that ended with al-Muqtadir's death in battle, he installed al-Qahir, who had him executed in August 933.

entries.name: Muhtasib
entries.desc: A muhtasib was the holder of the office of hisbah in classical Islamic administrations: a supervisor of bazaars and trade and inspector of public places and behaviour in towns, appointed by the sultan, imam or another authority to see that public business followed sharia. The office is commonly held to succeed the Byzantine agoranomos, a market overseer also known in Parthian and Sassanian Iran. In Mamluk Cairo the muhtasib regulated weights, money, prices, public morals and cleanliness, and had cheating merchants whipped and paraded; manuals such as al-Shayzari's guided the work. Muhammad Ali of Egypt abolished the office in Cairo and Alexandria in 1837.

entries.name: Murad III
entries.desc: Murad III was sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1574 until his death in 1595. Born in Manisa in 1546 to the future Selim II and Nurbanu Sultan, he had his five younger brothers strangled on his accession, and his reign saw the growing influence of the imperial harem, above all his mother and his favourite consort Safiye Sultan. He fought the Habsburgs and the Safavids, a war of 1578–1590 that brought temporary gains, and Morocco was for a time a vassal until 1582. Silver from the New World brought inflation and unrest among the Janissaries, while relations with Elizabethan England were cemented and he commissioned illustrated manuscripts such as the Siyer-i-Nebi.

entries.name: Nadītu
entries.desc: The nadītu were a social class of women in ancient Mesopotamia, attested only in the Old Babylonian period and dedicated to the tutelary gods of particular cities; they are often called priestesses, though that is disputed. The best documented community lived from around 1880 BCE in a cloister, the gagû, near the temple of Shamash at Sippar, where about 200 are presumed to have resided; they could not marry or have biological children, though adoption was allowed. Women did not become nadītu by choice, yet some managed their own affairs, leasing fields, hiring labourers and extending loans, and some grew richer. The economic position of the class declined by the seventeenth century BCE.

entries.name: Naunakhte
entries.desc: Naunakhte was an Egyptian woman of the 20th Dynasty who lived in the workers' village at Deir el-Medina and is known from her will. Married at 12 to Qenhirkhopsef, the head scribe of the village, then in his 50s, she later married the workman Khaemnun and had four sons and four daughters. In October 1145 BCE, in the 3rd year of Ramses V, she declared before the village court, probably at around 80, that four of her children would inherit nothing from her because they had not cared for her in her old age. The four papyri recording it, found in the 1920s, show that a woman could keep property inherited from her father through her marriages.

entries.name: Nicholas I of Russia
entries.desc: Nicholas I was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Finland from 1825 to 1855, the third son of Paul I and younger brother of Alexander I. His reign began with the failed Decembrist revolt and is remembered for expansion, centralisation and the repression of dissent in Russia and among its neighbours. He took Iğdır and the rest of present-day Armenia and Azerbaijan from Qajar Iran in 1826–1828, helped create an independent Greek state, crushed the November Uprising in Poland in 1831 and aided Austria against the Hungarian Revolution of 1848. He led Russia into the disastrous Crimean War and died of pneumonia in 1855, succeeded by his son Alexander II.

entries.name: Nur Jahan
entries.desc: Nur Jahan, born Mehr-un-Nissa, was the twentieth wife and chief consort of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, and is considered by some historians the real power behind the throne for more than a decade. Born in Kandahar in 1577 to the Persian noble Mirza Ghiyas Beg, she married Sher Afgan Khan in 1594 and Jahangir in 1611. She held honours no other Mughal empress enjoyed, including coinage struck in her name, and in 1626 led a unit against the rebel Mahabat Khan, who had captured her husband. After Jahangir died in 1627 the war of succession went to Shah Jahan, and she lived under house arrest in Lahore until her death in 1645.

entries.name: Ortogh
entries.desc: An ortogh, also ortoq, was a merchant in partnership with the state and individual aristocrats in the Mongol Empire, the name coming from the Turkic ortak, partner. The institution began when Chinggis Khan had his family members and commanders entrust gold and silver ingots to Muslim merchants, mainly Uyghurs or West Turkistanis, who received high commissions and low-interest loans; pooling resources reduced the risk of failed caravans. In 1268 Kublai Khan created the General Administration for the Supervision of Ortogh to lend to them. The Chinese resented their privileges and high-interest moneylending, and by the Ming dynasty the word simply meant merchant.

entries.name: Ostsiedlung
entries.desc: The Ostsiedlung, East settlement, was the medieval migration of ethnic Germans into areas populated by Slavic, Baltic and Uralic peoples, chiefly Germany east of the Saale and Elbe, Lower Austria and Styria, Poland and the Czech Republic. Larger treks of settlers moved east from the mid-12th century, often invited by local princes, and towns were granted German town law, above all the Magdeburg and Lübeck laws; the movement ended in the beginning of the 14th century. In the 20th century German nationalists, most notoriously the Nazis, exploited it for territorial claims, and after World War II it was reversed east of the Oder as Germans were driven out.

entries.name: Ouyang Xiu
entries.desc: Ouyang Xiu was a Chinese historian, calligrapher, epigrapher, essayist, poet and politician of the Song dynasty, considered the central figure of the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song. Largely self-taught, he passed the jinshi exam in 1030 and revived the Classical Prose Movement begun by Tang masters two centuries before, promoting it in the imperial examinations. A leading proponent of the Qingli Reforms of the 1040s, he was demoted when Fan Zhongyan fell in 1045, and later headed the compilation of the New Book of Tang, completed in 1060, and wrote the Historical Records of the Five Dynasties on his own. He retired in 1071 after opposing the New Policies of Wang Anshi.

entries.name: Pact of Umar
entries.desc: The Pact of Umar is a treaty traditionally said to have been made between the Muslims and the non-Muslims conquered by Umar in the Levant in 637, which later gained canonical status in Islamic jurisprudence. It sets out rights and restrictions for dhimmis, protected non-Muslims such as Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians, in the form of a petition promising submission in return for protection: no new churches or monasteries, no crosses shown outside, distinctive dress, no weapons or saddles. Several versions exist, none datable earlier than the tenth or eleventh century, and scholars question its attribution to Umar I, linking parts of it to Umar II (r. 717–720) or to 9th-century scholars.

entries.name: Parakoimomenos
entries.desc: The parakoimōmenos, Greek for the one who sleeps beside the emperor's chamber, was a Byzantine court position usually reserved for eunuchs. Probably created no later than the reign of Leo IV the Khazar (775–780), it began as a modest post for chamber servants who slept outside the emperor's room as a security measure, but from the mid-9th century it became the highest post for eunuchs; holders such as Samonas, Joseph Bringas and Basil Lekapenos acted as chief ministers, and Basil the Macedonian used it to usurp the throne. It declined in the 12th century, was divided in two under the Palaiologoi, and by the 14th century was essentially an honorific dignity.

entries.name: Parysatis
entries.desc: Parysatis was a Persian queen of the Achaemenid dynasty, consort of Darius II, with great influence during the reign of her son Artaxerxes II. A daughter of Artanes, brother of Xerxes I, she helped Darius II to the throne and, according to her physician Ctesias, used a network of spies and supporters to remove those who threatened it; she held lands and villages in Syria, Media and Babylon. She favoured her son Cyrus the Younger and, after his death at Cunaxa, had those she blamed killed, though the cruelties Ctesias reports are historically doubtful. Said to have poisoned the queen Stateira, she was banished to Babylon but returned; the year of her death is unknown.

entries.name: Pavel Kiselyov
entries.desc: Count Pavel Kiselyov was a Russian officer and statesman, generally regarded as the most brilliant reformer of the conservative reign of Nicholas I. After serving at Borodino and marching to Paris in the Napoleonic Wars, he governed Wallachia and Moldavia as plenipotentiary president of their Divans from 1829 to 1834, when the two got their first constitutions, the Organic Statute, in 1831 and 1832. As Minister of State Properties for 18 years he reformed the administration of state-owned peasants and set up schools for their children, while his plans to emancipate the serfs were laid to rest. Sent to Paris as envoy after the Crimean War, he retired in 1862 and died there in 1872.

entries.name: Pedro II of Kongo
entries.desc: Pedro II Nkanga a Mvika was king of Kongo from 1622 to 1624, the first of the Kinkanga lineage, known as the House of Nsundi, and a descendant of Alfonso I on his mother's side. Formerly Duke of Mbamba, he was elected as a compromise candidate on the death of Álvaro III. The governor of Angola, João Correia de Sousa, invaded Kongo with Imbangala allies, but Pedro's army crushed them at Mbanda Kasi and drove them out; his protests to Rome and the king of Spain led to Sousa's recall and the return of some 1,200 slaves from Brazil. He proposed an alliance with the Dutch against Luanda and died in 1624, succeeded by his son Garcia I.

entries.name: Philaret Drozdov
entries.desc: Philaret, born Vasily Mikhaylovich Drozdov, was Metropolitan of Moscow and Kolomna and the most influential figure in the Russian Orthodox Church from 1821 to 1867. Born in Kolomna to a clerical family, he taught at the Troitse-Sergiyeva Lavra and the academy of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra, became Archbishop of Tver in 1819, moved to Moscow in 1821 and became metropolitan in 1826. A leading preacher and author of many theological works, he worked toward a Russian translation of the Bible and is said to have prepared Alexander II's proclamation freeing the serfs; he also had Old Believer churches sealed and their clergy imprisoned. He was canonized in 1994.

entries.name: Plaçage
entries.desc: Plaçage was a recognized extralegal system in the French slave colonies of North America and the Caribbean in which European men entered into unions with women of African, Native American and mixed-race descent, known as placées. The unions, called left-handed marriages among free people of colour, were often settled by contracts that gave property to the woman and her children, and sometimes freedom if they were enslaved. It developed first in Saint-Domingue amid a shortage of European women, was most widely practised in New Orleans and reached its height between 1769 and 1803. Emily Clark sees it as a broad range of relationships rather than a contractual system.

entries.name: Qiyan
entries.desc: The qiyān (singular qayna) were a social class of women trained as entertainers in the pre-modern Islamic world, who flourished under the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates and in al-Andalus. Often called singing slave girls, they were trained in singing, dancing, composing music and verse, reciting anecdotes and calligraphy, and included free women, among them the Abbasid princess Ulayya bint al-Mahdi, as well as enslaved women, who were legally sexually available to their owners. A significant share of the medieval Arabic women poets whose work survives were qiyān. The institution declined with the waning fortunes of the Abbasid Caliphate, as austerity left the arts unfunded.

entries.name: Repartimiento
entries.desc: The repartimiento ('distribution') was a colonial labour system imposed on the Indigenous peoples of Spanish America and the Philippines, under which Amerindians of the pueblos de indios were drafted to work on farms, in mines, in workshops and on public projects. Instated with the New Laws of 1542 to replace the encomienda, it was not slavery: workers were not owned, were paid wages and served in turns, with only 7-10% of the adult men to be assigned at once. Yet it created slavery-like conditions in places, most notoriously in the silver mines of 16th-century Peru under the mita. As Indigenous populations collapsed and workers left their pueblos, wage labour came to dominate in New Spain.

entries.name: Rígsþula
entries.desc: Rígsþula (The Lay of Ríg) is an Eddic poem, preserved incomplete in the 14th-century Codex Wormianus, in which a god named Ríg fathers the social classes of mankind. Visiting three couples in turn, he fathers Þræll, ancestor of the thralls, Karl, ancestor of free farmers and craftsmen, and Jarl, ancestor of the warrior nobility; Jarl's youngest son Konr ungr, skilled in runes and magic, stands for the origin of the word konungr, king. The prose introduction identifies Ríg with Heimdall, though some scholars think the role fits Odin better. Datings of the poem range from the 10th to the 13th century, and it breaks off as a crow urges Konr to seek the halls of Dan and Danþír.

entries.name: Rōnin
entries.desc: A rōnin ('drifter' or 'wandering man') was a samurai of feudal and early modern Japan who had no lord or master, having lost him through death or through the loss of his favour or legal privilege. The word first named serfs who had fled their master's land in the Nara and Heian periods. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 confiscated fiefs made many samurai rōnin, and as many as a hundred thousand fought for Toyotomi Hideyori at the Siege of Osaka. The Edo shogunate forbade them new masters until the Keian Uprising of 1651, and many became mercenaries, bodyguards or criminals; the status ended when Emperor Meiji abolished the samurai class in the 19th century.

entries.name: Samuel Kamakau
entries.desc: Samuel Mānaiakalani Kamakau was a Hawaiian historian and scholar whose writings, published in Hawaiian-language newspapers and later compiled into books, became an invaluable resource on the Hawaiian people, culture and language. Born at Mokulēia on Oʻahu, he studied at Lahainaluna Seminary under Sheldon Dibble from 1833 and in 1841 helped form the first Hawaiian historical society, with King Kamehameha III as its president. From 1866 to 1871 he wrote serial histories of Kamehameha I, the House of Kamehameha and Hawaiʻi, while serving as a judge and legislator. They appeared in English as Ruling Chiefs of Hawaiʻi (1961) and Ka Poʻe Kahiko (1964).

entries.name: Sangmin
entries.desc: Sangmin, short for p'yŏngsangjimin, is a Korean term for the commoners of the Joseon period (1392–1897), everyone who was not of noble background. Its synonyms include yangmin, p'yŏngmin and sŏin, and it was sometimes also used for innocent people as against criminals. Under the two-class system called yangch'ŏnje, enacted in the latter half of the 17th century, the sangmin made up the lower class, though in practice they were divided into various subgroups. In principle they had equal access to education and to the gwageo civil service examinations, but the nobility restricted that access; some sangmin were so well off that they were hard to tell from nobles.

entries.name: Savva Morozov
entries.desc: Savva Timofeyevich Morozov was a Russian textile magnate and philanthropist of an Old Believer merchant family, the fifth-richest in Russia at the beginning of the 20th century. He studied physics and mathematics at Moscow University and chemistry at the University of Cambridge, where he studied the British textile industry. As the largest shareholder of the Moscow Art Theatre he funded the improvement of its building on Kamergersky Lane in 1902 and its electrification in 1903. Influenced by Maxim Gorky, he funded the Bolsheviks, including the newspaper Iskra. He died of a gunshot wound in Cannes in 1905; his death was ruled a suicide, though various murder theories exist.

entries.name: Scythian archers
entries.desc: The Scythian archers were a hypothesised police force of 5th- and early 4th-century BCE Athens, said to have numbered 300 Scythians who were public slaves of the city. Known from Attic vase paintings and the comedies of Aristophanes, they are said to have kept order in the Assembly and the council, acting for the Eleven, the elected magistrates responsible for arrests and executions. Scholars agree that a Scythian police force of some sort existed in 5th-century Athens, but not when it began or how long it lasted. Despite the name they probably did not use bows: the archery expert Mike Loades has called the vase paintings fantasy dress, and archaeology points to horse-whips.

entries.name: Selim II
entries.desc: Selim II was Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1566 until his death in 1574, a son of Suleiman the Magnificent and Hürrem Sultan. He secured the succession by defeating his brother Bayezid near Konya in 1559; Bayezid fled to Safavid Persia and was handed over and executed with his four sons in 1561. Selim did not lead his armies in person, and his grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha conducted much of the government. His reign saw the conquest of Cyprus from Venice in 1570–1571, a heavy naval defeat at Lepanto in 1571, the recovery of Tunis from Spain in 1574 and the building of the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne. He died after a fall on a marble floor while drunk.

entries.name: Shaghab
entries.desc: Shaghab was the mother of the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir (r. 908–932) and one of the most powerful figures of his reign. Reportedly of Greek origin, she was a slave who became a concubine of Caliph al-Mu'tadid and was freed after bearing al-Muqtadir in 895. When her thirteen-year-old son became the first underage caliph in Muslim history, she sat on his regency council, according to al-Tanukhi, and ran a parallel bureaucracy from the harem, influencing the appointment and dismissal of officials through stewardesses such as Umm Musa and Thumal. Later historians usually portrayed her as a rapacious schemer; she also spent large sums on public charity.

entries.name: Shreni
entries.desc: A shreni was an association of traders, merchants or artisans in ancient and early medieval India, usually one for each vocation, which acted as an economic body, a largely self-governing community and, within limits, a tribunal for its members. Commonly translated as 'guild', though scholars caution against the comparison with European guilds, shrenis are attested from the 6th century BCE to the 12th century CE and reached their height under the Mauryan and Gupta empires. Wealthy shrenis lent money and kept religious endowments; the ivory carvers of Vidisha are credited with sponsoring the southern gateway of the stupa at Sanchi. Their hereditary crafts may have fed into the caste system.

entries.name: Shu'ubiyya
entries.desc: The Shu'ubiyya was a social, cultural, literary and political movement in the early Muslim world that opposed the privileged status of Arabs and claims of Arab ethnic and cultural superiority. Its name comes from the Quran's word for 'peoples'; its antecedents appeared under the Umayyads, and the controversy peaked in the 8th and 9th centuries under the early Abbasids. Some Shu'ubis, many of them Persian scholars and bureaucrats writing in Arabic, called for equality between Arabs and non-Arabs, others for Persian superiority. Under the Samanids the sentiment fed a revival of Persian literature. Al-Jahiz and Ibn Qutaybah wrote against it, and a later form arose in al-Andalus.

entries.name: Sin-Iddinam
entries.desc: Sîn-iddinam ('Sîn gave to me') was a king of the Mesopotamian city-state of Larsa, who ruled from about 1849 to 1843 BCE (middle chronology) and was deified throughout his reign. The son of Nur-Adad, with whom he may have co-ruled for a time, he styled himself King of Sumer and Akkad, King of Larsa and Provider of Ur. His seven known year names record the founding of the Ebabbar temple, the defeat of an army of Babylon, the destruction of the land of Eshnunna and the building of the great wall of Mashkan-shapir. A later liver omen has been taken to mean that he died suddenly when a stone slab fell on him; his cult statue at Ur was still anointed under Rim-Sin.

entries.name: Sokollu Mehmed Pasha
entries.desc: Sokollu Mehmed Pasha was an Ottoman statesman, grand vizier from 1565 to 1579 under Suleiman the Magnificent, Selim II and Murad III. Born into an Orthodox Christian family in Ottoman Herzegovina, he was taken as a boy through the devşirme and rose to be High Admiral of the Fleet, Governor-General of Rumelia and vizier. As grand vizier he kept Suleiman's death at Szigetvár secret in 1566 until Selim II could take power, made peace with the Habsburgs at Edirne in 1568 and rebuilt the fleet after Lepanto. He helped restore the Serbian Patriarchate of Peć in 1557, endowed the eleven-arched bridge at Višegrad and was assassinated on 11 October 1579.

entries.name: Strateia
entries.desc: Strateia was a term in the Byzantine Empire for enrolment in state, military or church service and its obligations, the analogue of the Latin militia. In middle Byzantine times it chiefly meant the duty of a stratiotes either to serve as a soldier himself or to pay for a soldier's upkeep, alone or with co-givers. By the 10th century the duty was attached to military lands, with strateiai for sailors, infantry, cavalry and, from the 960s under Nikephoros II Phokas, heavy cavalry, and emperors restricted the sale of such lands. By the 11th century it had become a purely fiscal obligation whose proceeds increasingly paid for mercenaries.

entries.name: Sukbin Choe
entries.desc: Sukbin Choe, of the Haeju Choe clan, was a consort of King Sukjong of Joseon and the mother of King Yeongjo. Born into the cheonmin, the lowest class of Joseon society, she entered the palace young and, in the most accepted account, came to the king's notice as a maid praying for the deposed Queen Min. She rose through the consorts' ranks from 1693, bore the future Yeongjo in 1694 and in 1699 became a consort of the senior first rank with the title suk, 'pure'. Her low birth threatened her son at the start of his reign; as king, Yeongjo fought his officials until she was recognised as his public mother.

entries.name: Ségur Ordinance
entries.desc: The Ségur Ordinance was a French regulation of 1781 that required candidates for officer commissions to prove four generations of nobility in the male line, or to be the son of an officer holding the Cross of Saint-Louis. Named after the minister of war Philippe Henri de Ségur, who had advised against it, it was approved by Louis XVI for the French infantry, cavalry and dragoons and extended in 1784 to the hussars, mounted chasseurs and foreign infantry regiments. Rich commoners and nobles of the robe could no longer buy their way in as officers. The Third Estate's outcry and the resentment of the robe nobility fed the crisis that led to the French Revolution.

entries.name: Taille
entries.desc: The taille was a direct land tax on the peasantry and other non-nobles of the Third Estate in Ancien Régime France, levied on each household according to the land it held and paid directly to the state. At first an exceptional tax raised in times of need, it became permanent in 1439, when Charles VII was granted the right to tax for a standing army during the Hundred Years' War. Clergy, nobles, crown officers, soldiers, magistrates and towns such as Paris were exempt. Roughly half of royal income in the 1570s, it rose from 2.5 million livres in 1515 to a record 21 million in 1589, and became one of the most hated taxes of the Ancien Régime.

entries.name: Takedda
entries.desc: Takedda was a town and former kingdom in present-day Niger, west of the Aïr Massif; the archaeological site of Azelik wan Birni is believed to hold its ruins. Founded by the Sanhaja, a Berber tribal confederation of the Maghreb, the Tuareg-controlled kingdom played a prominent role in long-distance trade in the 14th century, chiefly because of its copper mines. Ibn Battuta visited it in 1353 on his return from the Mali Empire, and Mansa Sakoura of Mali took his army east to subjugate the copper-producing area. Excavations by the French archaeologist Danilo Grébénart have found evidence of copperworking at the site dating to the first millennium BCE.

entries.name: Taras Shevchenko
entries.desc: Taras Shevchenko was a Ukrainian poet, writer, artist and ethnographer whose poetry collection Kobzar (1840) is regarded as the foundation of modern Ukrainian literature and, to some degree, of the modern Ukrainian language. Born a serf in Kiev Governorate under Russian rule, he was bought free in 1838 with 2,500 rubles raised by a lottery for Karl Briullov's portrait of Vasily Zhukovsky, and studied at the Imperial Academy of Arts. Arrested in 1847 with the Brotherhood of Saints Cyril and Methodius, he was exiled as a private to Orenburg and Orsk, forbidden to write or paint. Amnestied in 1857, he died in Saint Petersburg and was reburied at Kaniv.

entries.name: Theodora Porphyrogenita
entries.desc: Theodora Porphyrogenita was Byzantine empress from 1042 until her death in 1056, and sole ruler from 1055, the last sovereign of the Macedonian dynasty. The youngest daughter of Constantine VIII, she refused to marry Romanos Argyros and, accused of plotting against her sister Zoë, was confined in the monastery of Petrion in 1031. A popular uprising against Michael V in 1042 brought her out to reign jointly with Zoë, until Zoë's marriage to Constantine IX passed power to him. On his death in 1055 she took the throne again and presided in the Senate herself; she died refusing to marry or name an heir, ending the dynasty's 189-year rule.

entries.name: Tithe
entries.desc: A tithe (from Old English teogoþa, 'tenth') is a tenth part of something paid as a contribution to a religious organisation or as a compulsory tax to government; historically tithes were required and paid in kind, such as agricultural produce, while modern tithes are normally voluntary. Tithing was a widespread practice in the ancient Near East, and the Torah commands several agricultural tithes, among them the first tithe given to the Levites. The Third Council of Mâcon in 585 prescribed excommunication for those who did not pay. In Ireland the collection of tithes for the Anglican Church of Ireland was resisted in the Tithe War of 1831–36, and Spain abolished the tithe in 1841.

entries.name: Trierarchy
entries.desc: A trierarchy was a liturgy, a public service levied on the very wealthy of ancient Athens, that made a citizen, the trierarch, responsible for outfitting, maintaining and leading a trireme warship, usually for a year, while the state provided the ship, its equipment and its crew. Aristotle dates it to at least the tyranny of Hippias (527–510 BCE), and Athens was levying it by 480 BCE. By 408 BCE the burden could be shared in a syntrierarchy; Periandros's Law of 358/7 BCE spread it over 1,200 registered men in twenty divisions, and a law of Demosthenes in 340 BCE raised the register to 2,000. Trierarchs were still appointed as late as 224/3 BCE.

entries.name: Ulayya bint al-Mahdi
entries.desc: Ulayya bint al-Mahdi was an Abbasid princess, poet and musician, a daughter of the caliph al-Mahdi and the singer Maknuna, a slave concubine. Apparently brought up by her half-brother Harun al-Rashid after their father's early death, she was, like her half-brother Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, a noted musician, and has been called the most gifted of the princesses who composed poetry and songs. Her poems, mostly short pieces made to be sung, treat love, friendship and longing for home, praise Harun and celebrate wine. As a free Arab woman she performed only at private family gatherings. She died in 824 or 825; the main source for her life is the Kitāb al-Aghānī.

entries.name: Ulf Jarl
entries.desc: Ulf Thorgilsson, known as Ulf Jarl, was a Danish jarl of Skåne and regent of Denmark, the father of King Sweyn II and so the progenitor of the House of Estridsen, which ruled Denmark from 1047 to 1375. He took part in Cnut the Great's invasion of England in 1016 and married Cnut's sister Estrid; from about 1024 he governed Denmark as Cnut's regent and guardian of Cnut's son Harthacnut. In 1026 he persuaded the freemen to elect Harthacnut king, a ruse that would have made him ruler, and the sources disagree on his side around the Battle of the Helgeå. After a quarrel over chess, Cnut had him killed in Roskilde at Christmas 1026.

entries.name: Vincent Ogé
entries.desc: Vincent Ogé was a merchant, military officer and revolutionary of Saint-Domingue who led a failed uprising against French colonial rule in 1790, shortly before the Haitian Revolution. Born at Dondon to a white French father and a free woman of colour, he became the richest merchant of African descent in Cap-Français and part-owner of his family's slave plantation. In revolutionary Paris he campaigned with Julien Raimond for the rights of free people of colour, while supporting slavery. When the colony refused to apply the law of March 1790, he and Jean-Baptiste Chavannes raised about 300 free men of colour; captured, he was broken on the wheel on 6 February 1791.

entries.name: Virji Vora
entries.desc: Virji Vora was a merchant of Surat in Mughal India whom the English East India Company's records describe as the richest merchant in the world at the time, with a personal worth estimated at 8 million rupees. A wholesale trader, moneylender and banker with agents across India and in the ports of the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea and South-East Asia, he often bought up the whole stock of a commodity such as pepper or coral and dictated its price. He was the greatest creditor of the English Company, and much of the capital lent to the Dutch company in India came from him. Shivaji's raid on Surat in 1664 looted his house and warehouses; he is last recorded in 1670.

entries.name: Waqf
entries.desc: A waqf, also called a ḥabs, is an irrevocable trust in Islamic law, usually an endowment of real estate or other assets whose revenues serve a specified purpose, such as a mosque, school, fountain or the founder's family. Once declared, the property cannot be sold, transferred or given away and is legally held to belong to God; the founder appoints a trustee to manage it. The practice rests on hadiths, among them Umar's endowment of land at Khaybar on Muhammad's advice, but the formal system emerged from the 9th century: the oldest dated deed, of 876 CE, concerns a Qur'an now in Istanbul. The Jerusalem Waqf manages the al-Aqsa Mosque.

entries.name: War of the Two Capitals
entries.desc: The War of the Two Capitals, or Tianli Incident, was a war of succession in the Yuan dynasty fought in 1328 between forces based at the capital Khanbaliq (Dadu, modern Beijing) and at the summer capital Shangdu after the death of the emperor Yesün Temür. At Shangdu his favourite retainer Dawlat Shah installed Yesün Temür's son Ragibagh, while at Khanbaliq the Qipchaq commander El Temür enthroned Tugh Temür, a son of Khayishan. The Khanbaliq side held the richer central provinces; its allies surrounded Shangdu on 14 November and the loyalists there surrendered the next day. It was the bloodiest succession in Yuan history, and the last loyalists did not give up until 1332.

entries.name: Wen Yanbo
entries.desc: Wen Yanbo, courtesy name Kuanfu, was a scholar-official of the Song dynasty who served four emperors over more than five decades and was a grand councilor under Emperor Renzong. After passing the imperial examination in 1027 he was magistrate of Yicheng County and controller-general of Jiang Prefecture before serving as a censor in the capital, Kaifeng. When the Tanguts declared their state of Western Xia in 1038 and invaded, he advised that front-line marshals be allowed to punish subordinate generals for desertion and cowardice without first asking the court. In 1040 he showed that General Huang Dehe, who had fled and accused the captured General Liu Ping of defecting, had lied.

credit.source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:歷代聖賢名人像-25-宋丞相文潞公彦博.jpg

entries.name: What Is the Third Estate?
entries.desc: What Is the Third Estate? is a political pamphlet by the French writer and clergyman Abbé Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, written between 6 November and 12 December 1788 and published in January 1789, shortly before the French Revolution. It answered finance minister Jacques Necker's invitation to say how the Estates-General should be organised. Sieyès argued that the third estate, the common people, formed a complete nation in itself, that the clergy and nobility were unnecessary, and that the nation was sovereign; he asked for representation equal to the other two orders together and votes by head. Some 300,000 copies were printed, and it made Sieyès one of the leaders of the Estates-General.

entries.name: Women's March on Versailles
entries.desc: The Women's March on Versailles, also called the October Days, was one of the earliest and most significant events of the French Revolution. On 5 October 1789 market women in Paris, rioting over the high price of bread, grew into a crowd of thousands that seized weapons at the city hall and marched on the Palace of Versailles, followed by fifteen thousand National Guardsmen under Lafayette. Early on 6 October protesters broke into the palace, killing at least two of the royal guards, and the crowd forced Louis XVI and his family to return with them to Paris, where they lived in the Tuileries. Most of the National Constituent Assembly followed, and the march ended the king's independence.

entries.name: Xiaolian
entries.desc: Xiaolian was the system of nominating civil officials begun by Emperor Wu of the Han in 134 BCE. On the advice of Dong Zhongshu, Emperor Wu ordered each commandery to put forward one filial and one incorrupt candidate, in keeping with the Confucian view that filial piety was the fundamental virtue. Emperor He later set one candidate for every 200,000 residents in most areas and one for every 100,000 in non-Sinicized regions, and a nominator could be punished if his nominees proved corrupt or if he nominated no one. After the Han it lost importance to the nine-rank system, and under the Sui dynasty both gave way to the imperial examination.

entries.name: Yalbugha al-Umari
entries.desc: Yalbugha al-Umari was a senior Mamluk emir of the Bahri period who became the strongman of Egypt in the 1360s. Bought as a mamluk by Sultan an-Nasir Hasan, he rose to the highest rank of emir of one hundred, and in 1361 he defeated his master, who was never heard from again; al-Maqrizi says Yalbugha had him tortured and killed. As commander in chief under al-Mansur Muhammad and al-Ashraf Sha'ban he built a household of some 3,000 mamluks, among them the future sultan Barquq, rebuilt the navy after the Cypriot attack on Alexandria in 1365 and patronised the Hanafi school. His harsh discipline turned his own mamluks against him, and they killed him in December 1366.

entries.name: Yohl Ikʼnal
entries.desc: Yohl Ikʼnal was queen regnant of the Maya city-state of Palenque, ancient Lakamha, from her accession on 23 December 583 CE until her death on 7 November 604. She is the first definitively identified woman in recorded Maya history to have held full royal authority and the complete royal title of kʼuhul ajaw, divine lord or lady. In 599 Palenque was sacked by Calakmul, probably on the orders of its ruler Scroll Serpent, and likely paid it tribute, but she went on ruling and was succeeded by Ajen Yohl Mat, apparently her son. Her grandson or great-grandson Kʼinich Janaab Pakal I stressed his descent from her, and she is shown twice on his sarcophagus.

entries.name: Zabeau Bellanton
entries.desc: Zabeau Bellanton was a slave trader in the French colony of Saint-Domingue and its most successful businesswoman before the Haitian Revolution. A free woman of colour of Cap-Haïtien, officially listed as a jam maker, she built her business herself rather than on money left by a white lover, as most such women had. She bought the cheapest enslaved Africans straight from the slave ships, the young and the sick, pawned them out for some months until they were fit to sell, then sold them, and during the American Revolutionary War she also bought from smuggling British ships. The method was thought immoral even in the colony, but it made her rich in town houses, and in 1782 she left for France.

entries.name: Zhao Mengfu
entries.desc: Zhao Mengfu was a Chinese calligrapher, painter and scholar of the Yuan dynasty and a descendant of the imperial family of the Song dynasty. Recommended by the censor-in-chief Cheng Jufu, he had an audience with Kublai Khan at Dadu in 1286 but received no important office; his work was later greatly appreciated by Emperor Renzong. Turning from the refined brushwork of his own era to the cruder style of the eighth century, he is considered to have brought about a revolution that created the modern Chinese landscape painting, and he was known for his paintings of horses. He was married to the poet, painter and calligrapher Guan Daosheng and the maternal grandfather of the painter Wang Meng.

entries.name: Zhao Tingmei
entries.desc: Zhao Tingmei, formally Prince Fudao, was an imperial prince of the Song dynasty and the younger half-brother of Zhao Kuangyin and Zhao Jiong. The fourth son of Zhao Hongyin by his concubine Lady Geng, he was first Prince of Qi, served as governor of Kaifeng and was named Prince of Qin in 979. In 981 Chai Yuxi accused him of arrogance and Zhao Pu had Li Fu, head of the Kaifeng government, accuse him falsely; he was exiled to Xijing and demoted to Duke Xian of Fuling. He went to Fangzhou in 984 and died there of anxiety at thirty-eight. Emperor Zhenzong restored his title of Prince of Qin, and Emperor Huizong posthumously named him Prince of Wei.

entries.name: Zoe Porphyrogenita
entries.desc: Zoe Porphyrogenita was a member of the Macedonian dynasty who briefly reigned as Byzantine empress regnant in 1042 with her sister Theodora. A daughter of Constantine VIII, she was married at fifty to Romanos Argyros in 1028, and the couple took the throne the next day on her father's death. Romanos III was found dying in his bath in 1034, a death variously blamed on Zoe, her lover Michael or both; she married Michael that day and he became Michael IV. When his nephew Michael V, whom she had adopted, exiled her, a popular revolt in 1042 deposed him and made the sisters joint empresses. After two months she married Constantine IX, and she died in 1050.

credit.artist: File:Empress_Zoe_mosaic_Hagia_Sophia.jpg : Photographer: Myrabella derivative work: Myrabella

entries.name: Álvaro II of Kongo
entries.desc: Álvaro II Nimi a Nkanga was king of Kongo from 1587 to 1614 and one of its most powerful and important kings. He succeeded his father Álvaro I after a dispute with his brother, settled by single combat at M'banza-Kongo (São Salvador) to avoid bloodshed. After a poorly documented civil war in 1590–91 he had to accept the virtual independence of Miguel, count of Soyo, and rewarded loyal nobles with habits of the Order of Christ, which Kongo kings went on granting through the 19th century. In 1596 M'banza-Kongo became the seat of a diocese, though the kings of Portugal chose its bishop, and in 1604–1608 he sent Emanuele Ne Vunda as ambassador to Pope Paul V.

entries.name: Álvaro III of Kongo
entries.desc: Álvaro III Nimi a Mpanzu was king, or manikongo, of the Kingdom of Kongo from August 1615 to 4 May 1622. A son of King Álvaro II and formerly Duke of Mbamba, he was the fourth ruler of the royal house of Kwilu founded by Álvaro I. Around 1619 he formalized the construction of a Jesuit college in São Salvador. Relations with the Dutch soured in the 1610s after the closure of a Dutch factory in Soyo, but he revived them as a check on Portuguese expansion, and Dutch factories reopened at Soyo in 1621. He died in 1622 while his son was too young to rule, and the nobles elected the Duke of Mbamba, beginning the short House of Nsundi.

entries.name: Ōoku
entries.desc: The Ōoku, the great interior, was the women's quarters of Edo Castle, where the women connected to the reigning shōgun lived. It was established under the second shogun, Tokugawa Hidetada, for his official wife Oeyo, and under Tokugawa Iemitsu was expanded at the suggestion of his nurse Lady Kasuga into a vast harem with nearly 1,000 women working as maidservants. Its women were strictly ranked, from the shogun's official wife down to servants from the townspeople and peasants, and a senior lady of the rank of Jōrō Otoshiyori held power equal to a Rōjū. Adult men were generally forbidden to enter. The Ōoku lasted until the Tokugawa shogunate was dissolved in 1868.

entries.name: ʻAhu ʻula
entries.desc: The ʻahu ʻula, the feather cape or cloak of ancient Hawaii, was with the mahiole, the feather helmet, a symbol of the highest rank of the aliʻi, the chiefly class. Made of a netting of olonā fibre to which small bundles of red, yellow and sometimes black and green feathers of native birds were tied, hundreds of thousands to a cloak, it was reserved for royals and high chiefs, and its size showed rank. It was believed to give spiritual protection and to take on the wearer's mana. In 1779 the chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu placed his cloak and helmet on James Cook. Over 160 are in museums; Kamehameha I's cloak in the Bishop Museum holds 450,000 mamo feathers from 80,000 birds.

credit.artist: Haalelea's_Feather_Cape_(Fig._105).jpg : William T. Brigham Bishop Museum derivative work: nagualdesign ( talk )

entries.name: ʻAi Noa
entries.desc: The ʻAi Noa, literally free eating, was a period of taboo-breaking in the Hawaiian Islands in October 1819 that overturned the kapu, the strict rules of Hawaiian religion and society. After the death of Kamehameha I, his son Liholiho, later Kamehameha II, tried to reimpose the kapu suspended during mourning, but was opposed by his mother Keōpūolani, Kamehameha's other wives including Kaʻahumanu, and the kahuna-nui Hewahewa. He then ate a feast the chiefesses had prepared, and messengers announced that the kapu had fallen: women could eat forbidden food and eat with men, and human sacrifice was to end. A revolt led by Keaoua Kekuaokalani was defeated at the Battle of Kuamo'o in December 1819.

entries.name: Liturgy (ancient Greece)
entries.desc: The liturgy, Greek leitourgia, was a public service in the ancient Greek city-states by which the richest residents, citizens or resident aliens, more or less voluntarily funded the state from their own wealth. In Athens the recurring liturgies belonged to religious festivals and games, chief among them the choregia, the upkeep of a chorus for the dramatic competitions, and the gymnasiarchy; the trierarchy, equipping and maintaining a trireme and its crew for a year, was called on when needed. A careful count gives at least 97 civilian liturgists a year in Athens. The trierarchy fell into disuse by the end of the 4th century BCE, and in the Hellenistic period euergetism eclipsed the system.

entries.name: Obshchina
entries.desc: The obshchina or mir was the peasant village community of Imperial Russia, made up of serfs, later emancipated serfs, state peasants and their descendants, usually of a single village. Title to the land lay with the mir, not the individual: each household farmed its own holding, which it could not sell or bequeath without the mir's consent, and the mir could repartition the land from time to time. Its assembly, the skhod, also levied recruits, punished minor crimes and answered for its members' taxes. Slavophiles hailed it as ancient and purely Russian, while the Western school of Boris Chicherin held it a later creation for tax collection; the Stolypin reforms of 1906–1914 undermined it.

entries.name: Bardas Phokas the Younger
entries.desc: Bardas Phokas the Younger was a Byzantine general of the Phokas family who took part in three revolts for and against the ruling Macedonian dynasty. A nephew of Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, he was proclaimed emperor by troops at Caesarea after his uncle's death in 969, but Bardas Skleros put the revolt down and he spent seven years in exile on Chios. Freed in 978 to fight Skleros, who had himself rebelled, he defeated him with the help of a Georgian army and in single combat, and became Domestic of the Scholae. In 987 he rebelled again and overran most of Asia Minor, but facing Basil II at Abydos in 989 he suffered a seizure and fell dead from his horse.

entries.name: Bardas Phokas the Elder
entries.desc: Bardas Phokas the Elder was a Byzantine general of the first half of the 10th century, father of Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas and of the kouropalates Leo Phokas the Younger, and maternal grandfather of Emperor John I Tzimiskes. A son of the general Nikephoros Phokas the Elder, he fought at the disastrous Battle of Acheloos in 917, and in 941, as governor of the Theme of Armeniakon, held off the Rus' who had landed in Bithynia until John Kourkouas drove them out. Made supreme commander in the East in 945, he was repeatedly defeated by Sayf al-Daula, emir of Aleppo, and was replaced by his son Nikephoros in 954/955. As emperor, Nikephoros made him Caesar; he died about 968, aged 90.

entries.name: Thing (assembly)
entries.desc: A thing was a governing assembly of the free people of a community in early Germanic societies, presided over by a lawspeaker and held regularly at prominent places. Tacitus gave the first detailed description in 98 CE, and the oldest written reference is a pillar at Housesteads on Hadrian's Wall dedicated to Mars Thincsus, the Mars of the Thing. In the Viking Age things served as parliaments and courts at local, regional and wider levels, settling disputes, electing chieftains and kings and judging by the law the lawspeaker recited. As royal power grew they became mainly courts, but the name lives on in the Icelandic Althing, the Norwegian Storting and the Manx Tynwald.

entries.name: John Young
entries.desc: John Young was a British subject who became a military adviser to Kamehameha I during the formation of the Kingdom of Hawaii. Boatswain of the American fur-trading ship Eleanora, he was detained ashore at Kealakekua Bay in 1790 and left behind, and with the Welshman Isaac Davis became Kamehameha's friend and adviser, bringing knowledge of naval and land warfare; at the Battle of Nuʻuanu he was in charge of the cannon. Between 1802 and 1812 he ruled as Royal Governor of Hawaii Island while Kamehameha was on other islands. His granddaughter Emma married Kamehameha IV, and he died in Honolulu in 1835.

entries.name: Banu'l-Furat
entries.desc: The Banu'l-Furat were a Shia family of civil functionaries of the Abbasid Caliphate in the late 9th and early 10th centuries, several of whom held the office of vizier; the sources often call its members simply Ibn al-Furat. With their rivals the Banu'l-Jarrah they controlled the caliphate's central government in the early 10th century. Abu'l-Hasan Ali ibn al-Furat (855–924) was vizier in 908–912, 917–918 and 923–924, until he and his son al-Muhassin were deposed and executed for abuse of power in 924. Al-Fadl ibn Ja'far was the last vizier of al-Muqtadir, and Ja'far ibn al-Fadl (921–1001), called Ibn Hinzaba, headed the administration of the Ikhshidids of Egypt before the Fatimid conquest.

entries.name: Jarrahids
entries.desc: The Jarrahids were an Arab dynasty, rulers of the Tayy tribe, who intermittently ruled Palestine and held Transjordan and northern Arabia in the late 10th and early 11th centuries. First allies of the Qarmatians, they rose under Mufarrij ibn Daghfal, who won the governorship of Ramla from the Fatimid Caliphate; driven out of Palestine in 981, they raided Hajj caravans and shifted between the Fatimids, Byzantines and Syrian rulers. In 1011–12 they held interior Palestine up to Tiberias and proclaimed their own caliph at Ramla. Defeated by the Fatimids in 1029, Mufarrij's son Hassan led the tribe to Byzantine territory near Antioch; a descendant, Fadl ibn Rabi'ah, founded the Al Fadl dynasty.

entries.name: Bukhtishu
entries.desc: The Bukhtishu were a family of Persian or Syrian Eastern Christian physicians spanning six generations and 250 years, from the 7th to the 9th centuries; their name, part Middle Persian and part Syriac, can be translated 'Jesus has redeemed'. Like most physicians of the early Abbasid court they came from the Academy of Gondishapur. Jurjis, director of its hospital, was called to Baghdad in 765 to treat the caliph al-Mansur; his son Bukhtishu II became physician-in-chief to Harun al-Rashid, and his grandson Jibril ibn Bukhtishu advised Harun on building Baghdad's first hospital. In the 9th and 10th centuries the family had a virtual monopoly on the practice of medicine in Baghdad.

entries.name: Radhanites
entries.desc: The Radhanites were early medieval Jewish merchants active in the trade between Christendom and the Muslim world from roughly the 8th to the 10th centuries. They are known chiefly from the Book of Roads and Kingdoms of Ibn Khordadbeh, written in about 870, which describes them as multilingual and traces four routes from the Rhône valley in southern France to China. They carried goods of small bulk and high demand, such as spices, perfumes, jewellery and silk, and also furs, swords and slaves. Whether the name meant a guild, a clan or Jewish merchants in general is unclear. Their activity appears to cease in the 10th century, after the fall of Tang China and the collapse of the Khazar state.

entries.name: Pharnaces (son of Arsames)
entries.desc: Pharnaces was a member of the Achaemenid family of Persia, a son of Arsames and younger brother of Hystaspes, and so an uncle of Darius I. According to the fortification tablets found at Persepolis, he was the chief economic official of Darius between 506 and 497 BCE, a Mayor of the Palace whose attribute was a short stick, probably of a precious metal; he likely appears on some of the Persepolis reliefs. Aristotle records that he introduced mules into Hellespontine Phrygia, in Asia Minor. His son Artabazus was made satrap of the region by Xerxes I around 477 BCE, and Artabazus's heirs, the Pharnacid dynasty, ruled it into the 4th century BCE, until Alexander the Great took it over.

credit.artist: A.Davey from Portland, Oregon, EE UU

entries.name: Intaphrenes
entries.desc: Intaphrenes was a Persian, one of the seven who in September 522 BCE helped Darius I seize the throne of the Achaemenid Empire from Bardiya. He then became Darius's bow carrier, a high position in which the Behistun Inscription shows him. In 521 BCE Darius sent him at the head of an army against Arakha, who had claimed the throne of Babylon as Nebuchadnezzar IV; Babylon was taken without much fighting on 27 November, and Arakha and his chief followers were impaled. In the account of Herodotus, Intaphrenes was later put to death after he cut off the ears and noses of two officers who barred his way to the king, and Darius, fearing a revolt, killed his family except his wife's brother and son.

entries.name: Bardiya
entries.desc: Bardiya, called Smerdis by Herodotus, was a son of Cyrus the Great and the younger brother of Cambyses II, both Persian kings. Views of him are sharply divided: either he ruled the Achaemenid Empire for a few months in 522 BCE, or he had been secretly killed by Cambyses and was impersonated by a magus called Gaumata. The second version is that of Darius the Great's Behistun Inscription, Herodotus and Ctesias, in which seven nobles killed the ruler in September 522 BCE and Darius took the throne. Most modern historians assume that the man who ruled was the real Bardiya and that Darius invented the impostor to justify his seizure of the throne. Bardiya's only daughter, Parmys, married Darius.

entries.name: Zubaidah bint Ja'far
entries.desc: Zubaidah bint Ja'far was an Abbasid princess, a granddaughter of the caliph al-Mansur and the wife and double cousin of Harun al-Rashid, whom she married in 781–82; their son became the caliph al-Amin. She is remembered above all for the wells, reservoirs and pools she built for Muslim pilgrims on the route from Baghdad to Mecca and Medina, renamed the Darb Zubaidah in her honour. After a drought she had the Zamzam Well deepened and spent over 2 million dinars on the water supply of Mecca, including an aqueduct from the spring of Hunayn, 95 kilometres to the east. She also rebuilt Tabriz after an earthquake in 791. Her son was killed by supporters of al-Ma'mun in 813, and she died in 831.

entries.name: Nobles of the Robe
entries.desc: The Nobles of the Robe were the aristocrats of Ancien Régime France whose rank came from holding certain judicial or administrative offices, as distinct from the older Nobles of the Sword. The class arose in the 16th century, named after the gowns of the university-trained judges, and the term first appeared in writing in 1603. Offices first given as rewards for service to the king became venal, and the edict of la Paulette, a tax paid to keep an office hereditary, made this official; by 1789 most holders had inherited their posts. The most influential were the 1,100 members of the 13 parlements; Montesquieu was one. They lost their place when the parlements were abolished in 1790.

entries.name: Nobles of the Sword
entries.desc: The Nobles of the Sword were the oldest class of the French nobility, dating from the Middle Ages: the knightly class, they owed military service, usually to the king, in return for feudal landed estates, and took their name from their right to bear a sword. In later centuries a family had to hold the status for at least three generations. From the Renaissance onwards kings created a new nobility of the robe through judicial and administrative offices, to the old nobility's anger. Under Louis XIV the nobles of the robe largely replaced them at Versailles; the nobles of the sword kept greater prestige, tax exemption and much of the officer class, but usually had lower incomes.

entries.name: Lettres de cachet
entries.desc: Lettres de cachet were letters signed by the king of France, countersigned by one of his ministers and closed with the royal seal, carrying the king's orders, often beyond appeal. Written orders of this kind arose in the 14th century from the principle that the king was released from the laws. The best known were penal: a subject could be imprisoned without trial or defence, confined or exiled, often at a family's request, as with the Marquis de Sade, held from 1777 to 1790, and Mirabeau, whose attack on them was published in 1782. A symbol of the abuses of the Ancien Régime, they were suppressed during the French Revolution, though Napoleon revived their penal equivalent in 1801.

entries.name: Teccalli
entries.desc: A teccalli was a noble household or lineage in the city-states, or altepetl, of ancient Mexico; the Nahuatl word joins teuctli, lord, and calli, house, and means 'lord-house'. The ruler, the tlatoani, and other nobles, the pipiltin, lived in it, while commoners, the macehualtin, worked its land, and the nobles received goods and services from them as tribute. Its head was the teuctli; succession passed mostly by direct descent or to his brothers, and up to six generations in the male line, 22 to 47 members, could live in one house. Western city-states built it into their housing compounds; eastern ones did not. It has been called the fundamental political subunit of the city-state.

entries.name: Slavery in the Aztec Empire
entries.desc: Slavery in the Aztec Empire and the surrounding Mexica societies was widespread; a slave was called a tlacotli in Nahuatl. Slaves did not inherit their status, and their children were set free: people were enslaved as a punishment, as captives of war, or voluntarily to pay debts, among them gambling debts, and during a famine in the 1450s many sold themselves into slavery. Most served in the palaces of lords; they could marry and own property, and owners had to feed and shelter them. War captives fared worst, being sold or sacrificed at religious festivals. Slaves were sold at Tenochtitlan and above all at Azcapotzalco and Itzocan, those judged incorrigible wearing wooden collars.

entries.name: Tagma
entries.desc: The tagmata were the elite regiments of the Byzantine Empire's central army in the 8th to 11th centuries; from the 4th century the Greek word tagma had meant an infantry battalion of 200–400 men. After putting down the revolt of Artabasdos in 741–743, Emperor Constantine V reformed the old guard units of Constantinople into professional heavy cavalry regiments, garrisoned around the capital as a central reserve. In the 9th and early 10th centuries there were four: the Scholai, the Excubitors, the Vigla and the Hikanatoi. New units followed, among them the Varangian Guard of about 988; the older tagmata declined after about 1050 and had mostly vanished by about 1100.

entries.name: Born in the purple
entries.desc: Born in the purple was a category of members of royal families born while their parent reigned, later extended to children of any prominent parents. In the Byzantine Empire the honorific porphyrogennetos, Latinized Porphyrogenitus, was given to a son or daughter born after the father had become emperor; the Byzantines linked it to the imperial purple or to the porphyry-lined room of the Great Palace where empresses gave birth. The idea was known from the 6th century, but the word is first securely used in 846 and was common by the 10th century, notably for Constantine VII. Porphyrogeniture favoured such sons over older brothers, as Henry I of England argued against Robert Curthose.

entries.name: De Ceremoniis
entries.desc: De Ceremoniis, in full De cerimoniis aulae Byzantinae and in English the Book of Ceremonies, is a Greek book of the ceremonial protocol of the Byzantine emperors' court at Constantinople, written in the middle of the 10th century. Emperor Constantine VII wrote or at least commissioned it, probably around 956–959, and it was partly revised under Nikephoros II; it includes chapters from a 6th-century manual by Peter the Patrician. It sets out the processions, stations, costumes and acclamations of religious feasts and of secular rites such as coronations, weddings, births and funerals, as well as the reception of ambassadors. An English translation in two volumes was published in 2012.

entries.name: Agraharam
entries.desc: An agraharam or agrahara was a grant of land and of the royal income from it, typically made by a king or noble family in India for religious purposes, particularly to Brahmins to maintain temples or a pilgrimage site and to support their families. Dynasties such as the Pandya, Cholas, Kadambas, Pallavas and Vijayanagara built and maintained them; they were also called Chaturvedimangalams, and Sāsana in Odisha. By traditional town-planning an agraharam was two rows of houses on either side of a road, with a temple to Shiva at one end and Vishnu at the other. An early description appears in the 3rd-century CE Sangam work Perumpāṇāṟṟuppaṭai, and many places in southern India bear the name.
