entries.name: Ministeriales
entries.desc: The ministeriales were a legally unfree but socially elite class of knights, administrators and officials in the Holy Roman Empire in the High Middle Ages, serving secular and church lords. Recruited at first from household serfs, they managed estates, finances and castles and held the household offices of seneschal, butler, marshal and chamberlain; Emperor Conrad II (990–1039) first referred to them as a distinct class. Their lords decided whom they might marry, and children of mixed marriages usually took the status of the lesser parent. In the 13th century their status was assimilated to that of the free nobility, and in the 15th century they formed the core of the German knightly class.

entries.name: Adalberon of Laon
entries.desc: Adalberon, also called Ascelin, was a French bishop and poet who became bishop of Laon in 977; he was a nephew of Adalberon, Archbishop of Reims. The chronicler Richer reports that he was accused that year of adultery with Queen Emma, whose son Louis V removed him from Laon in 981. Imprisoned when Charles, Duke of Lower Lorraine, took Laon in 988, he escaped to Hugh Capet, was restored to his see, and in 991 handed Laon, Charles and Archbishop Arnulf of Reims to Hugh. His satirical poem Carmen ad Rotbertum regem, addressed to Robert II, opposed monastic reform and names three orders of society, those who pray, fight and labour, an idea later built into the Ancien Régime's three orders.

entries.name: Panakas
entries.desc: The panakas were the royal kin groups of the Inca Empire, each formed by the descendants of a Sapa Inca or his wife: a noble form of the ayllu, the Andean kinship group descended from a common ancestor. The crown prince did not belong to his father's panaka; on becoming emperor he left his original panaka and formed his own. The panakas made up the court and aristocracy of Cusco, held estates and palaces across the realm, tended shrines along the ceque lines and kept the mummy (mallki) of their founder, in whose name they took part in politics. Eleven are listed, five of Hurin (lower) and six of Hanan (upper) Cusco, and scholars still dispute what the word first meant.

entries.name: Villac Umu
entries.desc: The Villac Umu (Willaq Umu, 'priest who recounts') was the High Priest of the Sun in the Inca Empire, the chief priest of Inti, the most important god of the Inca pantheon. Holders were usually brothers of the Sapa Inca and most likely the second most powerful person in the empire; in some accounts the office was created during the reign of Pachakuti. By the end of the empire the high priest was also the emperor's field marshal in war. Few holders' names survive; a Villac Umu joined Diego de Almagro's expedition to Chile in 1535 until he defected by night and returned to Cusco to aid the Inca uprising.

entries.name: Chungin
entries.desc: The chungin ('middle people') were the upper middle class of Joseon Korea, a small, privileged group of commoners below the yangban aristocracy and above the sangmin. They included government-employed specialists, military officers from or married into technical families, hereditary functionaries, and illegitimate children of aristocrats; entry usually required passing the chapkwa examination in practical skills. They were not taxed or conscripted, lived in the central part of the city and married within their class or into the yangban. From the late seventeenth century chungin poets formed societies, and in the late nineteenth century many chungin welcomed Western institutions and ideas.

entries.name: Paekchŏng
entries.desc: The paekchŏng were an untouchable caste in Korea, descended from minority, nomadic groups of disputed ethnicity, who worked as butchers, tanners, basket weavers and executioners. Under Goryeo (918–1392) the word meant common people; King Sejong of Joseon merged the outcaste groups with ordinary farmers under that name and settled them, but discrimination continued: they could not live in tiled houses, wear silk or take surnames, and were buried in separate graveyards. The Kabo Reform abolished the caste system in 1894, yet discrimination persisted. The Hyeongpyeongsa, founded in Jinju on 23 April 1923, campaigned for equality until 1935; today the word simply means a butcher.

entries.name: Kisaeng
entries.desc: Kisaeng, also called ginyeo, were enslaved women from outcast or enslaved families in Korea who were trained as courtesans to provide artistic entertainment and conversation to upper-class men. They emerged under the Goryeo dynasty and served the state at court and in the provinces, trained in music, dance, poetry and prose; some also worked in medicine and needlework, and many sijo by kisaeng survive. Their cheonmin status was hereditary, most careers were over by age 22, and in 1650 all kisaeng were made slaves of the government. The Gabo Reform of 1895 made them nominally free, and under Japanese rule the Kisaeng Regulation Order of 1908 grouped them with licensed prostitutes.

entries.name: Shin Saimdang
entries.desc: Shin Saimdang, born Shin In-seon, was a Korean artist, writer, calligrapher and poet of the Joseon period, born in Gangneung, where her birth home, Ojukheon, still stands. Taught by her maternal grandfather Yi Sa-on as he would have taught a grandson, she learned Neo-Confucian thought, history and literature as well as painting, calligraphy and embroidery. She married Yi Won-su in 1522 and had eight children, among them the Confucian scholar Yi I, and died in 1551 at the age of 46. About 40 of her paintings of insects, flowers, grapes, fish and landscapes remain. Long held up as a model of Confucian ideals, she became in 2009 the first woman on a South Korean banknote, the 50,000 won note.

entries.name: Lady Hyegyŏng
entries.desc: Lady Hyegyŏng of the Pungsan Hong clan was a Korean writer and Crown Princess of the Joseon period, the wife of Crown Prince Sado and mother of King Jeongjo. Put forward for selection in 1743 at the age of nine, she married Sado in 1744 and lived through his worsening mental illness, during which he grew violent. In 1762 King Yeongjo had Sado sentenced, and he was pronounced dead eight days later; she chose to stay alive to support her son and grandson. Between 1795 and 1806 she wrote The Memoirs of Lady Hyegyŏng (Hanjungnok, 'A Record of Sorrowful Days') in Hangul, four narratives on her life, her family and her husband's illness and death.

entries.name: Hong Kyŏngnae
entries.desc: Hong Kyŏngnae was a Korean rebel leader who led a rising in Pyongan Province against the central government of Joseon, which ended with his death in 1812. Born in Yonggang to the Namyang Hong clan, he was probably an educated commoner and professional geomancer rather than a fallen yangban, and his travels to find gravesites taught him his clients' discontents. He drew supporters with the Confucian argument that hardship and disasters showed the dynasty had lost the Mandate of Heaven, and with the Jeonggamnok's prophecy of a True Man named Jeong. The rebels were besieged in the walled town of Jeongju; Hong was shot and killed when it fell, in the battle that ended the rebellion.

entries.name: Gim Man-deok
entries.desc: Gim Man-deok was a Korean merchant of Joseon from Jeju Island who used her fortune to feed the island in a famine. Orphaned young, she became a gisaeng; at 22 she had her name removed from the gisaeng registry, regained her yangmin status and opened an inn for merchants and a commission agency for trade between Jeju and the mainland, becoming by 50 one of the two richest people in Joseon. When famine struck Jeju from 1792 and 170,000 people died of starvation, she imported and distributed rice, saving 18,000 lives. King Jeongjo granted her wish to visit the capital and Mount Geumgang, though Jeju women had been forbidden to leave the island for 200 years; she left her belongings to the poor.

entries.name: Dawatdar
entries.desc: Dawatdar (Persian) or dawadar (Arabic), 'the keeper of the inkpot', was a senior court office in medieval Islamic states, created under the Seljuk Empire for the head of the chancery and named after the royal inkpot, the symbol of office of the Abbasid caliphs' viziers. In the Mamluk Sultanate it was at first a lowly office, but under the Burji dynasty it became one of the seven most important, the 'Grand Keeper of the Inkpot' (dawadar kabir), with junior dawadars as aides. Its holders variously oversaw tax and harvest collection in Upper Egypt or mustered soldiers for campaigns, and some rose to be sultans. In the Ottoman and Safavid empires dawatdars were mere chancery scribes.

entries.name: Shadhili Order
entries.desc: The Shadhili Order is a Sufi order (tariqah) founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili in the 13th century, historically important in the Maghreb and Egypt and followed today by millions of people around the world. Its writers include Ibn Ata Allah al-Iskandari, author of the Hikam, and the commentators Ahmad Zarruq and Ahmad ibn Ajiba, and many head lecturers of al-Azhar in Cairo have followed it. Its branches include the Fassiyya, widespread in India, Sri Lanka and Pakistan, the Darqawiyya, founded in Morocco in the late 18th century, and the Alawi-Darqawiyya of Ahmad al-Alawi, which spread from Algeria to Syria, Jordan, France and English-speaking communities.

entries.name: Ryot
entries.desc: Ryot (also raiyat) was a general term used throughout India for peasant cultivators, from the Arabic ra'iyah, 'flock' or 'peasants': where zamindars were landlords, ryots were tenants and cultivators. Under the Mughal system khudkasta ryots were permanent cultivators of a village with heritable rights in land, while paikasta ryots moved from village to village for a crop season and paid much lower rent. In March 1859, under Company rule, thousands of ryots in Bengal refused to grow indigo. Under British rule the ryotwari system of Bombay, Madras, Assam and Burma assessed land revenue on the actual occupants, who held land of the crown in a heritable and transferable right of occupancy.

entries.name: Satnampanth
entries.desc: Satnampanth, or the Satnami movement, is a name for several Indian religious movements influenced by Kabirpanth and connected with Dalits, named after Satnam, the 'true name'. The first was founded by Bir Bhan at Narnaul in 1657; its followers, mostly farmers and traders from the low-caste leatherworkers, rejected ritual and caste distinctions. In 1672 the Satnamis rose against the Mughal Empire over taxation, took Narnaul and Bairat and defeated Mughal forces until Aurangzeb sent 10,000 troops with artillery; 2,000 Satnamis were killed in battle and many more in pursuit. The movement revived under Jagjivan Das in Uttar Pradesh and under Ghasidas in Chhattisgarh in the 1820s.

entries.name: Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Younger
entries.desc: Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Younger was grand vizier of the Ottoman Empire from 1439 to 1453, under Murad II and in the first years of Mehmed II, the fourth of the Çandarlı family to hold the office. When Murad abdicated in favour of the young Mehmed in 1444, and again during the Buçuktepe rebellion of 1446, Halil Pasha brought Murad back to the throne, which left Mehmed with a lasting resentment. He opposed the siege of Constantinople and was suspected of taking bribes from the Byzantines. After the city fell on 29 May 1453, Mehmed had him imprisoned and executed on 10 July, the first Ottoman grand vizier to be executed by a sultan.

entries.name: Kazasker
entries.desc: A kazasker or kadıasker ('military judge') was a chief judge of the Ottoman Empire, so named because his jurisdiction at first extended to the cases of soldiers, who were later tried only by their own officers. Two were appointed, the Rumeli Kazaskeri for the European part of the empire and the Anadolu Kazaskeri for the Asian part, and neither had jurisdiction over the city of Constantinople. Subordinate to the Grand Vizier and later to the Şeyhülislam, they attended the meetings of the Imperial Council, heard appeals against the decisions of kadıs, had the power to overrule them, and proposed candidates for the office of kadı to the Grand Vizier.

entries.name: Ziamet
entries.desc: The ziamet was a form of land tenure in the Ottoman Empire between the 14th and 16th centuries: a grant of lands or revenues by the sultan to an individual in return for services, especially military. The holder was an agent of the central government, supervising the possession, transfer and rental of lands in his territory and collecting tax revenue. The system was introduced by Osman I, who granted land tenure to his troops, and expanded by Murad I for his Sipahi cavalry; an institution taken over from the Seljuq sultanate. As central control weakened in the 16th and 17th centuries, ziamets were enlarged, given to fewer holders for longer tenures and converted into tax farms or iqta.

entries.name: State peasant
entries.desc: State peasants were a social estate of the peasantry in 18th- and 19th-century Russia who lived on public land and paid taxes to the treasury; unlike private serfs they were considered personally free, though their freedom of movement was restricted. Created by decrees of Peter I, they grew through Catherine II's confiscation of church lands, conquests and runaway serfs, from 19% of the population at the first census in 1724 to 45% at the last in 1858. They could appear in court, trade, own property and open factories. Pavel Kiselyov's reforms of 1837–41 placed them under a new Ministry of State Property, and a law of 24 November 1866 let rural communities hold their land in ownership.

entries.name: Military settlement
entries.desc: Military settlements were an organization of the Russian army from 1810 to 1857 that combined military service with farming, introduced by Alexander I to create an inexpensive reserve of trained troops. Alexei Arakcheyev set up the first in the Mogilev Governorate in 1810–1812 and headed all of them from 1817; by 1825 they made up almost a quarter of the army by some accounts. Life was strictly regulated, corporal punishment was common, and drill left the farm work late. Settlers rose in the Chuguyev regiment in 1819 and near Staraya Russa in July 1831, when the rebels executed their superiors; both risings were harshly put down, and all the settlements were abolished in 1857.

entries.name: Praskovia Kovalyova-Zhemchugova
entries.desc: Praskovia Kovalyova-Zhemchugova was a Russian serf actress and soprano opera singer, born into the family of a serf blacksmith owned by the Sheremetevs, probably in the province of Yaroslavl. Trained for the opera company of Count Pyotr Sheremetev and his son Nikolai, she debuted at the serf theatre of Kuskovo in 1779 and from 1780 appeared under the stage name Zhemchugova, "the Pearl". Her most important role was Eliane in Grétry's Les Mariages samnites, which she sang for 12 years and performed for Empress Catherine II in 1787. Nikolai Sheremetev freed her from serfdom in 1798 and married her in secret in 1801; she died in 1803, weeks after giving birth to their son Dmitry.

entries.name: Emperor Xiaozong of Song
entries.desc: Emperor Xiaozong of Song, personal name Zhao Shen, was the 11th emperor of the Song dynasty of China and the second of the Southern Song, a seventh-generation descendant of its founder, Emperor Taizu. Adopted by Emperor Gaozong in 1160, he came to the throne in 1162 when Gaozong abdicated, although the retired emperor remained the de facto ruler until his death in 1187. Xiaozong rehabilitated Yue Fei posthumously, made peace with the Jin dynasty in 1165, kept close control over his ministers and worked to stabilise the paper currency, the huizi, whose value was steadied by 1175. He abdicated in 1189 in favour of his son, Emperor Guangzong, and died in 1194.

entries.name: Mothax
entries.desc: The mothakes (singular mothax, a Doric Greek word meaning "stepbrother") were a sociopolitical class in ancient Sparta, prominent particularly during the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE). They were mostly the sons of Spartiate fathers and helot mothers, or the children of impoverished Spartiates. Free but not citizens, they were brought up alongside Spartan boys as their foster brothers, usually at the expense of wealthy families; since they could not contribute to the syssitia, the citizens' common messes, they could not hold equal status, but they were allowed to fight alongside the perioeci. Some rose to prominence, among them Gylippus, Lysander and Callicratidas.

entries.name: Neodamodes
entries.desc: The neodamodes were helots of Sparta who were freed after serving for a time as hoplites in the Spartan army. When the category first appeared is uncertain: the historian Jean Ducat concluded that their status was largely modelled on the measures taken for the Brasidians, the helots freed after taking part in the expedition of Brasidas in 424 BCE. Their existence is attested from 420 to 369 BCE, and 2,000 of them are recorded in the campaign of Agesilaus II in Ionia between 396 and 394 BCE. The name joins neos, "new", and demos, but they never acquired full citizenship, and the only community they joined was that of the perioeci.

entries.name: Conspiracy of Cinadon
entries.desc: The conspiracy of Cinadon was an attempted coup d'état in Sparta in 399 BCE, early in the reign of King Agesilaus II. Its leader, Cinadon, was a member of the king's bodyguard but not one of the homoioi, the full citizens, and he drew helots, neodamodes, hypomeiones and perioeci into a plot to break the power of the Spartan elite. The informer who betrayed it to the ephors said that Cinadon had counted only 40 full citizens among some 4,000 people in the agora. The ephors sent Cinadon to Aulon in Messenia on a pretext, had him questioned there and arrested his accomplices; he was whipped through the city and possibly executed. The main source is Xenophon's Hellenica.

entries.name: Gothi
entries.desc: A goði (plural goðar, feminine gyðja) was a chieftain of the Icelandic Commonwealth; the title first meant a pagan leader responsible for a religious structure and communal feasts, and outside Iceland survives mainly on runestones. The office, the goðorð, could be bought, shared, traded or inherited, and its holders organised the local assemblies, sat in the Lögrétta of the Althing and named judges; every free landowner of some property had to follow a goði of his choice. After the conversion of 1000 the title lost its religious meaning. By the 13th century five or six families held them all, and the system ended when the leading goðar swore fealty to King Haakon IV of Norway in 1262–1264.

entries.name: Leidang
entries.desc: The leidang (Old Norse leiðangr) was a form of conscription in medieval Scandinavia that raised coastal fleets for seasonal expeditions and the defence of the realm. The Icelandic sagas link its introduction to King Haakon I of Norway in the 10th century, and it is first mentioned in 985 by the court poets of Jarl Haakon and his son Erik, though its age is disputed: Niels Lund held that Denmark had no real leiðangr until 1170. The land was divided into ship districts (skipreiða), each bound to build, equip and crew a ship for two or three months; Norway had 279 in 1277. From the 12th and 13th centuries it became in many places a tax, paid by free farmers until the 19th century.

entries.name: Eiríkr Hákonarson
entries.desc: Eiríkr Hákonarson, also known as Eric of Hlathir, was Earl of Lade, governor of Norway and Earl of Northumbria, the son of Earl Hákon Sigurðarson. According to Heimskringla he commanded 60 ships at the Battle of Hjörungavágr in 986, where a Danish invasion fleet was defeated. Exiled to Sweden when Óláfr Tryggvason took power in 995, he burned Staraya Ladoga, and in 1000 he joined King Sweyn and King Olof of Sweden to defeat Óláfr at the Battle of Svolder, capturing his ship, the Long Serpent. He ruled Norway with his brother Sveinn under Sweyn Forkbeard until 1012, then joined Cnut's conquest of England and received Northumbria; he is not mentioned in English documents after 1023.

entries.name: Khongirad
entries.desc: The Khongirad were one of the major divisions of the Mongol tribes, with a homeland near Lake Hulun in Inner Mongolia and the Khalkha River in Mongolia. Their clans never united under a single leader, and they are known above all as the chief consort clan of the house of Genghis Khan: his mother Hoelun, his great-grandmother and his first wife were Khongirads, as were the wives of most rulers of the Yuan dynasty and the Golden Horde. Their power at the Yuan court peaked under Dagi and Temüder in the reign of Gegeen Khan. In the west, Khongirad elites founded the Sufi dynasty of Khwarazm (1359–1388), and later Qongirat inaks ruled the Khanate of Khiva, whose last khan abdicated in 1920.

entries.name: Gegeen Khan
entries.desc: Gegeen Khan, born Shidibala and known by the temple name Emperor Yingzong of Yuan, was an emperor of the Yuan dynasty and nominally the ninth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire. The eldest son of Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan, he was installed as crown prince in 1316 by his grandmother Dagi and succeeded his father in 1320, while Dagi and her protégé Temüder held much of the power. After both died in 1322 he broke the Khunggirad faction and, with the grand councillor Baiju, recruited Chinese scholar-officials and pressed reforms on Confucian principles. In 1323 Temüder's adopted son Tegshi killed him and Baiju at Nanpo, the first violent succession struggle in the dynasty's history.

entries.name: Shell money
entries.desc: Shell money was a medium of exchange made of whole or partial sea shells, often worked into beads, and used in the Americas, Asia, Africa and Australia. The shell most widely used was that of the money cowry, Monetaria moneta, found chiefly in the Indian Ocean. In China cowries served as currency from over three thousand years ago until the Qin dynasty standardised coinage. European traders imported cowries into West Africa to buy goods and slaves, at least 30 billion reaching the Bight of Benin between 1500 and 1875, and the growing imports brought inflation. In North America Indigenous peoples made wampum from quahog shells, and Ghana's cedi, introduced in 1965, is named after the cowrie.

entries.name: Pete Seeger
entries.desc: Pete Seeger was an American singer, songwriter, musician and social activist, a founding member of the folk groups the Almanac Singers and the Weavers, whose recording of Lead Belly's "Goodnight, Irene" topped the charts for 13 weeks in 1950. The Weavers were blacklisted in the McCarthy era; called before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1955, Seeger refused to name his associations and was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1961, a verdict overturned in 1962. He wrote or co-wrote "Where Have All the Flowers Gone?", "If I Had a Hammer" and "Turn! Turn! Turn!", helped popularise "We Shall Overcome", and in 1966 founded the Hudson River Sloop Clearwater.

credit.artist: Fred Palumbo , World Telegram staff photographer

entries.name: Paul Robeson
entries.desc: Paul Robeson was an American bass-baritone concert artist, actor, professional football player and activist. At Rutgers College, where he was the only African-American student, he was twice named a consensus All-American, and he took his law degree at Columbia while playing in the National Football League. His "Ol' Man River" in the London premiere of Show Boat in 1928 became the benchmark for the song, and he played Othello in London and on Broadway; between 1925 and 1961 he recorded about 270 songs. His support for the Spanish Republic and for the Soviet Union brought FBI scrutiny, and the State Department withdrew his passport until the Supreme Court's 1958 ruling in Kent v. Dulles.

credit.artist: Gordon Parks , Office of War Information; cropped by Beyond My Ken ( talk ) 07:13, 3 February 2011 (UTC)

entries.name: Woody Guthrie
entries.desc: Woody Guthrie was an American singer, songwriter and composer of folk music whose work dealt with American socialism and anti-fascism; his guitar often carried the words "This machine kills fascists". Raised in Okemah, Oklahoma, he joined the migrants who left the Dust Bowl for California and worked on Los Angeles radio before moving to New York, where in 1940 he recorded the album Dust Bowl Ballads and wrote "This Land Is Your Land" in answer to Irving Berlin's "God Bless America". He sang with the Almanac Singers, joined the Merchant Marine in 1943 and wrote the autobiography Bound for Glory. Huntington's disease, diagnosed in 1952, kept him in hospitals from 1956 until his death in 1967.

credit.artist: Al Aumuller/ New York World-Telegram and the Sun (uploaded by User:Urban )

entries.name: Hanns Eisler
entries.desc: Hanns Eisler was an Austrian and German composer, a pupil of Arnold Schoenberg and the first of his disciples to compose in the twelve-tone technique. In Berlin from 1925 he supported the Communist Party of Germany and began a collaboration with Bertolt Brecht that lasted until Brecht's death, writing music for The Decision and The Mother and the "Solidarity Song". Banned by the Nazis, he went into exile and in 1938 settled in the United States, where his scores for Hangmen Also Die! and None but the Lonely Heart were nominated for Oscars. Accused before the House Un-American Activities Committee, he was deported in 1948; in East Berlin he composed the national anthem of East Germany.

entries.name: Bertolt Brecht
entries.desc: Bertolt Brecht was a German theatre practitioner, playwright and poet. In Berlin, where he moved in 1924, he wrote The Threepenny Opera with Elisabeth Hauptmann and Kurt Weill, began a lifelong collaboration with Hanns Eisler and became a leading theorist of epic theatre, which sought the audience's critical reflection rather than its emotional identification. He fled Nazi Germany in 1933, first to Scandinavia and later to Southern California, and in exile wrote Life of Galileo and Mother Courage and Her Children. Questioned by the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1947, he returned to Europe and co-founded the Berliner Ensemble in East Berlin with Helene Weigel.

entries.name: Alan Lomax
entries.desc: Alan Lomax was an American ethnomusicologist and folklorist, known for his field recordings of folk music. The son of the folklorist John Lomax, he joined his father's collecting trips for the Library of Congress as a teenager and from 1937 to 1942 was Assistant in Charge of its Archive of Folk Song, recording Woody Guthrie, Lead Belly and, in the Mississippi Delta, Muddy Waters and Son House. After Congress ended that funding in 1942 he collected independently in Britain, Ireland, Italy, Spain and the Caribbean. His recordings, radio shows and concerts helped start the American and British folk revivals, and he later developed Cantometrics and argued for what he called cultural equity.

entries.name: John Lomax
entries.desc: John Lomax was an American teacher, musicologist and folklorist who worked to preserve American folk music. Raised in central Texas, he studied at the University of Texas and Harvard, where George Lyman Kittredge urged him to collect ballads in the field; his Cowboy Songs and Other Frontier Ballads appeared in 1910 with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt. From 1933 he made recording trips for the Library of Congress with his son Alan, recording Huddie Ledbetter, Lead Belly, at the Louisiana State Penitentiary, and from 1934 until his death he was honorary curator of the Archive of American Folk Song. He also directed the gathering of ex-slave narratives for the Federal Writers' Project.

entries.name: Miriam Makeba
entries.desc: Miriam Makeba, nicknamed Mama Africa, was a South African singer, songwriter, actress and civil rights activist who campaigned against apartheid. Born near Johannesburg, she sang with the Manhattan Brothers and the Skylarks in the 1950s, and a role in the anti-apartheid film Come Back, Africa (1959) took her to London, where Harry Belafonte became her mentor, and to New York. In 1960 her passport was cancelled when she tried to return for her mother's funeral, and she remained in exile until 1990. She recorded "Pata Pata" (1967), shared a Grammy with Belafonte and testified against the South African government at the United Nations; she died of a heart attack at a concert in Italy in 2008.

entries.name: Kim Jong Il
entries.desc: Kim Jong Il was a North Korean politician and dictator who was the second supreme leader of North Korea from the death of his father, Kim Il Sung, in 1994 until his own death in 2011. Born in the far east of the Soviet Union, he rose through the Workers' Party of Korea, helped develop the Juche ideology and the cult of personality, and was designated his father's successor in 1980. He took power amid a catastrophic economic crisis and famine, ruled a repressive and totalitarian dictatorship and made the army central through his Songun (military-first) policies. North Korea conducted its first nuclear test in 2006 under his rule; he promoted his third son, Kim Jong Un, as his successor.

entries.name: Hua Guofeng
entries.desc: Hua Guofeng was a Chinese politician who succeeded Mao Zedong as chairman of the Chinese Communist Party and also served as premier of China. Born in Jiaocheng, Shanxi, he fought as a guerrilla in the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Chinese Civil War, rose to lead Hunan province during the Cultural Revolution and became Minister of Public Security in 1973. Mao made him premier and first vice chairman after Zhou Enlai's death in January 1976, and in October 1976, a month after Mao's death, Hua had the Gang of Four arrested. Still committed to the Maoist line and a command economy, he was gradually forced from power by Deng Xiaoping and his supporters between December 1978 and June 1981.

entries.name: Lyndon B. Johnson
entries.desc: Lyndon Baines Johnson was the 36th president of the United States, serving from 1963 to 1969, who as vice president assumed the presidency after the assassination of John F. Kennedy. A Southern Democrat from Texas, he served in both houses of Congress and became Senate majority leader in 1954. His Great Society programmes and War on Poverty created Medicare and Medicaid, and he signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Civil Rights Act of 1968. He also escalated US involvement in the Vietnam War, and after disappointing results in the 1968 New Hampshire primary he withdrew his candidacy; he retired to his Texas ranch and died in 1973.

entries.name: Robert F. Kennedy
entries.desc: Robert Francis Kennedy was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 64th United States attorney general from 1961 to 1964 and as a senator from New York from 1965 until his assassination in 1968. He managed the campaigns of his brother John F. Kennedy and was his closest adviser, and as attorney general he supported the civil rights movement and fought organized crime. As a senator he opposed US involvement in the Vietnam War and sponsored legislation against poverty. A leading candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1968, he was shot by Sirhan Sirhan shortly after winning the California primary and died 25 hours later.

entries.name: Carl Schurz
entries.desc: Carl Schurz was a German-American revolutionary, statesman, journalist and reformer. Born in the Rhine Province of Prussia, he fought in the German revolutions of 1848–1849, fled after their suppression and, like many other Forty-Eighters, settled in the United States in 1852. An opponent of slavery and an early Republican, he served as a Union general in the American Civil War, fighting at Gettysburg, and became the first German-born American elected to the US Senate, for Missouri. He helped found the Liberal Republican Party, served as the 13th Secretary of the Interior under Rutherford B. Hayes, where he sought a civil service based on merit, and later led the Mugwump movement.

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.desc: Jeremy Bentham was an English philosopher, jurist and social reformer regarded as the founder of modern utilitarianism, which took the greatest happiness of the greatest number as the measure of right and wrong. His An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) was the first major book on the subject. A political radical, he advocated freedom of expression, equal rights for women and the abolition of slavery and of capital punishment, while dismissing natural rights as nonsense upon stilts. His students included James Mill and John Stuart Mill, and after his death in 1832 his body was preserved as an auto-icon, now on display at University College London.

entries.name: John Brown
entries.desc: John Brown was an American abolitionist and evangelical Christian who believed he was an instrument of God raised to strike the death blow to slavery, the leading exponent of violence in the abolitionist movement. During the Bleeding Kansas crisis he and his sons killed five supporters of slavery in the Pottawatomie massacre of May 1856. In October 1859 he led a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, meaning to arm enslaved people, but few joined and his men were killed or captured by militia and US Marines under Robert E. Lee. Hanged for treason in December 1859, Brown was viewed as a hero in the North, and the raid escalated the tensions that led to the American Civil War.

entries.name: Julia Ward Howe
entries.desc: Julia Ward Howe was an American author, poet and social activist who wrote the Battle Hymn of the Republic as new words to the song John Brown's Body. She wrote them in November 1861 after visiting Washington, D.C., and meeting Abraham Lincoln; published in the Atlantic Monthly in February 1862, the song became one of the most popular of the Union during the American Civil War. She held that freeing the slaves was right but did not believe in racial equality. After the war she worked for pacifism and women's suffrage, co-leading the American Woman Suffrage Association with Lucy Stone from 1869, and her Mothers' Day Proclamation called on women around the world to unite for peace.

entries.name: Liliʻuokalani
entries.desc: Liliʻuokalani was the only queen regnant and the last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ruling from 1891 until the monarchy was overthrown in 1893. Born in Honolulu, she succeeded her brother David Kalākaua and sought a new constitution to restore the power of the monarchy and the voting rights of the economically disenfranchised. Pro-American residents organised as the Committee of Safety overthrew her in January 1893, backed by the landing of US Marines, and after a failed uprising she was placed under house arrest and forced to abdicate in 1895. She composed Aloha ʻOe and wrote the autobiography Hawaiʻi's Story by Hawaiʻi's Queen (1898).

entries.name: Isaac Watts
entries.desc: Isaac Watts was an English Congregational minister, hymn writer, theologian and logician, credited with some 750 hymns, among them When I Survey the Wondrous Cross, Joy to the World and Our God, Our Help in Ages Past. Born in Southampton to a nonconformist family, he was barred from Oxford and Cambridge, then restricted to Anglicans, studied at the Dissenting Academy at Stoke Newington and became pastor of the Mark Lane Congregational Chapel in London. His Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707) and his metrical psalter of 1719, which rendered the Psalms in the language of the New Testament, helped bring new hymns into English worship. His Logick (1724) was printed in twenty editions.

entries.name: John Newton
entries.desc: John Newton was an English evangelical Anglican cleric and abolitionist who had earlier been a captain of slave ships and an investor in the Atlantic slave trade. He went to sea young, was pressed into the Royal Navy in 1743 and was for a time a servant in West Africa; after a conversion to Christianity he renounced the trade, was ordained and served as parish priest at Olney, Buckinghamshire, for two decades. With the poet William Cowper he published Olney Hymns in 1779, including the hymn now known as Amazing Grace. His pamphlet Thoughts Upon the Slave Trade (1788) described the conditions of the Middle Passage, and he lived to see Britain abolish the slave trade in 1807.

entries.name: Thomas Arne
entries.desc: Thomas Augustine Arne was an English composer of the late Baroque and early Classical periods and a leading British theatre composer of the 18th century, working at Drury Lane and Covent Garden in London. Born in Covent Garden, he wrote many operatic entertainments for the London theatres and pleasure gardens as well as concertos, sinfonias and sonatas. His song Rule, Britannia! was first heard in the Masque of Alfred at Cliveden, the country house of Frederick, Prince of Wales, in 1740. His Artaxerxes (1762) was one of the most successful English operas of the century and the only known attempt at an Italianate opera seria in English, with recitative in place of spoken dialogue.

entries.name: Henry Purcell
entries.desc: Henry Purcell was an English composer and organist of the middle Baroque era whose music, English in style, incorporated Italian and French elements. A former chorister of the Chapel Royal, he became organist of Westminster Abbey in 1679, when John Blow resigned the office in his favour, and organist of the Chapel Royal in 1682. His works include more than 100 songs, the opera Dido and Aeneas, the semi-operas Dioclesian, King Arthur and The Fairy-Queen, odes such as Come Ye Sons of Art, and music for the funeral of Queen Mary in 1695. He died at his home in Marsham Street in November 1695, at the height of his career, and is buried beside the organ in Westminster Abbey.

entries.name: Edward Elgar
entries.desc: Sir Edward Elgar was an English composer, born at Lower Broadheath near Worcester, many of whose works entered the British and international concert repertoire. Self-taught, a Roman Catholic in Protestant Britain and sensitive about his humble origins, he struggled for success until his forties, when the Enigma Variations (1899) became popular in Britain and abroad, followed by the choral work The Dream of Gerontius (1900). He also wrote the Pomp and Circumstance Marches, two symphonies and concertos for violin and cello, and was appointed Master of the King's Musick in 1924. Described as the first composer to take the gramophone seriously, he recorded most of his major orchestral works.

entries.name: Hector Berlioz
entries.desc: Hector Berlioz was a French Romantic composer, conductor and critic, born at La Côte-Saint-André, who left medical studies in Paris for music against his family's wishes. His refusal to follow traditional rules set him at odds with the conservative musical establishment of Paris, though he won the Prix de Rome in 1830. His works include the Symphonie fantastique, inspired by the actress Harriet Smithson, Harold in Italy, the Requiem, La Damnation de Faust and the operas Benvenuto Cellini, Les Troyens and Béatrice et Bénédict. Meeting only occasional success in France, he gained an international reputation as a conductor, and his Treatise on Instrumentation (1844) was influential.

entries.name: Anton Bruckner
entries.desc: Anton Bruckner was an Austrian composer and organist, born at Ansfelden near Linz, known for his symphonies and sacred music, including Masses, a Te Deum and motets. He worked as a teacher and organist at Sankt Florian, studied with the theorist Simon Sechter, and in 1868 took over Sechter's post teaching music theory at the Vienna Conservatory. His long symphonies, with their rich harmony, strong polyphony and unprepared modulations, are regarded as emblematic of the final stage of Austro-German Romanticism. Critics led by Eduard Hanslick attacked their size and repetition, and he revised many of his works, leaving several versions; he died in Vienna in 1896.

entries.name: Antonín Dvořák
entries.desc: Antonín Dvořák was a Czech composer, born in Nelahozeves near Prague, who drew on the rhythms and other features of the folk music of Moravia and Bohemia, following the nationalist example of Bedřich Smetana. Recommended by Johannes Brahms to the publisher Simrock, he won international success with the Slavonic Dances, Op. 46, and his Stabat Mater was widely performed after a London performance in 1883. From 1892 he directed the National Conservatory of Music of America in New York, where he wrote the Symphony From the New World and his Cello Concerto, before returning to Bohemia in 1895. Of his ten operas, most with Czech librettos, the most successful is Rusalka (1901).

entries.name: Bedřich Smetana
entries.desc: Bedřich Smetana was a Czech composer, born in Litomyšl in Bohemia, whose music became closely identified with his people's aspirations to a cultural and political revival; in his homeland he is regarded as the father of Czech music. After taking part briefly in the 1848 Prague uprising and working as a teacher and choirmaster in Gothenburg, he returned to Prague in the early 1860s to champion Czech opera, and The Bartered Bride (1866) achieved great popularity. Completely deaf by the end of 1874, he went on composing, notably the cycle of six symphonic poems Má vlast, which includes Vltava. A mental collapse early in 1884 led to his confinement in an asylum and his death.

entries.name: Camille Saint-Saëns
entries.desc: Camille Saint-Saëns was a French composer, organist, conductor and pianist of the Romantic era who made his concert debut at the age of ten. After studying at the Paris Conservatoire he was a church organist, from 1858 at La Madeleine, the official church of the French Empire, and later a freelance pianist and composer in Europe and the Americas. His works include Danse macabre (1874), the opera Samson and Delilah (1877), the Third (Organ) Symphony (1886) and The Carnival of the Animals (1886). At the École Niedermeyer he taught Gabriel Fauré; committed to classical structures, he was often regarded as a reactionary late in life, and he died in Algiers in 1921.

entries.name: Robert Schumann
entries.desc: Robert Schumann was a German composer, pianist and music critic of the early Romantic era, born in Zwickau in Saxony, who composed in all the main musical genres of his time. He studied law at Leipzig and Heidelberg and piano with Friedrich Wieck from 1829, but a worsening problem with his right hand turned him to composition, and in 1834 he co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, which he edited for ten years. In 1840 he married Wieck's daughter Clara against her father's bitter opposition, then wrote song cycles such as Dichterliebe and, in 1841, the first of his four symphonies. In 1854 he threw himself into the Rhine and died two years later in a sanatorium near Bonn.

entries.name: Clara Schumann
entries.desc: Clara Schumann, born Clara Wieck in Leipzig, was a German pianist, composer and piano teacher whose 61-year concert career changed the piano recital by giving less room to purely virtuosic works. Trained as a child prodigy by her father Friedrich Wieck, she made her official debut at the Leipzig Gewandhaus in 1828 and was named Royal and Imperial Austrian Chamber Virtuoso in Vienna in 1838. She married Robert Schumann in 1840; they had eight children and encouraged the young Johannes Brahms, and she gave the public premieres of many works by both men. After Robert's death she toured Europe for decades, often with Joseph Joachim, and from 1878 taught at Dr. Hoch's Konservatorium in Frankfurt.

entries.name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
entries.desc: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was an Italian composer of late Renaissance music and the central figure of the Roman School, born in Palestrina in the Papal States. In 1551 Pope Julius III made him maestro di cappella of the Cappella Giulia at St. Peter's Basilica; his book of masses of 1554 was the first by a native Italian composer. Barred as a married layman when Pope Paul IV required papal choristers to be clerics in 1555, he worked at St John Lateran and Santa Maria Maggiore before returning to St Peter's in 1571 until his death in 1594. He left 105 masses and more than 300 motets, and his counterpoint, codified by Johann Joseph Fux, became a model for later composers.

entries.name: Josquin des Prez
entries.desc: Josquin des Prez was a French or Franco-Flemish composer of the Renaissance and a central figure of the Franco-Flemish School, born around 1450 in present-day northeastern France or Belgium. A singer by training, he served René of Anjou, Cardinal Ascanio Sforza, Popes Innocent VIII and Alexander VI, Louis XII and Ercole I d'Este of Ferrara, for whom he wrote the Missa Hercules Dux Ferrariae. His masses, motets and chansons developed an imitative polyphony of independent voices closely tied to the text, and many were printed by Ottaviano Petrucci. From 1504 he was provost of the collegiate church of Notre-Dame at Condé-sur-l'Escaut, and he died in 1521.

entries.name: Johannes Ockeghem
entries.desc: Johannes Ockeghem was a Franco-Flemish composer and singer of the early Renaissance, the leading European composer between Guillaume Du Fay and Josquin des Prez. Probably born in Saint-Ghislain in the County of Hainaut, he is first recorded as a singer at Antwerp's cathedral in 1443, and from around 1452 spent most of his career at the French royal court under Charles VII, Louis XI and Charles VIII. Some 14 masses, five motets and 21 chansons are reliably attributed to him, among them the canon-based Missa prolationum and the earliest surviving polyphonic Requiem. His death in 1497 was lamented by Erasmus, Jean Molinet and Josquin, who wrote Nymphes des bois for him.

entries.name: Marc-Antoine Charpentier
entries.desc: Marc-Antoine Charpentier was a French Baroque composer under Louis XIV, born in or near Paris, whose sacred vocal music was especially admired in his lifetime. After studying in Rome with Giacomo Carissimi, probably between 1667 and 1669, he was for seventeen years house composer to Marie de Lorraine, duchesse de Guise, writing Italianate oratorios and motets, and wrote music for Molière's The Imaginary Invalid. From late 1687 he was music master to the Jesuits in Paris, and from 1698 until his death in 1704 maître de musique of the Sainte-Chapelle. More than 500 of his works survive in 28 autograph volumes, and the prelude of his Te Deum H.146 has opened Eurovision broadcasts since 1954.

entries.name: Zoltán Kodály
entries.desc: Zoltán Kodály was a Hungarian composer, ethnomusicologist and music educator, born in Kecskemét, known for the Kodály method of music teaching. From 1905 he recorded folk songs in remote villages on phonograph cylinders and introduced his friend Béla Bartók to folk-song collecting. His works blend Western European styles with Hungarian folk music; his first major success was the Psalmus Hungaricus in 1923, followed by Háry János (1926) and the Dances of Galánta (1933). From 1935 he worked to reform music teaching in Hungary's schools, and his principles, built on singing and on folk songs in the pupils' mother tongue, spread after the Second World War. He died in Budapest in 1967.

entries.name: Heinrich Heine
entries.desc: Heinrich Heine was a German poet, writer and critic, born Harry Heine into a Jewish family in Düsseldorf, who converted to Lutheran Christianity in 1825. His early lyric poetry, collected in the Buch der Lieder of 1827, was set to music by Schubert, Mendelssohn, Robert Schumann and others; his later verse and prose are marked by satire and irony. Associated with the Young Germany movement, he settled in Paris in 1831, and in 1835 the German Diet banned his works with theirs; bedridden from 1848, he died in Paris in 1856. Nazi Germany burned and later banned his books, and a line from his play Almansor on burning books and people is engraved at the site of the 1933 Berlin book burning.

entries.name: Clemens Brentano
entries.desc: Clemens Brentano was a German poet and novelist and a major figure of German Romanticism, born into a wealthy merchant family in Frankfurt and brother of the writer Bettina von Arnim. With Achim von Arnim he collected the folk songs of Des Knaben Wunderhorn (1805–1808), which Gustav Mahler later drew upon. In 1818 he returned to the Catholic faith and until 1824 took down at Dülmen the visions of the nun Anne Catherine Emmerich, published as The Dolorous Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ in 1833, though later investigations made it uncertain how much was his own. His works also include the romance Godwi (1801) and the Romanzen vom Rosenkranz, published in 1852; he died in Aschaffenburg.

entries.name: Venantius Fortunatus
entries.desc: Venantius Fortunatus was a Latin poet and hymn writer at the Merovingian courts and later Bishop of Poitiers, venerated as a saint. Born between 530 and 540 near Treviso in Italy and educated in Ravenna, he came to Metz in 566 and performed a poem at the wedding of King Sigibert and Queen Brunhild. At Poitiers he became a close friend of Queen Radegund, writing poems in her honour, and enjoyed the patronage of Gregory of Tours. His eleven surviving books of poetry include panegyrics and epitaphs, and his hymns Pange lingua gloriosi proelium certaminis and Vexilla Regis prodeunt entered the Catholic liturgy. He became Bishop of Poitiers around 599–600 and died early in the 7th century.

entries.name: Hilary of Poitiers
entries.desc: Hilary of Poitiers was a 4th-century Bishop of Poitiers and a Doctor of the Church, called the Hammer of the Arians for his opposition to Arianism. Born at Poitiers to distinguished pagan parents, he turned from Neoplatonism to Nicene Christianity through study of the Scriptures. Banished to Phrygia after the synod of Béziers in 356, he spent nearly four years in exile, writing De synodis and De trinitate, the first successful expression in Latin of the Nicene theology worked out in Greek. Back in his diocese in 361, he opposed the homoion creed in Gaul and encouraged Martin, the future bishop of Tours, to found a monastery at Ligugé; according to Jerome he died in Poitiers in 367.

entries.name: Bonaventure
entries.desc: Bonaventure, born Giovanni di Fidanza at Civita di Bagnoregio in the Papal States, was an Italian Franciscan theologian and philosopher, Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor, cardinal and Bishop of Albano. He entered the Franciscan Order in 1243, studied at the University of Paris and was received there as master in 1257. As the order's seventh Minister General he defended it against its critics and steered it on a moderate and intellectual course, and he wrote a life of Francis of Assisi. His theology, set out in works such as The Mind's Road to God, sought to integrate faith and reason. He died suddenly at the Second Council of Lyon in 1274 and was canonised in 1482.

entries.name: Myles Coverdale
entries.desc: Myles Coverdale was an English reformer, Bible translator and preacher who in 1535 produced the first printed translation of the complete Bible into Early Modern English, completing the work of William Tyndale. A Cambridge-educated Augustinian friar, he left the order to preach reform and in 1528 fled to the Continent; knowing little Hebrew or Greek, he translated from Latin and German sources and from Tyndale. He oversaw the Great Bible of 1539, and his Psalms are still used in the 1662 Book of Common Prayer. Bishop of Exeter from 1551, he was ejected under Mary I in 1553 and went into exile again, contributing to the Geneva Bible, before returning to London in 1559.

entries.name: Kazi Nazrul Islam
entries.desc: Kazi Nazrul Islam was a Bengali poet, writer, journalist and musician, later honoured as the national poet of Bangladesh. Born in Churulia in the Bengal Presidency, he worked as a muezzin and with a travelling folk theatre group as a young man, and served in the British Indian Army from 1917. In Calcutta his poem Bidrohi (The Rebel, 1922) earned him the name Rebel Poet, and his bi-weekly Dhumketu and other writings against British rule led to repeated imprisonment. He wrote and composed nearly 4,000 songs, known as Nazrul Gīti, brought the ghazal into Bengali and opposed religious, caste and gender bigotry. Ill from 1942, he was brought to Dhaka in 1972 and died there in 1976.

entries.name: Ram Prasad Bismil
entries.desc: Ram Prasad Bismil was an Indian poet, writer and revolutionary against British rule who wrote in Urdu and Hindi under the pen names Ram, Agyat and Bismil. Born in Shahjahanpur district in the North-Western Provinces, he formed the revolutionary group Matrivedi and took part in the Mainpuri Conspiracy of 1918, then lived in hiding. A founding member of the Hindustan Republican Association, he planned the Kakori train robbery of 9 August 1925, in which ten revolutionaries stopped a train near Lucknow to seize the government treasury it carried. After 18 months of legal process he was sentenced to death and hanged at Gorakhpur Jail on 19 December 1927.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Krantmlverma at Hindi Wikipedia .

entries.name: Lata Mangeshkar
entries.desc: Lata Mangeshkar, born Hemalata in Indore, was an Indian playback singer whose career in film music spanned eight decades and who recorded songs in more than thirty-six Indian languages. The daughter of the classical singer and actor Deenanath Mangeshkar, she began working after his death in 1942 and moved to Mumbai in 1945; her song Aayega Aanewaala in the film Mahal (1949) helped win recognition for playback singers, until then uncredited. In 1963, during the Sino-Indian War, she sang Aye Mere Watan Ke Logo before Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. She received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1989 and the Bharat Ratna in 2001, and died in 2022 after treatment for COVID-19 and pneumonia.

entries.name: M. S. Subbulakshmi
entries.desc: M. S. Subbulakshmi was an Indian Carnatic singer from Madurai and in 1998 the first musician to be awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour. The daughter of the veena player Shanmukhavadivu Ammal, of the devadasi community, she first performed in public in 1927 at the Rockfort Temple in Tiruchirappalli and sang at the Madras Music Academy in 1929, at 13. Her title role in the Tamil film Meera (1945) brought her national prominence. Her concerts abroad included the United Nations General Assembly in 1966, and in 1974 she received the Ramon Magsaysay Award. She stopped performing after her husband Kalki Sadasivam died in 1997, and died in Chennai in 2004.

entries.name: Umm Kulthum
entries.desc: Umm Kulthum, born Fatima Ibrahim es-Sayyid el-Beltagi in the village of Tamay al-Zahayra in Egypt's Dakahlia Governorate, was an Egyptian singer and film actress known by the honorific Kawkab el-Sharq, Planet of the East. The daughter of a rural imam, she sang religious hymns in her father's ensemble as a child, dressed as a boy, and moved to Cairo in the early 1920s, working with the poet Ahmed Rami and composers such as Mohammed Abdel Wahab. From 1934 she gave a broadcast concert on the first Thursday of every month for forty years, and after the 1967 war she sang abroad to raise funds for the Egyptian war effort. Her funeral in Cairo in 1975 drew a crowd of over 4 million people.

entries.name: Sayed Darwish
entries.desc: Sayed Darwish was an Egyptian singer and composer from Alexandria, considered the father of Egyptian popular music, who set to music Bilady, Bilady, Bilady, the song that became Egypt's national anthem. Trained in Quran recitation and for two years at al-Azhar, he worked as a bricklayer and café singer before turning in 1918 to musical theatre in Cairo, composing operettas for Naguib el-Rihani's company, for Munira al-Mahdiyya and others. His songs of the 1919 revolt against British occupation, mostly with words by the poet Badi' Khayri, voiced national feeling, and light melodies such as Salma ya Salama passed into Egyptian folklore. He died in September 1923, aged thirty-one.

entries.name: Ahmed Shawqi
entries.desc: Ahmed Shawqi was an Egyptian poet and linguist, born in Cairo in 1868, whom his peers crowned Amir al-Shu'ara, the Prince of Poets, in 1927. After studying law at Montpellier and Paris, he served at the court of the Khedive Abbas II, and his early verse praised the Khedive. Exiled to Andalusia in Spain in 1914 for his opposition to the British, he wrote patriotic poems on Egypt and the Arab world until his return in 1920. He was the first in modern Arabic literature to write poetic plays, among them Majnun Laila and The Death of Cleopatra, and scholars count him the leading poet of Arabic Neoclassicism. He died in 1932.

entries.name: Tian Han
entries.desc: Tian Han was a Chinese playwright, translator and poet and a leader of left-wing drama, music and film, counted by drama historians among the three founders of Chinese spoken drama. After studying in Japan from 1916 to 1922, he founded the Southern Society in Shanghai, joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1932 and wrote plays on workers' struggles and resistance to Japan. In 1934 he wrote the lyrics of March of the Volunteers, set to music by Nie Er, which was adopted as the provisional national anthem of the People's Republic of China in 1949. Denounced and jailed in the Cultural Revolution, he died in 1968; he was rehabilitated in 1979, and his words were restored to the anthem in 1982.

entries.name: Enoch Sontonga
entries.desc: Enoch Sontonga was a Xhosa composer and teacher, born in Uitenhage in the Eastern Cape Colony, who wrote the hymn Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika (God Bless Africa). Trained at the Lovedale Institution, he taught and led the choir at a Methodist mission school in Nancefield, near Johannesburg, and composed the first verse and chorus in 1897 as a school anthem; the poet Samuel Mqhayi later added seven verses. The African National Congress adopted it as its closing anthem in 1925, Tanganyika and Zambia took versions of it as national anthems, and since 1994 it has formed the first half of South Africa's anthem. Sontonga died in 1905, and his grave was declared a national monument in 1996.

entries.name: Solomon Linda
entries.desc: Solomon Linda was a South African singer and composer from Natal whose song Mbube, improvised in a Johannesburg recording studio in 1939 with his group the Evening Birds, reshaped the isicathamiya style of choral singing. A migrant worker in Johannesburg, he introduced a falsetto lead voice over several bass singers. Mbube reportedly sold more than 100,000 copies in South Africa, but Linda had sold his rights to Eric Gallo for ten shillings. The Weavers recorded it as Wimoweh in 1951 and the Tokens as The Lion Sleeps Tonight in 1961, neither crediting him. He died poor in 1962; after his family sued Disney in 2004, a settlement gave them royalties and him a cowriting credit.

entries.name: Feodor Chaliapin
entries.desc: Feodor Chaliapin was a Russian bass singer, born into a peasant family in Kazan in 1873, who is often credited with establishing the tradition of naturalistic acting in opera. After success as Mephistopheles at the Mamontov Private Opera, he sang at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre from 1899 to 1914, and the title role of Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov became his signature part. From 1901 he sang abroad, at La Scala and later the Metropolitan Opera, and his advocacy made Russian operas such as Khovanshchina and Prince Igor well known in the West. He remained outside Russia after 1921, settled in Paris and died there in 1938; his remains were moved to Moscow in 1984.

entries.name: Arturo Toscanini
entries.desc: Arturo Toscanini was an Italian conductor, born in Parma in 1867, who began as a cellist and first conducted in Rio de Janeiro in 1886, leading Aida from memory at the age of 19. He conducted the world premieres of Leoncavallo's Pagliacci and Puccini's La bohème, was principal conductor and later music director of La Scala, and led the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. An opponent of Mussolini, he refused to conduct the Fascist anthem Giovinezza and was beaten by Blackshirts in Bologna in 1931. From 1937 to 1954 he was the first music director of the NBC Symphony Orchestra, whose broadcasts and recordings reached a mass audience. He died in New York in 1957.

entries.name: Marian Anderson
entries.desc: Marian Anderson was an American contralto from Philadelphia who sang music from opera to spirituals with leading orchestras in the United States and Europe between 1925 and 1965. In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let her sing to an integrated audience in Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C.; with the help of Eleanor and Franklin D. Roosevelt she sang instead on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, before more than 75,000 people. In 1955 she became the first Black American singer to perform at the Metropolitan Opera. She later served as a delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Committee, sang at the March on Washington in 1963 and died in 1993.

entries.name: Mahalia Jackson
entries.desc: Mahalia Jackson was an American gospel singer, born in poverty in New Orleans in 1911, the granddaughter of enslaved people, who was central to the development and spread of gospel blues in Black churches. In Chicago she sang with the Johnson Singers and drew on Thomas Dorsey and Bessie Smith; her 1947 recording Move On Up a Little Higher sold two million copies, a first for gospel music. She became the first gospel recording artist to tour Europe, turned down offers to record secular music, and is credited with influencing rhythm and blues, soul and rock and roll singing. A supporter of Martin Luther King Jr., she sang at the March on Washington in 1963. She died in 1972.

entries.name: Francis James Child
entries.desc: Francis James Child was an American scholar and folklorist at Harvard University, known for The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, the collection now called the Child Ballads. He became Boylston Professor of Rhetoric and Oratory in 1851, and in 1876 Harvard made him its first professor of English to keep him from Johns Hopkins. Using the methods of comparative philology and corresponding with the Danish scholar Svend Grundtvig, he gathered some 305 ballads with their variants, published in parts from 1882 to 1898, the last after his death in 1896. His studies also shaped how Chaucer's grammar and pronunciation are understood, and in 1888 he founded the American Folklore Society.

entries.name: Allan Ramsay
entries.desc: Allan Ramsay was a Scottish poet, playwright, publisher and librarian of early Enlightenment Edinburgh, born at Leadhills in Lanarkshire, who worked as a wig-maker before turning bookseller around 1718. His collections The Tea-Table Miscellany (1723–37), of Scots and English songs, and The Ever Green (1724), of Scots poems written before 1600, revived interest in vernacular literature. His pastoral drama The Gentle Shepherd (1725) went through several editions, and he is credited with creating the first circulating library in Britain in 1726. He is seen as the link between the makars of the 15th and 16th centuries and the later poets Robert Fergusson and Robert Burns. He died in 1758.

entries.name: Louis Armstrong
entries.desc: Louis Armstrong was an American jazz trumpeter, cornetist and singer from New Orleans, among the most influential figures in jazz, who shifted the music's focus from collective improvisation to solo performance. Raised in poverty, he followed his mentor King Oliver to Chicago in 1922, and his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings from 1925 showcased his solos. He was one of the first African-American entertainers to reach wide white and international audiences, toured Africa, Europe and Asia for the US State Department, and spoke out publicly during the Little Rock school desegregation crisis of 1957. His recording of Hello, Dolly! reached No. 1 in 1964. He died in Queens, New York, in 1971.

entries.name: Leonard Bernstein
entries.desc: Leonard Bernstein was an American conductor, composer, pianist and music educator, born in Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1918 to Jewish immigrant parents, and the first American-born conductor to win international acclaim. His unrehearsed debut with the New York Philharmonic in 1943, broadcast nationwide, made him famous, and he was its music director from 1957, jointly at first, until 1969. He composed the musical West Side Story (1957), On the Town, Candide, the Chichester Psalms and the score of On the Waterfront, and he was central to the modern revival of Gustav Mahler's music. His Young People's Concerts brought classical music to television audiences. He died in New York in 1990.

entries.name: Mercedes Sosa
entries.desc: Mercedes Sosa was an Argentine singer from San Miguel de Tucumán, rooted in Argentine folk music, who became a leading voice of the nuevo cancionero movement and was called the voice of the voiceless. After a performance at the Cosquín folklore festival in 1965 brought her national attention, she recorded songs by many Latin American writers, among them Violeta Parra's Gracias a la vida. Under the military junta of Jorge Videla she received death threats, was arrested on stage at La Plata in 1979 along with her audience and was barred from performing, and she went into exile in Paris and Madrid. She returned to Argentina in 1982 and toured widely until her death in 2009.

entries.name: Teresa Teng
entries.desc: Teresa Teng was a Taiwanese singer, born in Yunlin County in 1953 to parents from the mainland, who is credited as a pioneer of modern Chinese popular music. She recorded more than 1,700 songs in Mandarin, Hokkien, Cantonese, Japanese and other languages, and built a second career in Japan from 1974. From the late 1970s her songs, among them The Moon Represents My Heart, spread through mainland China on cassettes; banned there for some years in the early 1980s as bourgeois, they circulated on the black market until the restrictions ended. She never performed on the mainland, supported the Tiananmen student protests of 1989, and died in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in 1995.

entries.name: Revolutions of 1848
entries.desc: The revolutions of 1848, also called the springtime of the peoples, were a wave of uprisings across Europe between January 1848 and October 1849, the most widespread in European history. Beginning in Sicily in January and spreading after the February Revolution in Paris overthrew the July Monarchy, they reached Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Buda and Pest and more than fifty countries. Coalitions of workers and middle-class reformers sought constitutions, nation states, a free press and economic rights, after a food crisis from 1845 to 1847. Most were soon suppressed, with tens of thousands killed, but serfdom was abolished in Austria and Hungary and absolute monarchy ended in Denmark.

entries.name: Oxford Movement
entries.desc: The Oxford Movement was a high-church movement within the Church of England, begun in the 1830s by clergy mostly associated with the University of Oxford, which developed into Anglo-Catholicism. Prompted by the Irish Church Temporalities Bill and John Keble's Assize Sermon of 1833, its leaders, among them Keble, John Henry Newman and Edward Bouverie Pusey, published the Tracts for the Times, arguing that the church's authority came from God through apostolic succession rather than from the state. Newman's reception into the Catholic Church in 1845 shook the movement, yet it led to Anglican religious orders, a more central place for the Eucharist and the wider use of vestments.

entries.name: Division of Korea
entries.desc: The division of Korea began at the end of the Second World War in 1945, when the peninsula, annexed by Japan in 1910, was split at the 38th parallel into a Soviet occupation zone in the north and a US zone in the south. Two American officers chose the line on 10 August 1945 using a National Geographic map, placing Seoul in the American zone, and a four-power trusteeship agreed in Moscow that December was never carried out. In 1948 the Republic of Korea and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea were founded, each claiming the whole peninsula. North Korea's invasion in 1950 began the Korean War, and the 1953 armistice left Korea divided along the Demilitarized Zone, as it remains.

A caravel was a small, highly manoeuvrable sailing ship, often with lateen sails that allowed it to sail close to the wind. It developed from the fishing craft of Galicia, Portugal and Atlantic Andalusia, where the word is first recorded in Portuguese in 1255, and in the fifteenth century the Portuguese made it the ship of their voyages of exploration along the African coast.

Colonial powers used it heavily in the Scramble for Africa, and British forces used it in the conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate. Its destructive power has often been embellished by popular myth: modern accounts find it effective in pitched battles, as at Omdurman, but owing much of its significance to its psychological impact.

In the nineteenth century steam warships carried Western power to East Asia: a British fleet that included the iron steamer Nemesis overcame the Qing Empire's coastal defences in the First Opium War of 1839–1842, and in 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry's squadron, which included steam-powered warships, entered Edo Bay and demanded that the Tokugawa Shogunate open Japan's ports.

Griots are hereditary oral historians, praise-singers and musicians of West Africa who preserve genealogies and historical traditions. They held a recognised place in the social structure of the region's states. In the Jolof Empire they formed part of the caste-based social order and maintained the memory of rulers and lineages.

Griots are the hereditary oral historians, praise singers, storytellers and musicians of West Africa, who preserve genealogies and historical traditions; among the Mande peoples they are the jeli or jali. Historically an endogamous caste, they served higher-ranking families of warrior kings or emperors, advising them and mediating in disputes, yet were held apart: in the worst case they were buried in trees, not the ground, to avoid polluting the earth. In the Jolof Empire they were part of the caste-based social order. The Epic of Sundiata names Balla Fasséké as the griot given to Sundiata Keita as adviser, the founder of the Kouyaté line of griots, which still exists.

Sheikh ul-Islam was the title of the chief religious authority in the Ottoman Empire, who headed the learned hierarchy of Islamic scholars. The holder issued legal opinions (fatwas) on matters of law and state policy. Accounts of the Ottoman Empire treat the office as an important part of Ottoman governance, linking the state to Sunni religious legitimacy.

Sheikh ul-Islam, or Shaykh al-Islam ('elder of Islam'), was an honorific title for outstanding scholars of the Islamic sciences, which first appeared in Khurasan in the 10th century. In Syria and Egypt it was an informal title for jurists whose fatwas were especially influential, while under the Ilkhans, the Delhi Sultanate and the Timurids rulers conferred it on high-ranking ulama. In the Ottoman Empire it came to designate the chief mufti, head of a hierarchy of state-appointed ulama, who issued fatwas, advised the sultan, appointed judges and confirmed new sultans. The office was abolished with the Caliphate in 1924 and replaced by the Presidency of Religious Affairs.
mani

Mani was a Persian prophet of the third century CE and founder of Manichaeism. According to the Aksumite Empire's profile, he described Aksum as one of the four great powers of the world, alongside Rome, Persia and China. His statement is often cited as evidence of Aksum's international standing.

Mani was a prophet born in 216 in Mesopotamia, near the Persian capital Ctesiphon, who from about 240 preached the religion later called Manichaeism. He taught that the world is a mixture of light and darkness and that souls, sparks of light, can be freed through knowledge and discipline, and he presented himself as the last in a line of prophets after the Buddha, Zoroaster and Jesus. He died in prison under the Sasanian king Bahram I, around 274 to 277, and his faith spread from Roman North Africa to China. He described Aksum as one of the four great powers of the world, alongside Rome, Persia and China.
